Option 1: Immediately stop the entire factory and recalibrate every machine in the building.
Option 2: Investigate the process for "assignable causes" or special cause variation.
Option 3: Change the control limits to include the new point so the chart looks "normal."
Option 4: Ignore the point, as a single outlier is statistically irrelevant in a large sample.

Question Text: In the context of "Maintenance Engineering," what is the "Mean Time To Repair" (MTTR) used to measure regarding the equipment performance?
Option 1: The reliability of the machine, indicating how long it runs before it fails.
Option 2: The maintainability of the machine, indicating how quickly it can be fixed after failure.
Option 3: The total energy consumption of the machine during a standard eight-hour shift.
Option 4: The time it takes for a machine to produce one finished unit of the product.

Question Text: A plant manager wants to use "Linear Programming" to maximize profit. What does the "Objective Function" represent in this mathematical model?
Option 1: The physical constraints of the machines, such as maximum hours available.
Option 2: The mathematical expression that defines the goal, such as total profit or total cost.
Option 3: The list of all raw materials required to produce one unit of each product type.
Option 4: The graphical representation of the feasible region where all constraints are met.

Question Text: Under the "5S" framework, the step "Seiton" (Set in Order) focuses on which of the following activities on the production shop floor?
Option 1: Removing all unnecessary tools and materials from the immediate work area.
Option 2: Arranging necessary items so they are easy to find, use, and put away.
Option 3: Cleaning the workspace and equipment to identify potential leaks or issues.
Option 4: Standardizing the first three steps to ensure they are performed consistently.

Question Text: A "Fixed-Position Layout" is most likely to be used in which of the following industrial scenarios?
Option 1: The assembly of high-volume consumer electronics like smartphones.
Option 2: The construction of a massive naval ship or a large commercial aircraft.
Option 3: A bakery producing thousands of loaves of bread every single day.
Option 4: A plastic injection molding facility with dozens of identical machines.

Question Text: In "Supply Chain Management," the "Bullwhip Effect" refers to which phenomenon regarding demand signals moving upstream?
Option 1: The smoothing out of demand variability as it moves from the retailer to the factory.
Option 2: The amplification of demand variability as it moves from the retailer to the supplier.
Option 3: The reduction in shipping costs when orders are bundled into larger shipments.
Option 4: The increase in customer satisfaction when products are always available on the shelf.

Question Text: A "Simultaneous Engineering" (or Concurrent Engineering) approach in product development aims to achieve what specific outcome?
Option 1: To perform design and manufacturing planning activities in parallel to reduce time-to-market.
Option 2: To ensure that design engineers work in a separate building from the manufacturing team.
Option 3: To finish the entire design phase before ever talking to the production department.
Option 4: To hire multiple engineering firms to design the same product and pick the best one.

Question Text: Which of the following is a "Value-Added" activity in a manufacturing process according to Lean principles?
Option 1: Moving a part from the warehouse to the assembly line using a forklift.
Option 2: Inspecting a finished part to ensure that it meets the quality specifications.
Option 3: Machining a raw casting into the final shape requested by the customer.
Option 4: Storing finished goods in a climate-controlled room while waiting for an order.

Question Text: In "Operations Management," what is the primary purpose of an "Aggregate Plan"?
Option 1: To determine the exact sequence of jobs on a specific machine for the next shift.
Option 2: To develop a mid-term production strategy that balances capacity and demand.
Option 3: To track the real-time location of every pallet in the warehouse using RFID.
Option 4: To calculate the precise chemical composition of the raw materials used.

Question Text: A "Pareto Chart" used in Quality Engineering is based on the 80/20 rule. What does this rule imply about process defects?
Option 1: 80% of the defects are caused by 20% of the total number of different problem types.
Option 2: 80% of the workers are responsible for 20% of the total production volume.
Option 3: 80% of the machines should be running while 20% are undergoing maintenance.
Option 4: 80% of the profit comes from products that have a 20% defect rate or higher.

Question Text: "Ergonomics" in a workstation design specifically looks at the "Neutral Posture." Why is this posture important for an industrial worker?
Option 1: It allows the worker to exert the maximum possible force with their muscles.
Option 2: It minimizes the stress on joints and muscles, reducing the risk of injury.
Option 3: It makes the worker look more professional when customers visit the plant.
Option 4: It ensures that the worker stays awake and alert during a repetitive night shift.

Question Text: A "Flexible Manufacturing System" (FMS) is characterized by its ability to do what?
Option 1: Produce one single type of product at extremely high speeds with no variations.
Option 2: Adjust quickly to produce different product types and change production volumes.
Option 3: Operate without any electricity by using manual levers and steam power.
Option 4: Function only when the factory temperature is kept at exactly 22 degrees Celsius.

Question Text: In "Maintenance Engineering," "Predictive Maintenance" differs from "Preventive Maintenance" because it:
Option 1: Relies on scheduled intervals (like every 3 months) to change parts or oil.
Option 2: Uses sensor data (like vibration or heat) to intervene only when failure is imminent.
Option 3: Only involves fixing a machine after it has completely broken down and stopped.
Option 4: Focuses on buying new machines every year to avoid any potential repair work.

Question Text: Which of the following describes "Mura" in the context of the Three M's of Lean (Muda, Mura, Muri)?
Option 1: The waste associated with unnecessary motion or transportation of goods.
Option 2: The unevenness or fluctuations in work demand or production flow.
Option 3: The overburdening of equipment or people beyond their natural limits.
Option 4: The process of continuous improvement through small, incremental changes.

Question Text: An "Assembly Line Balancing" problem aims to distribute tasks among workstations so that:
Option 1: Each workstation has a different amount of work to keep things interesting for workers.
Option 2: The "Idle Time" at each workstation is minimized and the flow is synchronized.
Option 3: The most skilled worker does all the tasks while others watch and learn.
Option 4: The fastest workstation is placed at the very beginning of the entire line.

Question Text: In "Operations Research," the "Critical Path" in a PERT/CPM network represents:
Option 1: The shortest sequence of tasks that must be completed to finish the project.
Option 2: The longest sequence of dependent tasks that determines the project duration.
Option 3: The path that contains only the tasks with the highest financial costs.
Option 4: The sequence of tasks that can be delayed without affecting the project end date.

Question Text: A "Fishbone Diagram" (Ishikawa) is most useful during a brainstorming session to:
Option 1: Categorize potential causes of a specific problem into logical groupings.
Option 2: Calculate the statistical probability that a certain defect will occur in a batch.
Option 3: Schedule the delivery of parts from various suppliers across the globe.
Option 4: Compare the features of your product with those of your main competitors.

Question Text: "Kaizen" is a philosophy that encourages which type of behavior in a production environment?
Option 1: Making large, expensive capital investments to completely automate the plant.
Option 2: Encouraging every employee to make small, daily improvements to their work.
Option 3: Hiring external consultants to rewrite the entire company policy every five years.
Option 4: Only allowing the senior management to suggest changes to the production flow.

Question Text: A "Jidoka" enabled machine in an automated line will do what if it detects a defect?
Option 1: Automatically stop the process to prevent the defect from moving downstream.
Option 2: Ignore the defect but highlight it with a red marker for later inspection.
Option 3: Speed up the process to make up for the lost time caused by the bad part.
Option 4: Sound a loud alarm but continue producing to maintain the daily target.

Question Text: What is the primary purpose of "Safety Stock" in an inventory management system?
Option 1: To increase the total value of assets held by the company on the balance sheet.
Option 2: To protect against uncertainties in demand and lead time from the suppliers.
Option 3: To ensure the warehouse looks full when investors come for a facility tour.
Option 4: To take advantage of bulk-buy discounts even if the items are not needed.

Question Text: In "Work Study," a "Therblig" refers to which of the following concepts?
Option 1: A unit of measurement for the electrical consumption of an industrial motor.
Option 2: One of the 18 fundamental motions required for a worker to perform a task.
Option 3: A specific type of cutting tool used in high-speed lathe operations.
Option 4: The weight capacity of a standard industrial pallet used in international shipping.

Question Text: A "Cellular Layout" often uses a "U-shaped" line. What is a key ergonomic and operational advantage of this shape?
Option 1: It allows one operator to oversee multiple machines with minimal walking.
Option 2: It makes it easier to install long, straight overhead crane systems.
Option 3: It prevents workers from talking to each other, increasing their focus on tasks.
Option 4: It requires more floor space, which makes the factory look larger and busier.

Question Text: When applying "Six Sigma," what does the "Z-score" (Sigma level) represent?
Option 1: The number of standard deviations the process limit is from the process mean.
Option 2: The total number of employees trained in Green Belt and Black Belt levels.
Option 3: The ratio of the cost of quality to the total revenue generated by the line.
Option 4: The speed at which a product moves through the entire value stream.

Question Text: An "Industrial Robot" is typically categorized by its "Degrees of Freedom." What does this term refer to?
Option 1: The number of independent movements (joints) the robot arm can perform.
Option 2: The number of hours the robot can operate without needing a human to restart it.
Option 3: The ability of the robot to choose which tasks it wants to perform each day.
Option 4: The price of the robot relative to the average annual salary of a manual worker.

Question Text: A "Cross-Docking" strategy in Supply Chain Management involves:
Option 1: Storing goods in a warehouse for at least 30 days to ensure quality control.
Option 2: Moving products directly from incoming trucks to outgoing trucks with little storage.
Option 3: Shipping products across the ocean using specialized container ships and ports.
Option 4: Sorting products by color and size before putting them into long-term storage.

Question Text: In "Facility Planning," "CRAFT" (Computerized Relative Allocation of Facilities Technique) is used for:
Option 1: Improving an existing functional layout by swapping departments to minimize handling costs.
Option 2: Designing a brand-new factory from scratch using 3D modeling and virtual reality.
Option 3: Calculating the maximum load-bearing capacity of the concrete floors in a plant.
Option 4: Managing the payroll and attendance records of the facility maintenance staff.

Question Text: What is the "Overall Equipment Effectiveness" (OEE) if a machine has 100% Availability, 100% Performance, but only 80% Quality?
Option 1: The OEE would be 100% because the machine never stopped and ran at full speed.
Option 2: The OEE would be 80% because it is the product of Availability, Performance, and Quality.
Option 3: The OEE would be 90% which is the average of the three different factors.
Option 4: The OEE cannot be calculated without knowing the total number of parts produced.

Question Text: A "Single-Level Bill of Materials" (BOM) for a bicycle would show:
Option 1: Every single nut, bolt, and washer required to build the entire finished bike.
Option 2: Only the major assemblies like the frame, wheels, and handlebar set.
Option 3: The history of all price changes for the bicycle over the last five years.
Option 4: The names of the workers who are qualified to assemble the bicycle.

Question Text: In "Project Management," what is "Crashing" a project?
Option 1: Terminating a project because it has exceeded the budget and the deadline.
Option 2: Adding resources to critical path activities to shorten the total project duration.
Option 3: Moving the project deadline further into the future to reduce worker stress.
Option 4: Using a computer simulation to predict when the project might fail in the future.

Question Text: A "Heijunka" board is used in Lean manufacturing to achieve "Level Loading." This means:
Option 1: Producing the exact same product every day for an entire year to maximize efficiency.
Option 2: Smoothing out production volume and mix over time to reduce "Mura."
Option 3: Ensuring that every pallet weighs exactly the same before being loaded on a truck.
Option 4: Distributing the physical weight of machines evenly across the factory floor.

Question Text: In "Quality Engineering," the "Taguchi Method" emphasizes which of the following?
Option 1: Reducing loss to society by minimizing variation around a specific target value.
Option 2: Inspecting every single part at the end of the line to catch all defects.
Option 3: Increasing the tolerance limits so that more parts are accepted by the system.
Option 4: Using the cheapest possible materials to maximize the profit margin per unit.

Question Text: A "SCADA" (Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition) system is primarily used in industrial automation to:
Option 1: Write the low-level code that controls a single motor or pneumatic valve.
Option 2: Monitor and control large-scale processes from a centralized location.
Option 3: Design the physical mechanical components of a robot using CAD software.
Option 4: Calculate the annual tax returns for a manufacturing corporation.

Question Text: A "Work Sampling" study is preferred over a "Continuous Time Study" when:
Option 1: You need a highly precise measurement of a very short, repetitive task.
Option 2: You want to estimate the percentage of time a worker spends on various activities.
Option 3: You are measuring the speed of a fully automated robotic assembly arm.
Option 4: The worker being observed is new and does not yet know the standard method.

Question Text: If a company uses a "Make-to-Stock" strategy, their primary goal in production planning is to:
Option 1: Wait for a customer order before ordering any raw materials from suppliers.
Option 2: Maintain an inventory of finished goods to fulfill customer orders immediately.
Option 3: Only produce items that are custom-designed for a specific individual client.
Option 4: Reduce the warehouse size to zero by shipping parts as soon as they are made.

Question Text: In "Operations Research," the "Monte Carlo Simulation" is used to:
Option 1: Find a single perfect answer to a problem with no variable factors.
Option 2: Model the probability of different outcomes in a process with random variables.
Option 3: Determine the fastest route for a delivery truck using a GPS system.
Option 4: Organize a company's social events using a random selection process.

Question Text: "Group Technology" (GT) in manufacturing is based on the principle of:
Option 1: Grouping workers into teams based on their hobbies and personal interests.
Option 2: Identifying and grouping parts with similar shapes or processing requirements.
Option 3: Moving all machines into a single large room to save on heating and cooling.
Option 4: Having one manager supervise at least fifty workers to reduce overhead costs.

Question Text: Which of the following is a "Hard Automation" system?
Option 1: A CNC machining center that can be programmed to make many different parts.
Option 2: A specialized transfer line designed to produce only one specific engine block.
Option 3: A collaborative robot (cobot) that works alongside humans on various tasks.
Option 4: A manual assembly line where workers use power tools to build furniture.

Question Text: A "Kanban" system is often described as a "Visual Factory" tool because:
Option 1: It uses expensive cameras and AI to monitor the movements of the workers.
Option 2: It uses physical signals (cards, bins, lights) to communicate production needs.
Option 3: It requires the factory walls to be painted in specific bright colors for safety.
Option 4: It involves showing the workers movies of how the product should be built.

Question Text: In "Maintenance Engineering," "Reliability Centered Maintenance" (RCM) focuses on:
Option 1: Preserving the function of the system rather than just making the equipment run.
Option 2: Replacing every machine as soon as the manufacturer's warranty expires.
Option 3: Reducing the number of maintenance staff to save on the monthly payroll.
Option 4: Only fixing things when they break to ensure the maximum use of every part.

Question Text: A "P-chart" (Attribute Control Chart) is used to monitor:
Option 1: The average weight of a sample of cereal boxes over a period of time.
Option 2: The fraction or proportion of defective items in a series of samples.
Option 3: The variation in the diameter of a precision-ground steel shaft.
Option 4: The total number of hours a machine was down during the previous week.

Question Text: In "Ergonomics," the "NIOSH Lifting Equation" is used to calculate:
Option 1: The maximum speed at which a worker can run while carrying a heavy box.
Option 2: The Recommended Weight Limit (RWL) for a manual lifting task to prevent injury.
Option 3: The number of calories a worker burns during a standard eight-hour shift.
Option 4: The amount of weight a forklift can carry before it tips over on a ramp.

Question Text: A "Service Level" of 95% in inventory management means:
Option 1: 95% of the products produced are high quality and meet all specifications.
Option 2: There is a 95% probability that demand will be met during the lead time.
Option 3: 95% of the employees are satisfied with their current working conditions.
Option 4: The machines are running 95% of the time they are scheduled to operate.

Question Text: "Just-in-Time" (JIT) manufacturing requires which of the following to be successful?
Option 1: High levels of inventory to cover up any problems in the production process.
Option 2: Extremely reliable processes and high-quality parts from all suppliers.
Option 3: A large team of inspectors to check every part at every single workstation.
Option 4: Long lead times and large batch sizes to maximize the shipping efficiency.

Question Text: In "Operations Research," a "Dual Problem" in Linear Programming provides information about:
Option 1: The cost of hiring a second manager to supervise the production process.
Option 2: The "Shadow Price" or the value of increasing a constraint by one unit.
Option 3: A backup plan in case the first optimal solution cannot be implemented.
Option 4: The probability that the demand will double in the next fiscal year.

Question Text: "Vertical Integration" in a supply chain occurs when a company:
Option 1: Moves its headquarters to a taller building to house all its employees.
Option 2: Acquires its suppliers (backward) or its distributors (forward).
Option 3: Hires more managers to increase the number of layers in the hierarchy.
Option 4: Increases the speed of its elevators to move materials between floors.

Question Text: In "Quality Engineering," what is the difference between "Quality of Design" and "Quality of Conformance"?
Option 1: Design is how well it's planned; Conformance is how well it matches the plan.
Option 2: Design is about the price; Conformance is about the speed of the production.
Option 3: Design is done by engineers; Conformance is done by the marketing team.
Option 4: There is no difference; they both refer to the number of defects in a batch.

Question Text: A "DFA" (Design for Assembly) analysis aims to:
Option 1: Make the product look more attractive to the end customer in the store.
Option 2: Reduce the number of parts and simplify the assembly process steps.
Option 3: Increase the complexity of the product to prevent competitors from copying it.
Option 4: Ensure that the product can be disassembled easily for repair and recycling.

Question Text: "Total Quality Management" (TQM) is different from traditional "Quality Control" because:
Option 1: TQM focuses on inspection at the end, while QC focuses on the whole process.
Option 2: TQM involves every employee in improvement, while QC is a separate department.
Option 3: TQM is only for service industries, while QC is only for manufacturing plants.
Option 4: TQM requires more expensive machinery, while QC relies on manual labor.

Question Text: In "Industrial Automation," an "Actuator" is a device that:
Option 1: Senses the environment and sends data to a computer for processing.
Option 2: Converts a control signal (like electricity or air) into physical motion.
Option 3: Stores the logic program and decides when to turn the machines on.
Option 4: Protects the workers from getting their hands caught in moving parts.

Question Text: A "Product-Process Matrix" suggests that for "Project" type processes (like building a house), the volume is:
Option 1: Very high, and the product is highly standardized and rarely changes.
Option 2: Very low, and the product is highly customized and unique for each client.
Option 3: Moderate, and the product is made in batches of several hundred units.
Option 4: Continuous, like a refinery where the product flows through pipes 24/7.

Question Text: What is the main purpose of "Standard Work" in a Lean production environment?
Option 1: To provide a baseline for improvement and ensure consistency in the process.
Option 2: To ensure that every worker is paid the exact same salary regardless of skill.
Option 3: To make the job as boring as possible so that workers do not get distracted.
Option 4: To prevent workers from suggesting any changes to the way they do their work.

Question Text: In "Operations Research," the "Vogel’s Approximation Method" (VAM) is used to:
Option 1: Find a starting "Initial Feasible Solution" for a transportation problem.
Option 2: Determine the optimal number of servers in a bank's queuing system.
Option 3: Calculate the shortest path in a network of roads between two major cities.
Option 4: Predict the stock market trends based on historical manufacturing data.

Question Text: A "Systematic Layout Planning" (SLP) procedure uses an "Activity Relationship Chart." What does this chart show?
Option 1: The sequence of operations for a single product as it moves through the plant.
Option 2: The desired closeness between different departments based on various factors.
Option 3: The total cost of moving one ton of material between two specific machines.
Option 4: The electrical wiring diagram for the entire facility's automation system.

Question Text: In "Supply Chain Management," "Vendor Managed Inventory" (VMI) means:
Option 1: The buyer is responsible for going to the vendor's warehouse to pick up items.
Option 2: The vendor monitors the buyer's inventory and decides when to replenish it.
Option 3: The vendor and the buyer both own 50% of the inventory at all times.
Option 4: The government manages the inventory to ensure fair prices for all citizens.

Question Text: A "FMEA" (Failure Mode and Effects Analysis) assigns a "Risk Priority Number" (RPN) based on:
Option 1: Severity, Occurrence, and Detection of a potential failure mode.
Option 2: The cost of the machine, the age of the machine, and its total weight.
Option 3: The number of workers, the shift length, and the total production target.
Option 4: The height of the factory, the width of the aisles, and the number of exits.

Question Text: In "Work Study," the "Performance Rating" is applied to the "Observed Time" to calculate:
Option 1: The "Normal Time," which is the time a qualified worker takes at a normal pace.
Option 2: The "Standard Time," which includes all the allowances for personal needs.
Option 3: The "Down Time," which is the time the machine was not working during the study.
Option 4: The "Cycle Time," which is the total time from the start to the end of one unit.

Question Text: "Distributed Control Systems" (DCS) are most commonly found in which type of industry?
Option 1: Discrete manufacturing, like an assembly line for toys or small appliances.
Option 2: Process industries, like oil refineries, chemical plants, or power stations.
Option 3: Small-scale workshops where most of the work is done by hand tools.
Option 4: Retail environments where the focus is on point-of-sale transactions.

Question Text: A "Line of Balance" (LOB) technique is primarily used for scheduling:
Option 1: A single, unique project that will never be repeated by the company again.
Option 2: The production of a large number of identical items in a continuous flow.
Option 3: A small number of batches of items that are produced periodically.
Option 4: The maintenance schedule for the fleet of trucks used in the supply chain.

Question Text: In "Operations Management," the "Theory of Constraints" (TOC) suggests focusing on:
Option 1: Improving every single process in the factory at the same time to be efficient.
Option 2: Identifying and managing the most restrictive factor (bottleneck) in the system.
Option 3: Reducing the cost of every raw material by negotiating with all suppliers.
Option 4: Hiring more supervisors to ensure that every worker is working at 100% speed.

Question Text: What is the purpose of "Allowances" (Personal, Fatigue, Delay) in calculating Standard Time?
Option 1: To give workers extra money at the end of the month for working very hard.
Option 2: To account for legitimate non-productive time that occurs during a workday.
Option 3: To make the production target easier so that the manager looks successful.
Option 4: To penalize workers who take too many breaks during their eight-hour shift.

Question Text: "Six Sigma" uses the "DMAIC" methodology for existing processes. What is the equivalent for designing new processes?
Option 1: DMADV (Define, Measure, Analyze, Design, Verify).
Option 2: PDCA (Plan, Do, Check, Act).
Option 3: SMED (Single-Minute Exchange of Die).
Option 4: TPM (Total Productive Maintenance).

Question Text: An "AGV" (Automated Guided Vehicle) in a factory is typically used for:
Option 1: Performing high-precision welding on car bodies in an assembly line.
Option 2: Transporting materials between different locations without a human driver.
Option 3: Calculating the weekly payroll for the employees in the logistics department.
Option 4: Designing the 3D layout of the warehouse using specialized software.

Question Text: In "Maintenance Engineering," "Breakdown Maintenance" is acceptable when:
Option 1: The machine is the most expensive and critical piece of equipment in the plant.
Option 2: The cost of repair is low and the failure does not affect safety or production.
Option 3: The company has no money and cannot afford to buy any grease or oil.
Option 4: The operators are highly skilled and can fix any problem in under five minutes.

Question Text: A "Supply Chain" is considered "Agile" if it is designed to:
Option 1: Minimize every possible cost, even if it means long lead times for customers.
Option 2: Respond quickly to unpredictable changes in demand or market requirements.
Option 3: Use only one supplier for everything to simplify the communication process.
Option 4: Focus entirely on local markets and never export products to other countries.

Question Text: In "Quality Engineering," "Type I Error" (Producer's Risk) occurs when:
Option 1: A good lot is incorrectly rejected by the quality inspection process.
Option 2: A bad lot is incorrectly accepted by the quality inspection process.
Option 3: The inspector falls asleep and misses a defect on the assembly line.
Option 4: The machine produces a part that is much better than the specifications.

Question Text: "Work Measurement" is essential for a manufacturing organization primarily to:
Option 1: Determine how much they should charge the customer for each product.
Option 2: Establish time standards for planning, costing, and incentive schemes.
Option 3: Decide which workers should be promoted to management positions.
Option 4: Choose the best color for the uniforms worn by the production staff.

Question Text: In "Operations Research," "Sensitivity Analysis" in Linear Programming helps to:
Option 1: Determine how the optimal solution changes if the input parameters change.
Option 2: Measure the emotional state of the workers during a difficult production run.
Option 3: Calculate the exact temperature at which a chemical reaction will fail.
Option 4: Find the fastest way to shut down the factory in case of an emergency.

Question Text: A "Product Layout" (Flow Line) is often criticized for which of the following reasons?
Option 1: It is too difficult to manage because everyone is doing different tasks.
Option 2: It is highly inflexible; a breakdown in one machine can stop the whole line.
Option 3: It requires very high-skilled workers who can do every single job in the plant.
Option 4: It has very high material handling costs compared to a process layout.

Question Text: "Lean Manufacturing" identifies "Inventory" as a waste because:
Option 1: It takes up space and hides underlying problems in the production process.
Option 2: It is too difficult to count during the annual end-of-year financial audit.
Option 3: It makes the workers feel lazy because they know there are plenty of parts.
Option 4: It increases the taxes the company has to pay to the local government.

Question Text: In "Industrial Automation," what is the function of an "HMI" (Human Machine Interface)?
Option 1: To replace the human operator with a computer that makes all the decisions.
Option 2: To provide a graphical display for the operator to monitor and control a machine.
Option 3: To measure the heart rate of the worker to ensure they are not over-stressed.
Option 4: To translate the English instructions into the language used by the robot.

Question Text: "Enterprise Resource Planning" (ERP) systems are used in production to:
Option 1: Control the physical movements of a robot arm in a welding cell.
Option 2: Integrate all facets of an operation, including planning, manufacturing, and sales.
Option 3: Design new products using sophisticated three-dimensional modeling tools.
Option 4: Provide air conditioning and heating control for the corporate office building.

Question Text: In "Quality Engineering," the "Capability Index" (Cp) measures:
Option 1: The ability of a process to produce parts within the specified tolerance limits.
Option 2: The total number of years the quality manager has worked in the industry.
Option 3: The speed at which the inspection team can check a batch of one hundred parts.
Option 4: The ratio of the price of the product to the cost of the raw materials used.

Question Text: "Ergonomics" - The "Golden Zone" for manual assembly work refers to the area:
Option 1: Between the shoulders and the waist, where work is most comfortable.
Option 2: On the very top shelf of the warehouse where rare items are stored.
Option 3: Outside the factory gates where the workers go to have their lunch.
Option 4: Inside the manager's office where the temperature is always perfect.

Question Text: A "Balanced Scorecard" in operations management measures performance across:
Option 1: Financial, Customer, Internal Process, and Learning & Growth perspectives.
Option 2: Only the total amount of money the company made in the last three months.
Option 3: The weight of the products compared to the weight of the raw materials.
Option 4: The number of hours the CEO spends on the shop floor every single week.

Question Text: In "Maintenance Engineering," "Oiling and Greasing" a machine is a form of:
Option 1: Breakdown Maintenance, because you only do it when the machine squeaks.
Option 2: Preventive Maintenance, because it is done to prevent wear and tear.
Option 3: Predictive Maintenance, because you use your ears to predict a failure.
Option 4: Corrective Maintenance, because you are correcting a dry joint in the machine.

Question Text: "Mass Customization" is a strategy that attempts to:
Option 1: Produce high volumes of identical products to keep the unit cost very low.
Option 2: Provide custom-designed products at prices near those of mass-produced items.
Option 3: Hire thousands of workers to manually customize every item by hand.
Option 4: Convince customers that they don't really need customized products at all.

Question Text: In "Operations Research," the "Queuing Theory" helps a manager decide:
Option 1: Which workers should be fired during a company-wide downsizing event.
Option 2: The optimal balance between the cost of service and the cost of waiting.
Option 3: The best color for the chairs in the waiting room of a busy hospital.
Option 4: How many items to put in a box before shipping it to a far-away customer.

Question Text: "SMART" goals in Production Planning stand for:
Option 1: Simple, Manageable, Action-oriented, Robust, and Technical.
Option 2: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound.
Option 3: Small, Monthly, Annual, Recurring, and Targeted for the future.
Option 4: Strong, Meaningful, Adjusted, Reliable, and Tested by engineers.

Question Text: A "Job Shop" environment is most likely to have:
Option 1: A Product Layout with specialized machines for high-speed production.
Option 2: A Process Layout with general-purpose machines for high variety.
Option 3: A fixed-position layout where the product never moves from its spot.
Option 4: No machines at all, as everything is done by hand by master craftsmen.

Question Text: In "Supply Chain Management," "Third-Party Logistics" (3PL) involves:
Option 1: Hiring a relative to manage the company's internal delivery van fleet.
Option 2: Outsourcing some or all of the logistics operations to a specialized firm.
Option 3: Using three different shipping companies for every single order sent out.
Option 4: Building three separate warehouses in three different countries for safety.

Question Text: A "Control Plan" in Quality Engineering is used to:
Option 1: Describe the actions required at each phase of the process to ensure outputs are in control.
Option 2: Control the behavior of the employees to ensure they arrive at work on time.
Option 3: Plan the budget for the quality department for the next three to five years.
Option 4: Determine which suppliers should be allowed to bid on new material contracts.

Question Text: The concept of "Industry 4.0" is primarily focused on:
Option 1: The use of steam power and water wheels to mechanize the production flow.
Option 2: The integration of "Cyber-Physical Systems," Internet of Things (IoT), and Big Data.
Option 3: The move from manual labor to assembly lines using electricity and motors.
Option 4: The total elimination of all human workers from every factory in the world.

Question Text: You are managing a production line where a CNC machine has a 15% defect rate, but the manual assembly station downstream is starving for parts. Do you:
Option 1: Stop the CNC immediately to recalibrate, even if it halts the entire downstream flow for the shift.
Option 2: Run the CNC at a slower speed to see if precision improves while maintaining a minimum flow of parts.
Option 3: Implement a 100% inspection gate after the CNC to filter defects while the engineering team diagnoses the root cause.
Option 4: Increase the CNC speed to overproduce and compensate for the 15% loss to keep the assembly line busy.

Question Text: A warehouse operator reports that the most frequently picked items are stored on the top rack of a 5-meter shelf to "keep the floor clear." How do you respond?
Option 1: Praise the operator for keeping the floor clear and organized as per 5S "Sort" principles.
Option 2: Conduct a frequency analysis and move high-velocity items to the "Golden Zone" (waist-to-shoulder height).
Option 3: Purchase a faster forklift to ensure the high picking time from the top rack is mitigated.
Option 4: Instruct the operator to pick larger batches once a day to minimize the number of trips to the top rack.

Question Text: You find that a "Jidoka" (autonomation) sensor is frequently stopping the line due to minor dust interference. The operators are taping over the sensor to meet targets. What is your action?
Option 1: Reprimand the operators for safety violations and increase the production target to recover lost time.
Option 2: Permanentely disable the sensor since it is clearly too sensitive for a real-world factory environment.
Option 3: Relocate or shield the sensor and implement a 5-minute daily cleaning standard for that specific sensor.
Option 4: Replace the automated sensor with a manual inspection worker to ensure the line never stops unnecessarily.

Question Text: Your facility layout has high "cross-traffic" between forklifts and pedestrians near the canteen entrance. Budget for a total redesign is zero. What is the best immediate intervention?
Option 1: Issue whistles to all pedestrians and tell them to blow them loudly when crossing the forklift path.
Option 2: Install floor tape for dedicated walkways and convex mirrors at blind corners to improve visibility.
Option 3: Change the lunch breaks so that no one is allowed to walk while the forklifts are operating.
Option 4: Remove the forklifts and switch to manual hand-pallets to eliminate the risk of high-speed collisions.

Question Text: An assembly worker complains of wrist pain. You observe they are using a manual screwdriver 400 times a shift at an awkward 90-degree wrist angle. What do you do?
Option 1: Provide the worker with wrist braces and tell them to do stretching exercises every hour during their break.
Option 2: Replace the manual tool with a suspended, torque-controlled electric driver with a pistol grip.
Option 3: Rotate the worker to a different station that requires heavy lifting to "balance" the muscle usage.
Option 4: Ignore the complaint unless the worker provides a formal medical certificate from a specialist.

Question Text: A critical pump in a chemical plant has a "Mean Time Between Failure" (MTBF) of 40 days. The next scheduled maintenance is in 10 days, but sensors show rising vibration.
Option 1: Wait the 10 days for the scheduled window to avoid disrupting the production plan and losing volume.
Option 2: Increase the pump speed to finish the batch before it fails, then perform an emergency repair.
Option 3: Schedule an immediate controlled shutdown to replace the bearings before a catastrophic failure occurs.
Option 4: Reduce the lubrication frequency to see if "drying out" the bearings stabilizes the vibration.

Question Text: During a Value Stream Mapping (VSM) exercise, you see that parts sit in "In-Process Inspection" for 4 days, while actual machining takes 20 minutes. What is the priority?
Option 1: Buy a faster machining center to reduce the 20-minute cycle time to 10 minutes.
Option 2: Integrate inspection tools into the machining station (Self-Quality) to eliminate the 4-day wait.
Option 3: Hire 5 more inspectors to work in the inspection department to clear the backlog faster.
Option 4: Increase the batch size from 100 to 1000 to justify the 4-day wait in the inspection queue.

Question Text: Your supplier offers a 20% discount if you double your order size, but your warehouse is already at 90% capacity and the product has a short shelf life.
Option 1: Accept the discount and store the excess inventory in an outdoor tent to save on warehouse costs.
Option 2: Refuse the discount, as the holding costs and risk of obsolescence will likely exceed the 20% savings.
Option 3: Accept the discount and stop all production for two months until the excess stock is sold.
Option 4: Negotiate with the supplier to keep the 20% discount but deliver in smaller, frequent JIT batches.

Question Text: A "Single-Minute Exchange of Die" (SMED) project is failing because the heavy tools are stored in a locked room 200 meters away from the machine. What is the fix?
Option 1: Give the operator a faster motorized cart to drive to the tool room during the changeover.
Option 2: Move the required tools to a shadow board located within 2 meters of the machine's changeover point.
Option 3: Train the operators to run faster between the machine and the tool room to shave off seconds.
Option 4: Increase the production run size so that changeovers only happen once a month instead of daily.

Question Text: You are implementing a Pull system. Station B's bin is full, but Station A (upstream) wants to keep working because their "Efficiency" metric is low.
Option 1: Allow Station A to continue producing so their individual efficiency stays high for the month.
Option 2: Stop Station A and reassign the worker to 5S or training until Station B signals for more parts.
Option 3: Tell Station A to produce parts and store them in the hallway so they don't clutter the floor.
Option 4: Speed up Station B's machine beyond its safety limit to catch up with the production of Station A.

Question Text: A robot on the assembly line keeps "dropping" parts. You realize the part dimensions from the previous supplier have slightly changed, though still within tolerance.
Option 1: Reprogram the robot's grip pressure every time a new batch of parts arrives from the supplier.
Option 2: Work with the supplier to narrow the tolerance range specifically for the robotically handled features.
Option 3: Disable the robot and hire two manual laborers to perform the task until the parts are used up.
Option 4: Apply industrial glue to the robot's grippers to ensure the parts stay in place regardless of size.

Question Text: In an ERP system, you notice that "Work-in-Progress" (WIP) has tripled in a month, but finished goods output has stayed the same. What is the likely cause?
Option 1: The sales team is doing a great job and more orders are coming into the system than ever before.
Option 2: There is a major bottleneck or a "hidden factory" where parts are being reworked multiple times.
Option 3: The accounting department has changed the way they value the raw materials in the warehouse.
Option 4: The workers have become 300% faster at the beginning of the line but slower at the end.

Question Text: A Lean project has successfully reduced lead time by 50%. The CEO asks why the "Net Profit" hasn't increased immediately. What is the most honest answer?
Option 1: Lean doesn't actually improve profit; it only improves the "feeling" of the factory floor.
Option 2: The capacity gained from shorter lead times must now be sold to new customers to see a profit.
Option 3: We need to fire 50% of the workers now that the lead time is shorter to save on labor costs.
Option 4: We must have made a mistake in the lead time calculations because profit always rises with Lean.

Question Text: You are designing a layout for a new electronics repair center. There are 50 different types of repairs, each requiring different tools. Which layout is best?
Option 1: A straight assembly line where every unit passes through every single tool station.
Option 2: A "Cellular" layout where common repair types are grouped into dedicated, flexible workstations.
Option 3: A massive warehouse where units stay in one spot and tools are brought to them by hand.
Option 4: A circular conveyor belt that moves parts continuously until a technician grabs one.

Question Text: A "Six Sigma" project finds that temperature in the curing oven fluctuates by 10 degrees, causing 2% scrap. Fixing the oven costs $50k; the scrap costs $5k/year.
Option 1: Spend the $50k immediately because "Zero Defects" is the company's only mission statement.
Option 2: Monitor the oven but do not fix it, as the Return on Investment (ROI) would take 10 years.
Option 3: Look for a low-cost "Poka-Yoke" solution, like an alarm that triggers if the temp fluctuates.
Option 4: Fire the oven operator and hire someone with more experience in thermal management.

Question Text: You are using a "String Diagram" to track a nurse's movement in a clinic. The diagram looks like a "spaghetti" mess. What is the first design change you test?
Option 1: Increase the size of the clinic so the nurse has more room to walk between the patients.
Option 2: Move the medicine cabinet and the chart station closer to the center of the patient rooms.
Option 3: Give the nurse a pair of high-quality running shoes to reduce the fatigue from all the walking.
Option 4: Install more chairs so the patients can wait longer while the nurse moves between rooms.

Question Text: An automated PLC system keeps triggering an "Emergency Stop." You find that the light curtain is being tripped by the flickering of a nearby overhead fluorescent light.
Option 1: Tape a piece of cardboard over the light curtain sensor so it can't see the flickering light.
Option 2: Replace the light curtain with a physical metal gate that must be opened and closed manually.
Option 3: Move the light fixture or shield the light curtain to eliminate the optical interference.
Option 4: Change the PLC code to ignore the light curtain signal for the first 5 seconds of every cycle.

Question Text: Your "ABC" inventory analysis shows that "C" items (cheap, low volume) are taking up 60% of your shelf space. What is the strategic action?
Option 1: Move all "C" items to the front of the warehouse because there are so many of them to look at.
Option 2: Consolidate "C" items into high-density storage or consider "Vendor Managed Inventory" (VMI).
Option 3: Immediately throw away all "C" items to make room for more "A" items that are expensive.
Option 4: Build a second warehouse specifically for "C" items to keep the main warehouse for "A" items.

Question Text: An operator is consistently outperforming the "Standard Time" by 30%. Other operators are struggling. What is your first investigation?
Option 1: Check if the fast operator is skipping safety steps or quality checks to achieve the high speed.
Option 2: Immediately increase the "Standard Time" for everyone based on this one operator's performance.
Option 3: Give the fast operator a massive bonus and ignore the other workers who are much slower.
Option 4: Fire the slower workers and try to find more people who can work as fast as the star operator.

Question Text: You are in charge of a "Total Productive Maintenance" (TPM) rollout. The maintenance team feels threatened that operators are now doing "their jobs." How do you handle it?
Option 1: Explain that operators will now do the simple cleaning/oiling, allowing the skilled team to focus on high-level reliability engineering.
Option 2: Tell the maintenance team they are no longer needed and will be transferred to the shipping department.
Option 3: Force the operators to do the maintenance in secret so the maintenance team doesn't find out.
Option 4: Increase the maintenance team's workload so they are too busy to worry about what the operators are doing.

Question Text: A project is on the "Critical Path." The task "Design Review" is delayed by 2 days. What is the effect on the total project completion date?
Option 1: The project completion date will remain the same as long as the other tasks are done faster.
Option 2: The project completion date will be delayed by exactly 2 days unless the path is "crashed."
Option 3: The project will likely be cancelled because any delay on the critical path is a total failure.
Option 4: The project completion date will be moved forward by 2 days to compensate for the lost time.

Question Text: A production line has a "Takt Time" of 60 seconds, but the slowest station takes 80 seconds. What happens to the customer demand?
Option 1: The customer demand is met perfectly because the other stations are much faster than 60 seconds.
Option 2: The company will fail to meet customer demand unless the 80-second station is improved or split.
Option 3: The customer will naturally wait longer because they understand that manufacturing is a difficult process.
Option 4: The "Takt Time" will automatically change to 80 seconds to match the slowest part of the factory.

Question Text: You notice that 80% of your machine downtime is caused by "Lack of Raw Material" at the station. What is the core problem?
Option 1: The machines are too fast for the workers to keep up with the loading of the materials.
Option 2: The internal logistics and replenishment system (e.g., Kanban) are failing to signal needs.
Option 3: The machines are old and need to be replaced with newer models that don't need raw materials.
Option 4: The raw materials are of poor quality and are being rejected by the machines during the run.

Question Text: A "Pareto Analysis" shows that "Scratches" are the #1 defect. You find that parts are being tossed into metal bins without liners. What is the fix?
Option 1: Hire more inspectors to find the scratches earlier so the parts can be polished by hand.
Option 2: Buy expensive plastic parts instead of metal ones so that they don't show the scratches as easily.
Option 3: Line the bins with rubber mats or use "shadow foam" trays to prevent part-to-part contact.
Option 4: Slow down the entire production line so the workers have more time to put the parts down gently.

Question Text: You have to choose between a "Fixed Position Layout" and a "Product Layout" for building a 50-meter luxury yacht. Why choose Fixed Position?
Option 1: It is cheaper to move the workers and tools to the yacht than to move the yacht through a line.
Option 2: It is easier to train workers if they stay in one spot and the yacht moves past them on a belt.
Option 3: A yacht is a very small product and can easily be moved between different stations in a factory.
Option 4: Fixed position layouts always have the highest efficiency and lowest cost for any type of product.

Question Text: A "Kaizen" event identifies that an operator walks 5 kilometers a day just to fetch cardboard boxes. What is the "Lean" solution?
Option 1: Buy the operator a pedometer and give them a prize for the most steps taken during a shift.
Option 2: Move the box storage area to a flow-rack located directly behind the operator's workstation.
Option 3: Hire a dedicated "box runner" whose only job is to carry boxes to all the different operators.
Option 4: Tell the operator to carry more boxes at once so they only have to make two trips per day.

Question Text: Your "Maintenance" budget is being spent 90% on "Emergency Repairs" and 10% on "Preventive Maintenance." What is the long-term risk?
Option 1: The machines will eventually become "self-healing" because they are being repaired so often.
Option 2: The total cost of ownership will skyrocket as equipment reliability declines and downtime increases.
Option 3: The maintenance team will become the most skilled in the world because they fix so many things.
Option 4: The machines will last longer because they are getting fresh parts every time they break down.

Question Text: An "Industrial Robot" is programmed to move at 2 meters per second. A human must enter the cell to clear a jam. What is the safety protocol?
Option 1: The human should run into the cell very quickly and clear the jam before the robot can hit them.
Option 2: The system must use an interlocked gate that cuts all power to the robot motors before the door opens.
Option 3: The robot should be programmed to "wave" at the human to show that it knows they are there.
Option 4: The human must wear a thick padded suit that protects them from any impact from the robot arm.

Question Text: You are analyzing "Job Satisfaction" on a highly repetitive assembly line. Turnover is 40%. What "Work Study" change might help?
Option 1: Increase the speed of the line so the workers are too busy to think about being unhappy.
Option 2: Implement "Job Rotation" or "Job Enlargement" to provide variety in the daily tasks.
Option 3: Install more cameras to monitor the workers and ensure they are not talking to each other.
Option 4: Pay the workers on a "piece-rate" system so they are forced to work harder to make a living.

Question Text: In a "Six Sigma" project, the "p-value" for a change in process temperature is 0.01. What does this tell you?
Option 1: There is a 1% chance that the temperature change had no effect on the quality of the product.
Option 2: The temperature change is 99% likely to be the reason for the improvement in the quality.
Option 3: The temperature should be increased by exactly 0.01 degrees to achieve the best results.
Option 4: The project has failed because the p-value should always be higher than 0.50 for success.

Question Text: A factory uses a "Push" system. The warehouse is overflowing with "Part A," but the assembly line is stopped because they are missing "Part B."
Option 1: Tell the "Part A" machine to work overtime to ensure the warehouse stays completely full.
Option 2: Stop "Part A" production and switch that machine/operator to produce "Part B" immediately.
Option 3: Buy a bigger warehouse so that you can store even more of "Part A" while you wait for "Part B."
Option 4: Increase the price of "Part B" products so that customers will buy "Part A" products instead.

Question Text: You are asked to reduce "Material Handling" costs in a 3-story factory. Which solution is the most "Industrial Engineering" focused?
Option 1: Install a gravity-fed spiral chute to move finished parts from the 3rd floor to the 1st floor.
Option 2: Hire more people to carry the parts down the stairs in small, manageable plastic bags.
Option 3: Use the elevator for everything, even if people have to wait 20 minutes for it to arrive.
Option 4: Move all the heavy machines to the 3rd floor and all the light assembly to the 1st floor.

Question Text: A "Linear Programming" model for profit maximization has 5 constraints. You find a way to remove one constraint (e.g., hiring more staff). What happens?
Option 1: The profit will definitely decrease because the model has become simpler and less accurate.
Option 2: The "Feasible Region" expands, potentially allowing for a higher optimal profit than before.
Option 3: The model will crash because it requires at least 5 constraints to find a mathematical answer.
Option 4: Nothing will change, as the first constraint is always the only one that actually matters.

Question Text: You are conducting a "Method Study" on a worker. You notice they use their left hand only to hold a part while the right hand does all the work.
Option 1: Tell the worker they are doing a great job and should continue using their hands this way.
Option 2: Design a simple "fixture" or "jig" to hold the part, freeing the left hand to add value.
Option 3: Instruct the worker to try using their left hand for everything and keep the right hand in their pocket.
Option 4: Give the worker a heavier part to hold so that their left hand gets a better workout during the day.

Question Text: A "Kanban" card for "Steel Bolts" has been lost. The production line continues to run until they run out of bolts. What is the systemic fix?
Option 1: Use an electronic Kanban (e-Kanban) or a "Two-Bin" system where the empty bin is the signal.
Option 2: Tape the Kanban card to the wall so that it can never be moved or lost by the operators.
Option 3: Hire a "Kanban Manager" whose only job is to hold all the cards in a secure, locked briefcase.
Option 4: Stop using Kanban and go back to a system where you order 1 million bolts once a year.

Question Text: Your "Safety" audit finds that workers are removing the "Blade Guard" on a saw because it "slows them down." What is the correct response?
Option 1: Allow them to keep the guard off if they promise to be very careful and sign a waiver.
Option 2: Find a guard design that is transparent or spring-loaded, which doesn't impede the work speed.
Option 3: Remove the saw entirely and tell the workers to cut the wood using manual hand-saws.
Option 4: Increase the production target to see if they can work even faster without the guard.

Question Text: A "Maintenance" technician suggests using an ultrasound sensor to "listen" to bearing wear. This is an example of moving from:
Option 1: Preventive Maintenance to Predictive Maintenance to reduce unnecessary part changes.
Option 2: Breakdown Maintenance to Preventive Maintenance to ensure the machines are always oiled.
Option 3: Manual labor to Automation to reduce the number of people working in the factory.
Option 4: Six Sigma to Lean Manufacturing to reduce the amount of waste in the repair process.

Question Text: During a "5S" audit, you find that the "Red Tag" area has items that have been sitting there for 6 months. What is the next step?
Option 1: Leave them there for another 6 months to see if anyone finally decides to use them.
Option 2: Discard, sell, or relocate the items immediately, as they are clearly not "necessary."
Option 3: Move the Red Tag items back to the production floor to make the Red Tag area look clean.
Option 4: Paint the Red Tag items a different color so they don't look like they are part of a 5S audit.

Question Text: A "Supply Chain" risk assessment shows that your only supplier for a critical "Microchip" is in a flood-prone zone. What do you do?
Option 1: Do nothing and hope it doesn't rain in that country for the next ten or twenty years.
Option 2: Develop a "Dual Sourcing" strategy by qualifying a second supplier in a different region.
Option 3: Buy enough microchips to last for the next 50 years and store them in a secure vault.
Option 4: Tell the supplier to build a giant wall around their factory to protect your chips from water.

Question Text: You are calculating "OEE" (Overall Equipment Effectiveness). The machine is running at 50% of its rated speed to prevent overheating. This affects:
Option 1: The "Availability" score because the machine is not available to run at its full potential.
Option 2: The "Performance" score because the machine is running slower than its designed cycle time.
Option 3: The "Quality" score because running slow always produces parts that are of a lower quality.
Option 4: The "OEE" score cannot be calculated if the machine is running at a different speed.

Question Text: A worker is using a 5kg grinder for 4 hours a day. The vibration is causing "White Finger" syndrome. Which "Ergonomic" fix is best?
Option 1: Buy the worker thick wool gloves to keep their hands warm while they are grinding.
Option 2: Select a low-vibration grinder and implement "Job Rotation" to limit exposure time.
Option 3: Tell the worker to grip the grinder tighter so that the vibration doesn't move their fingers.
Option 4: Replace the grinder with a 10kg model so that the extra weight absorbs the vibration.

Question Text: You are implementing "Standard Work." The veteran worker says, "I have my own way, and it's better than your document." How do you proceed?
Option 1: Discipline the veteran worker for not following the new company rules immediately.
Option 2: Ask the veteran to demonstrate their "way"; if it's better, update the Standard to include it.
Option 3: Ignore the veteran and wait for them to retire so you can train a new person the "right" way.
Option 4: Tell the veteran they are wrong and that the document was written by a person with a degree.

Question Text: A "Control Chart" shows 7 consecutive points on one side of the mean, but all are inside the control limits. What does this indicate?
Option 1: The process is perfectly fine because no points have gone outside the red control lines.
Option 2: There is a "Run" or a shift in the process mean that requires investigation (non-random).
Option 3: The person drawing the chart has made a mistake and should start over with new data.
Option 4: The machine is getting better and better, and soon there will be no defects at all.

Question Text: You are choosing an "Automation" strategy for a product that changes design every 3 months. Which do you choose?
Option 1: Hard Automation (Fixed transfer lines) because it is the fastest way to produce parts.
Option 2: Programmable Automation (Industrial Robots/CNC) because it is flexible for design changes.
Option 3: Manual Labor only, because machines are never able to handle any design changes at all.
Option 4: A system of pulleys and gears that must be rebuilt every time the design changes.

Question Text: A "Heijunka" (Leveling) strategy results in producing small amounts of "Product A, B, and C" every day instead of a week of each. Why?
Option 1: It makes the warehouse look more colorful with different boxes arriving every day.
Option 2: It reduces the "Bullwhip Effect" and allows the factory to respond to actual daily demand.
Option 3: It is much easier for the workers to remember how to build all three products at once.
Option 4: It increases the total amount of inventory in the warehouse, which is good for the company.

Question Text: A "Facility Layout" study shows that workers spend 20% of their time waiting for the "Overhead Crane." What is the industrial engineering fix?
Option 1: Tell the workers to be more patient and use the waiting time to relax and rest.
Option 2: Install smaller "Jib Cranes" at individual workstations for localized heavy lifting.
Option 3: Hire a "Crane Manager" to decide who gets to use the big crane first every morning.
Option 4: Remove all the heavy parts from the product so that no one ever needs a crane again.

Question Text: Your "Maintenance" team finds a way to fix a machine in 2 hours instead of 10. This improvement specifically reduces which metric?
Option 1: MTBF (Mean Time Between Failure), because the machine will now break down more often.
Option 2: MTTR (Mean Time To Repair), which directly increases the "Availability" component of OEE.
Option 3: Takt Time, because the machine is now producing parts five times faster than before.
Option 4: The cost of electricity, because the machine is turned off for a shorter amount of time.

Question Text: A "Poka-Yoke" on an assembly line detects a missing screw and locks the part in the fixture. The operator complains it’s annoying.
Option 1: Remove the lock so the operator is happy, and hope they remember the screw next time.
Option 2: Explain that the "annoyance" prevents a $10,000 warranty claim from a frustrated customer.
Option 3: Tell the operator to work faster so they have more time to look for the missing screw.
Option 4: Move the Poka-Yoke to a different station where the operator is less likely to complain.

Question Text: You are using "Work Sampling" to check machine utilization. Out of 100 random observations, the machine was "Idle" 40 times. What is the estimate?
Option 1: The machine is being used 100% of the time, but the observer was unlucky with their timing.
Option 2: The machine utilization is approximately 60%, suggesting capacity for more work.
Option 3: The machine is broken and should be sold for scrap metal as soon as possible.
Option 4: The observer should be fired for not watching the machine for 100 hours in a row.

Question Text: A "Supply Chain" manager decides to move from "Sea Freight" to "Air Freight" for a heavy component. What is the most likely impact?
Option 1: The "Inventory Holding Cost" will go up because the parts arrive so much faster.
Option 2: The "Transportation Cost" will increase significantly, but "Lead Time" will decrease.
Option 3: The quality of the parts will improve because the air is cleaner at high altitudes.
Option 4: The company will save money because airplanes don't have to pay for fuel like ships do.

Question Text: A "Cellular Manufacturing" layout has 4 machines. The "Worker-Machine Chart" shows the worker is idle 50% of the time. What do you do?
Option 1: Add more machines to the cell or have the worker manage two cells (Multi-Machine handling).
Option 2: Give the worker a chair so they can sit down comfortably during their 50% idle time.
Option 3: Slow down the machines so that the worker is always busy watching them run slowly.
Option 4: Fire the worker and try to find a machine that can operate itself without any human help.

Question Text: In a "Six Sigma" project, "Standard Deviation" (Sigma) for a shaft diameter decreases. What does this mean for the process?
Option 1: The process has become more "precise," meaning the parts are more consistent with each other.
Option 2: The process has become more "accurate," meaning the parts are exactly on the target size.
Option 3: The machines are now using more electricity to produce the parts with a smaller sigma.
Option 4: The workers are now taking more breaks during the day to avoid making any mistakes.

Question Text: An "Industrial Automation" sensor fails every time it gets wet. The environment is naturally damp. What is the "Engineering" solution?
Option 1: Tell the workers to wipe the sensor with a dry towel every thirty seconds.
Option 2: Replace the sensor with one that has a higher "IP Rating" (e.g., IP67) for water resistance.
Option 3: Build a giant umbrella over the entire production line to keep all the sensors dry.
Option 4: Stop using water in the factory and find a way to make the products in a dry environment.

Question Text: You are using "Linear Programming" to schedule 50 jobs on 2 machines. The "Optimal" solution is 10.2 hours. Can you use this?
Option 1: Yes, you can tell the workers to work exactly 10.2 hours and then stop immediately.
Option 2: No, because jobs are "Integer" (discrete); you must use "Integer Programming" for a real plan.
Option 3: Yes, because 0.2 hours is just a few minutes and it doesn't matter in a big factory.
Option 4: No, you should always round the answer up to 100 hours to be safe with the schedule.

Question Text: A "Kaizen" suggestion says "Move the printer closer to the desks." This saves 10 minutes of walking per day for 20 people. Total time saved?
Option 1: 10 minutes, because only one person can use the printer at a time anyway.
Option 2: 200 minutes (over 3 hours) of collective "Non-Value Added" time per day.
Option 3: Zero minutes, because walking is good exercise and makes the employees healthier.
Option 4: 1000 minutes, because the printer will now print much faster than it did before.

Question Text: A "Maintenance" plan for a conveyor belt is "Replace every 6 months." It breaks after 3 months. What is the action?
Option 1: Change the plan to "Replace every 2 months" or use "Condition Monitoring" (e.g., belt tension).
Option 2: Keep the 6-month plan and just accept that it will break every once in a while.
Option 3: Stop using conveyor belts and use humans to carry the parts on their shoulders.
Option 4: Buy a conveyor belt that is made of solid gold so that it never breaks again.

Question Text: You are designing a "Dashboard" for a Plant Manager. Which "KPI" is the most "Actionable"?
Option 1: "Total Revenue" for the last 10 years shown in a giant colorful pie chart.
Option 2: "Current Hourly Output vs. Target" with a red/green indicator for the current shift.
Option 3: The "Average Age" of all the employees working in the maintenance department.
Option 4: The "Total Weight" of all the trash cans in the cafeteria for the last month.

Question Text: A "Process Layout" is causing high "Work-in-Progress" because parts must wait for a "Move Ticket" and a forklift. What is the fix?
Option 1: Hire 10 more forklift drivers so that no one ever has to wait for a move ticket.
Option 2: Convert the high-volume products to a "Product Layout" or "Cell" with integrated flow.
Option 3: Tell the workers to carry the 500kg parts by hand so they don't have to wait for a forklift.
Option 4: Increase the size of the "In-Box" at every station so that more parts can wait in the queue.

Question Text: An "Ergonomic" study finds that 60% of workers are taller than the "Fixed Height" assembly table. What is the best solution?
Option 1: Tell the tall workers to bend their knees more to reach the table comfortably.
Option 2: Install "Adjustable Height" workstations that can be customized for each shift's operator.
Option 3: Only hire short people to work at that specific assembly table from now on.
Option 4: Cut 10cm off the legs of all the chairs so that the workers feel taller at the table.

Question Text: A "Lean" consultant says "Inventory is the root of all evil." You have a 2-day lead time from your only supplier. Do you go to "Zero Inventory"?
Option 1: Yes, because the consultant is always right and inventory is a waste according to Lean.
Option 2: No, you must keep at least 2 days of "Safety Stock" to prevent a line shutdown.
Option 3: No, you should keep 100 days of inventory just to prove the consultant is wrong.
Option 4: Yes, and tell the supplier that they must now deliver parts every 5 minutes by drone.

Question Text: A "Simulation" model shows that adding a second "Inspection Station" reduces the queue from 50 units to 2 units. What is the trade-off?
Option 1: The trade-off is the extra cost of the second inspector and equipment vs. the cost of WIP.
Option 2: There is no trade-off; adding more stations is always the best thing to do in any factory.
Option 3: The trade-off is that the first inspector will become lazy because they have less work.
Option 4: The second station will make the factory too crowded and people won't be able to walk.

Question Text: In "Total Quality Management," a "Quality Circle" suggests a change. The manager dislikes the idea. What is the TQM approach?
Option 1: The manager should ignore the suggestion because they have more experience and a degree.
Option 2: The manager should allow the circle to "Pilot" the idea and collect data on the results.
Option 3: The manager should fire the members of the quality circle for challenging the authority.
Option 4: The manager should tell the circle to go back to work and stop thinking about improvements.

Question Text: You are using "Single-Level BOM" for a chair. You realize the "Screws" are missing from the list. What is the impact on "MRP"?
Option 1: The MRP will never order the screws, and the assembly line will stop when they run out.
Option 2: The MRP is "smart" and will realize that screws are needed to build a chair automatically.
Option 3: The workers will just find some screws in the parking lot and use those instead.
Option 4: The chair will be built without screws, and the company will hope the glue is strong enough.

Question Text: A "Time Study" shows a worker takes 10 minutes. Their "Rating" is 80% (they were slow). What is the "Normal Time"?
Option 1: 10 minutes, because the rating doesn't change the actual time recorded on the stopwatch.
Option 2: 8 minutes (10 * 0.8), which is the time a standard worker should take for the task.
Option 3: 12.5 minutes (10 / 0.8), because a slow worker needs more time to do the same job.
Option 4: 100 minutes, because the worker should be penalized for being so slow during the study.

Question Text: Your "Supply Chain" is suffering from the "Bullwhip Effect." What is the best way to "Dampen" the whip?
Option 1: Increase the lead times so that everyone has more time to react to the demand changes.
Option 2: Share real-time "Point-of-Sale" (POS) data from the retailer directly with the factory.
Option 3: Stop talking to the retailer and only guess the demand based on the weather patterns.
Option 4: Charge the retailer more money every time they change their order size or timing.

Question Text: A "Maintenance" engineer uses "Oil Analysis" to check for metal shavings in a gearbox. This is an example of:
Option 1: Predictive Maintenance, using the condition of the oil to predict internal component wear.
Option 2: Breakdown Maintenance, because you only look at the oil after the gearbox has exploded.
Option 3: Preventive Maintenance, because you are changing the oil every Tuesday regardless of its state.
Option 4: Corrective Maintenance, because the metal shavings are being removed from the gearbox.

Question Text: During a "5S" Seiri (Sort) phase, you find a machine that hasn't been used in 3 years. It's "just in case."
Option 1: Leave it where it is; you never know when a 20-year-old order might come back.
Option 2: Red tag it and move it to storage or sell it to free up valuable "Production Floor" space.
Option 3: Paint it a bright color so that it looks like it is a useful part of the factory.
Option 4: Hire a worker to stand next to it and pretend to use it whenever the boss walks by.

Question Text: You are automating a "Pick and Place" task. The part weighs 20kg. What is the most important "Robot" specification?
Option 1: The "Color" of the robot, so that it matches the company's brand and logo.
Option 2: The "Payload Capacity," ensuring the robot can safely lift the 20kg part plus the gripper.
Option 3: The "Memory" of the robot, so that it can remember the names of all the workers.
Option 4: The "Voice" of the robot, so that it can talk to the other machines on the line.

Question Text: A "Six Sigma" Green Belt wants to use a "Fishbone Diagram" for a defect. Who should be in the room?
Option 1: Only the Green Belt, because they are the only one who knows how to draw the diagram.
Option 2: A cross-functional team including the operators, maintenance, and the design engineer.
Option 3: The CEO and the Board of Directors, as they are the ones who pay for the project.
Option 4: No one; the diagram should be generated by an AI based on the factory's data.

Question Text: You are using "Jitoka" in a manual line. A worker pulls an "Andon" cord. What is the immediate result?
Option 1: A light flashes and the supervisor comes to help the worker solve the problem immediately.
Option 2: The worker is fired for stopping the line and wasting the company's valuable time.
Option 3: The entire factory power is cut and everyone is sent home for the rest of the day.
Option 4: A loud siren sounds and the worker is given a "Red Card" for their performance file.

Question Text: A "Layout" uses "U-Shaped Cells." You have 10 machines and 3 workers. How is this better than a straight line?
Option 1: Workers can easily move between machines on both sides of the "U" to balance the work.
Option 2: The "U-Shape" takes up more room, making the factory look more impressive to visitors.
Option 3: A straight line is always better because it's easier to walk in one single direction.
Option 4: The "U-Shape" prevents the workers from seeing each other, which increases their focus.

Question Text: A "Job Shop" receives a "Rush Order." The "Dispatching Rule" is "Shortest Processing Time" (SPT). Why use this?
Option 1: It minimizes the average time a job spends in the shop (Flow Time) and reduces WIP.
Option 2: It ensures that the most important and expensive customer always gets their order first.
Option 3: It is the easiest rule for the workers to understand because they like short jobs.
Option 4: It maximizes the total profit by only doing the jobs that are very quick to finish.

Question Text: You are analyzing "Plant Maintenance" data and find "Infant Mortality" failures in new motors.
Option 1: Increase the "Preventive Maintenance" frequency for all new motors to every day.
Option 2: Improve the "Installation and Commissioning" procedures and check supplier quality.
Option 3: Wait until the motors are at least 5 years old before you start using them in the plant.
Option 4: Stop buying new motors and only buy used ones that have already survived for 10 years.

Question Text: A "Safety Stock" calculation uses "Service Level." If you move from 90% to 99% Service Level:
Option 1: Your inventory costs will stay the same, but your customers will be 9% happier.
Option 2: Your inventory costs will increase exponentially as you try to cover the extreme "tails" of demand.
Option 3: Your inventory costs will decrease because you are being more "Service-Oriented."
Option 4: The "Lead Time" from the supplier will automatically decrease to help you meet the goal.

Question Text: You are using "Method Study" on a packaging station. You notice the worker reaches 80cm for a label.
Option 1: Move the label dispenser to within 25cm (the "Primary Work Zone") of the worker.
Option 2: Give the worker a longer arm or a tool to reach the 80cm label dispenser.
Option 3: Tell the worker to stretch more so that they become more flexible over time.
Option 4: Move the label dispenser even further away to encourage the worker to walk more.

Question Text: In "Project Management," you "Crash" a task by spending $1000 to save 1 day. When is this worth it?
Option 1: Always, because saving time is the only thing that matters in any engineering project.
Option 2: Only if the task is on the "Critical Path" and the "Penalty" for delay is > $1000.
Option 3: Only if the manager is angry and wants the project finished as soon as possible.
Option 4: Never, because spending extra money is a sign of poor planning and management.

Question Text: A "Six Sigma" process has a $C_{pk}$ of 0.5. What does this tell you about the process?
Option 1: The process is highly capable and is producing almost zero defects every single day.
Option 2: The process spread is much wider than the tolerance; it is producing many defects.
Option 3: The process is "Six Sigma" quality because 0.5 is half of 1.0, which is very good.
Option 4: The process mean is exactly on the target, but the workers are not working fast enough.

Question Text: You are implementing "Industrial Automation." A "Limit Switch" keeps breaking because the metal part hits it too hard.
Option 1: Replace the mechanical limit switch with a non-contact "Inductive Proximity Sensor."
Option 2: Make the limit switch bigger and stronger so that it can survive the heavy impacts.
Option 3: Tell the workers to catch the part by hand before it hits the limit switch.
Option 4: Program the PLC to ignore the limit switch signal and just guess when the part is there.

Question Text: A "Supply Chain" uses "Cross-Docking." What is the main benefit for a retail chain?
Option 1: It allows the retailers to store goods for a long time without paying for a warehouse.
Option 2: It reduces inventory "Dwell Time" and handling costs by bypassing long-term storage.
Option 3: It makes the trucks look more full and impressive when they are driving on the highway.
Option 4: It allows the company to hide the products from the government to avoid paying taxes.

Question Text: You are using "Standard Work Combination Sheets." You find the "Manual Time" + "Walking Time" > "Takt Time."
Option 1: This is fine; the worker will just have to work through their lunch break to catch up.
Option 2: The process is "Overburdened" (Muri); you must redistribute tasks or improve the method.
Option 3: You should increase the "Takt Time" so that the worker doesn't feel so rushed.
