Option 1: Continue testing other modules on Android 13 and ignore the Android 14 crash until the end of the sprint.
Option 2: Stop further testing on Android 14, report a "Blocker" bug, and investigate the OS-specific compatibility logs.
Option 3: Perform a full Regression Test on all previous versions of Android to see if the crash is widespread.
Option 4: Run a Performance Test to see if the Android 14 crash is caused by high memory consumption during the splash screen.

Question Text: You are tasked with testing a weather app that fetches data from a third-party API. The API is currently down for maintenance. How can you continue Functional Testing?
Option 1: Wait for the API to come back online before resuming any testing activities to ensure data accuracy.
Option 2: Use a Mock Server or "Stub" to simulate the API responses, allowing you to test how the UI handles different data.
Option 3: Manually enter the weather data into the app's local database using a SQL editor on a rooted device.
Option 4: Skip the weather data verification and focus solely on the app's "About Us" and "Settings" pages.

Question Text: In a mobile app, you need to verify that a "Terms and Conditions" link opens the correct URL in the system browser. This check falls under which category?
Option 1: Security Testing, to ensure the URL is using the HTTPS protocol and is not a malicious phishing site.
Option 2: Functional Testing, as you are verifying that a specific action (clicking a link) results in the expected behavior.
Option 3: Compatibility Testing, to ensure that every mobile browser (Chrome, Safari, Firefox) can render the link correctly.
Option 4: Load Testing, to see if the system browser can handle multiple tabs opening the same URL simultaneously.

Question Text: An automation script fails because a button's ID changed from btn_submit to button_login. What is the best industry practice to prevent such "brittle" tests?
Option 1: Hard-code the button coordinates (x, y) so the script clicks the same physical spot regardless of the ID.
Option 2: Use "Page Object Model" (POM) to centralize locators, making it easier to update the ID in one place for all tests.
Option 3: Ask the developers to never change an ID once it has been created, regardless of UI redesigns or refactoring.
Option 4: Record a new macro for every test run to ensure the locators are always up to date with the latest build.

Question Text: You are testing a navigation app. You need to ensure the app doesn't drain the battery excessively when running in the background for 4 hours. This is:
Option 1: Stress Testing, because you are pushing the battery to its limit until the phone eventually shuts down.
Option 2: Performance Testing (specifically Power Consumption testing) to monitor resource usage over an extended period.
Option 3: Usability Testing, because a fast-draining battery results in a poor user experience for the target audience.
Option 4: Integration Testing, to see how the GPS module interacts with the background service and the battery manager.

Question Text: While testing a "Dark Mode" feature, you notice that some text remains black on a dark background, making it unreadable. This is primarily a failure in:
Option 1: Accessibility Testing, which is a subset of Usability Testing focused on ensuring the app is usable by everyone.
Option 2: Compatibility Testing, as the dark mode might only be failing on specific OLED screens vs LCD screens.
Option 3: Regression Testing, because the black text was likely a default setting that wasn't updated for the new theme.
Option 4: Unit Testing, as the developer failed to write a test case for the text color property in the CSS/XML file.

Question Text: Your team is moving from Manual Testing to Automated Testing. Which types of test cases should you prioritize for automation first to get the best ROI?
Option 1: Complex, one-time edge cases that are difficult to reproduce and require significant manual setup.
Option 2: High-volume, repetitive Regression tests and "Happy Path" scenarios that are executed in every release.
Option 3: Usability tests that require human intuition to determine if a layout is "pleasing" or "intuitive."
Option 4: Security tests that require creative hacking techniques and manual exploration of the app's vulnerabilities.

Question Text: When a tester is looking for bugs by "wandering" through the app without pre-defined test cases or scripts, they are performing:
Option 1: System Testing, because they are evaluating the entire system's functionality from an end-user perspective.
Option 2: Exploratory Testing, which relies on the tester's experience and creativity to find defects in an unscripted way.
Option 3: User Acceptance Testing, because the tester is acting like a user to see if the app meets their needs.
Option 4: Ad-hoc Testing, which is a formal process used to find bugs that were missed during the initial requirement phase.

Question Text: In a "Test Summary Report," what is the most important metric to communicate to the stakeholders before a major app store release?
Option 1: The total number of test cases written, regardless of whether they were actually executed or passed.
Option 2: The "Pass/Fail" rate of critical features and the number of "Open High-Priority" defects remaining.
Option 3: The total number of hours the testing team worked during the sprint, including overtime and breaks.
Option 4: The number of lines of code written by the developers that were successfully covered by the unit tests.

Question Text: You are testing a chat application. You need to verify that when a user is in a tunnel (no signal), messages are queued and sent automatically once they exit. This is:
Option 1: Functional Testing focused on "Offline Synchronization" and "Data Persistence" during network state changes.
Option 2: Compatibility Testing to ensure that the 4G and 5G antennas on different phones handle the tunnel correctly.
Option 3: Stress Testing the message database to see how many unsent messages it can hold before the app crashes.
Option 4: Unit Testing the network listener class to ensure it returns a "False" value when the signal is lost.

Question Text: A bug is found where the app crashes only when the device is rotated from portrait to landscape during a video upload. What is the most likely cause?
Option 1: The server is unable to handle the change in the aspect ratio of the video metadata during the upload process.
Option 2: The activity or screen is being recreated by the OS, and the app is not properly saving the state or the upload thread.
Option 3: The device's accelerometer is faulty and is sending incorrect interrupt signals to the application's main thread.
Option 4: The performance of the CPU is spiking during rotation, causing the video encoder to run out of available memory.

Question Text: During "Integration Testing," you discover that the Payment Gateway returns a success code, but the Order Database doesn't update. Where is the defect?
Option 1: In the UI, because it should have shown a loading spinner until both the gateway and the database were synced.
Option 2: In the interface or middleware logic that handles the communication between the gateway and the database.
Option 3: In the Unit Test of the Payment Gateway, which should have caught this error before the integration phase.
Option 4: In the Load Balancer, which is likely misrouting the database update request to a non-existent server.

Question Text: You need to test how the app behaves when the internal storage of the smartphone is 99% full. This scenario is a part of:
Option 1: Performance Testing, specifically looking at how the app handles low-resource environments and caching.
Option 2: Security Testing, to ensure that the app doesn't leak sensitive data when it's unable to write to the log files.
Option 3: Stress Testing, as you are pushing the device's hardware constraints to see if the app can still function.
Option 4: Compatibility Testing, to see if different brands of SD cards or internal storage chips affect app stability.

Question Text: What is the main purpose of a "Traceability Matrix" (RTM) in a mobile testing project?
Option 1: To track the performance metrics of the automation scripts across different versions of the mobile operating system.
Option 2: To ensure that every business requirement has a corresponding test case, ensuring 100% requirement coverage.
Option 3: To map the developers' names to the specific bugs they fixed, allowing for better accountability in the team.
Option 4: To visualize the network path taken by a request from the mobile app to the backend server and back.

Question Text: An app requires a "Mandatory Update." You need to test if users on version 1.0 are successfully forced to upgrade to 2.0. This is:
Option 1: Regression Testing, as you are checking if the update process has broken any existing features from version 1.0.
Option 2: Functional Testing of the "Update Logic" and "Backward Compatibility" of the user's local data during the migration.
Option 3: Load Testing the update server to see if it can handle thousands of simultaneous download requests.
Option 4: User Acceptance Testing, to see if the users are happy with the new features introduced in version 2.0.

Question Text: In automated mobile testing, what does the term "Locator Strategy" refer to?
Option 1: The GPS coordinates used by the script to simulate the user's physical location in a location-based app.
Option 2: The method (ID, XPath, Accessibility ID) used by the script to find and interact with a UI element.
Option 3: The physical location of the testing lab where the real devices are kept for automated execution.
Option 4: The strategy used to find the best server to host the test automation results and HTML reports.

Question Text: You are testing a banking app. You must ensure that if the app is put in the background, the screen is blurred in the "Recent Apps" view. This is a:
Option 1: Usability requirement to ensure the user isn't confused by seeing their balance when switching apps.
Option 2: Security/Privacy requirement to prevent sensitive data leakage through screen captures or system previews.
Option 3: Performance requirement to reduce the memory footprint of the app while it is in a suspended state.
Option 4: Compatibility requirement to ensure the app looks consistent with the multitasking UI of Android and iOS.

Question Text: Which of the following is a key challenge unique to "Mobile Test Automation" compared to "Web Test Automation"?
Option 1: The need to handle multiple browser versions like Chrome, Firefox, and Safari on a Windows desktop.
Option 2: The fragmentation of hardware, OS versions, screen sizes, and varying network conditions (3G, 4G, 5G).
Option 3: The lack of open-source tools for mobile automation, forcing teams to use expensive proprietary software.
Option 4: The fact that mobile apps do not use HTML or CSS, making it impossible to use element selectors.

Question Text: During "System Testing," the QA team finds that the app consumes 40% of the CPU even when idle. This should be reported as:
Option 1: A Functional Bug, because the app is not functioning efficiently and might be performing hidden tasks.
Option 2: A Performance Defect, as high CPU usage leads to battery drain and device overheating, impacting quality.
Option 3: A Usability Issue, because the user will notice the device getting hot and might uninstall the application.
Option 4: A Design Flaw, as the UI is likely too complex for the mobile processor to render even in a static state.

Question Text: A "Beta Testing" phase is conducted by:
Option 1: The internal QA team using a specialized environment that mimics the production server settings.
Option 2: A selected group of real users in a real-world environment before the official release to the general public.
Option 3: The developers themselves, to ensure that the code is "clean" and follows the company's coding standards.
Option 4: The automated "Bots" that crawl the app looking for crashes and broken links in a controlled lab.

Question Text: You are testing a multi-language app. The German translation is much longer than the English one, causing the "Submit" button to disappear off-screen. This is a:
Option 1: Localization Bug (Usability/UI), requiring a redesign of the layout to handle dynamic text lengths.
Option 2: Functional Bug, because the user cannot click the button and therefore cannot complete the transaction.
Option 3: Compatibility Bug, as the German language might only be supported on specific European device models.
Option 4: Security Bug, because the disappearing button might prevent users from logging out of their accounts.

Question Text: When performing "Load Testing" on a mobile backend, what is the primary goal?
Option 1: To check if the mobile UI remains responsive while the server is being hammered with thousands of requests.
Option 2: To determine the maximum number of concurrent users the backend can handle before response times degrade.
Option 3: To ensure that the mobile app doesn't crash when it receives a "500 Internal Server Error" from the backend.
Option 4: To verify that the backend API can handle different image formats uploaded from various mobile devices.

Question Text: A tester discovers that the app works on Wi-Fi but fails to load images on cellular data. Which type of testing would have specifically targeted this?
Option 1: Compatibility Testing, focusing on different network types and carrier-specific data restrictions.
Option 2: Performance Testing, to see if the image loading is too slow on the lower bandwidth of cellular networks.
Option 3: Functional Testing, to ensure the image fetching logic doesn't have a hard-coded check for Wi-Fi only.
Option 4: Security Testing, to see if the cellular carrier is blocking the encrypted traffic from the app's servers.

Question Text: In the context of "App Quality Assurance," what does "Static Testing" involve?
Option 1: Running the application on a physical device and checking if the UI elements remain static and don't move.
Option 2: Reviewing requirements, design documents, and source code without actually executing the application.
Option 3: Testing the application in an environment where the network and data remain static and do not change.
Option 4: Using a simulator that doesn't simulate hardware sensors, keeping the environment "static" for the app.

Question Text: You are testing a music streaming app. You need to ensure the music continues playing even when the user switches to another app. This is a test of:
Option 1: System Testing (specifically Background Processing) to ensure the service persists as per mobile OS rules.
Option 2: Unit Testing the audio player class to ensure the play() method is called correctly by the UI.
Option 3: Regression Testing, as adding a new playlist feature might have broken the background playback logic.
Option 4: Usability Testing, to see if the user finds it easy to control the music from the notification shade.

Question Text: What is the primary difference between a "Simulator" and an "Emulator" in mobile testing?
Option 1: Simulators mimic the hardware of a device, while Emulators only mimic the software environment of the OS.
Option 2: Emulators mimic both hardware and software, whereas Simulators only mimic the software's internal behavior.
Option 3: Simulators are used only for iOS testing, while Emulators are used exclusively for Android and Windows.
Option 4: There is no difference; the terms are used interchangeably by industry professionals in all documentation.

Question Text: During "Regression Testing," you find a bug in a feature that wasn't even touched in the current sprint. What does this suggest?
Option 1: The developers have accidentally introduced a "side effect" in a shared component or a global library.
Option 2: The QA team is wasting time testing things that are unrelated to the current changes and should stop.
Option 3: The original requirement for that feature was poorly written and has finally been caught by the testers.
Option 4: The testing environment has been corrupted and needs to be wiped and re-installed from scratch.

Question Text: A "Sanity Test" is typically performed:
Option 1: After a major release to the App Store to ensure that the production environment is stable for all users.
Option 2: After receiving a bug fix to verify that the specific bug is fixed and the logic of that module is still sound.
Option 3: Before the start of a project to ensure that the testing team has all the necessary devices and tools.
Option 4: Every morning by the automated build system to check if the code still compiles and the app can boot.

Question Text: Which of the following is a "Non-Functional" requirement for a mobile application?
Option 1: The user should be able to reset their password by clicking the "Forgot Password" link on the login screen.
Option 2: The application must load the user's dashboard in less than 2 seconds over a standard 4G connection.
Option 3: The "Add to Cart" button must change its color to green once an item has been successfully added.
Option 4: The system should send a push notification to the user whenever they receive a new private message.

Question Text: While performing "Compatibility Testing," you find that the app's font size is too small to read on a high-density (QHD) display. This is a:
Option 1: Functional defect, because the user cannot read the text and therefore cannot use the app's features.
Option 2: UI/UX defect related to Screen Density (DPI) handling, which needs to be fixed using scalable units like 'sp'.
Option 3: Performance defect, as the high-resolution screen is likely causing the app to render fonts incorrectly.
Option 4: Regression defect, as the font size was likely correct in the previous version before the UI was updated.

Question Text: You are creating a "Test Case" for a login screen. Which of the following is a "Negative Test Case"?
Option 1: Entering a valid username and a valid password and checking if the user is redirected to the dashboard.
Option 2: Entering a valid username and an incorrect password and checking if the app displays an error message.
Option 3: Clicking the "Show Password" icon and checking if the password text becomes visible to the user.
Option 4: Checking if the "Login" button is disabled until both the username and password fields are filled.

Question Text: In "Mobile Security Testing," what is "Reverse Engineering"?
Option 1: The process of converting the compiled app (APK/IPA) back into a readable source code to find vulnerabilities.
Option 2: The process of testing the app's features in the reverse order of the user flow to find hidden logical bugs.
Option 3: A technique where developers write the test cases first and then write the code to pass those tests.
Option 4: Using an older version of the OS to see if the app's security features are still functional on legacy systems.

Question Text: A "User Story" says: "As a user, I want to upload a profile picture so that others can recognize me." Which test is missing?
Option 1: Testing the upload with a 20MB high-resolution image to see if the app handles large files gracefully.
Option 2: Testing if the user can change their username, as it is a related feature in the "Profile" section.
Option 3: Testing if the app's color scheme matches the company's branding on the profile upload screen.
Option 4: Testing if the "Upload" button has a nice animation when clicked by the user during the process.

Question Text: What is the main benefit of "Continuous Integration" (CI) for a mobile QA team?
Option 1: It allows the testers to manually run all the regression tests every time a developer commits a line of code.
Option 2: It automatically triggers builds and automated tests on every code change, providing fast feedback on quality.
Option 3: It eliminates the need for any manual testing, as the CI system is capable of finding all types of bugs.
Option 4: It provides a central location for storing all the physical mobile devices used by the testing team.

Question Text: During "Usability Testing," several users try to "swipe" to delete an item, but the app only supports "long-press." This is:
Option 1: A Functional Bug, because the swipe action is a standard gesture in mobile apps and must be supported.
Option 2: A Usability Finding, suggesting that the app's gestures are not aligned with standard user expectations.
Option 3: A Compatibility Bug, as swiping might work on iOS devices but not on Android devices due to OS differences.
Option 4: A Performance Issue, because the app is taking too long to recognize the long-press gesture from the user.

Question Text: In "Integration Testing," what is the "Top-Down" approach?
Option 1: Testing the low-level modules first and then moving up to the complex user interfaces and system modules.
Option 2: Testing the high-level UI and main modules first, using "Stubs" to represent the lower-level components.
Option 3: Starting the testing process from the backend database and moving towards the mobile application's UI.
Option 4: Testing the most critical features of the app first, regardless of their position in the software architecture.

Question Text: You are testing an app that uses a lot of data. You need to ensure the app doesn't exceed the user's monthly data limit without warning. This is:
Option 1: Performance Testing, to ensure the app is efficient in its data usage and doesn't waste bandwidth.
Option 2: Functional Testing of the "Data Usage Monitor" and "Alert System" within the application's settings.
Option 3: Security Testing, to ensure the data is not being sent to unauthorized servers without the user's consent.
Option 4: Load Testing the data server to see if it can handle the large amounts of data being sent by the app.

Question Text: What is "Monkey Testing" in the context of mobile application development?
Option 1: A formal testing process where professional testers follow a strict script to find bugs in the application.
Option 2: Using automated tools to send random, unpredictable user inputs to the app to see if it crashes.
Option 3: A type of Usability Testing where people who have never seen a smartphone are asked to use the app.
Option 4: Testing the app on ancient "Legacy" devices to see how it performs on very slow and outdated hardware.

Question Text: A "Bug Life Cycle" typically starts with which status?
Option 1: "In Progress," when a developer starts working on a fix for the defect reported by the QA team.
Option 2: "New" or "Open," when a tester first discovers and documents a discrepancy in the application's behavior.
Option 3: "Fixed," when the developer has successfully resolved the issue and is ready for the tester to verify it.
Option 4: "Closed," when the tester has verified that the bug no longer exists and the feature is working as expected.

Question Text: You are testing a fitness app. You notice that the step counter increases even when you are just shaking the phone while sitting. This is a:
Option 1: Accuracy issue in "Sensor Fusion" logic, requiring better filtering of the accelerometer data.
Option 2: Performance issue, as the app is processing data too quickly and picking up "noise" from the sensor.
Option 3: Compatibility issue, as the accelerometer in this specific phone is more sensitive than in other models.
Option 4: Functional issue, because the app is correctly recording the movement it detects from the hardware.

Question Text: Why is "Test Planning" crucial for a mobile project with a short 2-week release cycle?
Option 1: To ensure that every single line of code is manually tested by at least two different people before release.
Option 2: To define the scope, prioritize critical features, and allocate limited time and device resources effectively.
Option 3: To provide a long document that the developers can read to understand how the app is supposed to work.
Option 4: To delay the start of the testing phase so the developers have more time to finish their features.

Question Text: In "Compatibility Testing," what is a "Device Farm"?
Option 1: A physical location where mobile phones are grown and harvested for use in the testing department.
Option 2: A cloud-based service that provides access to hundreds of real physical devices for remote testing.
Option 3: A specialized software that can simulate multiple different mobile devices on a single desktop computer.
Option 4: A group of testers who all use the same type of device to ensure consistency in their bug reports.

Question Text: You find a bug where the app crashes only when the "Language" is set to "Arabic" (a Right-to-Left language). This is a:
Option 1: Localization and UI Mirroring issue, likely due to improper handling of layout directions in the code.
Option 2: Functional issue, as the app should work the same regardless of the language selected by the user.
Option 3: Security issue, because the Arabic text might be hiding a malicious script that is crashing the app.
Option 4: Performance issue, as rendering Right-to-Left text requires more CPU power than Left-to-Right text.

Question Text: What is the purpose of "Exploratory Testing" in a high-speed Agile environment?
Option 1: To replace all formal test cases, as they take too long to write and maintain in a fast-moving project.
Option 2: To complement scripted testing by finding "unforeseen" bugs that formal test cases might miss.
Option 3: To provide a way for non-testers (like managers) to help find bugs without needing any training.
Option 4: To test the app's features in a random order to see if any "hidden" features can be discovered.

Question Text: You are testing an app's "Push Notifications." You receive the notification, but tapping it takes you to the home screen instead of the specific article. This is:
Option 1: A Deep Linking failure, where the notification payload does not contain the correct routing information.
Option 2: A Performance issue, as the app is taking too long to load the article and defaults to the home screen.
Option 3: A Usability issue, as the user might find it annoying to have to navigate to the article manually.
Option 4: A Compatibility issue, because push notifications work differently on Android than they do on iOS.

Question Text: In "Automated Testing," what is "Parallel Execution"?
Option 1: Running the same test script multiple times in a row on a single device to ensure it is consistent.
Option 2: Running different test scripts on different devices at the same time to reduce the total execution time.
Option 3: Having two different testers run the same manual test case simultaneously to see if they find the same bugs.
Option 4: Running the automated tests while the developer is still writing the code for the feature being tested.

Question Text: You are testing a mobile game. You need to ensure the game doesn't crash when the phone receives an incoming call. This is a:
Option 1: "System Interrupt" test, crucial for mobile apps to ensure they handle OS events gracefully.
Option 2: "Load Test," to see if the phone can handle both the game and the phone call at the same time.
Option 3: "Security Test," to ensure the game doesn't record the phone call without the user's permission.
Option 4: "Usability Test," to see if the user can easily switch between the game and the phone call.

Question Text: What is the "Golden Path" (or Happy Path) in a mobile test plan?
Option 1: The most expensive and difficult path to test, requiring specialized hardware and expert knowledge.
Option 2: The primary, successful sequence of actions a user takes to achieve a goal, without any errors.
Option 3: The path that leads to the most bugs being found by the QA team during the initial testing phase.
Option 4: The sequence of screens that have the most visually appealing design and the best user experience.

Question Text: You are testing a "Photo Editor" app. You need to verify that it can handle images of various formats (JPG, PNG, HEIC) and sizes. This is:
Option 1: Compatibility Testing (File Format) and Functional Testing (Boundary Value Analysis for file sizes).
Option 2: Performance Testing, to see how long it takes the app to load and process a large high-resolution image.
Option 3: Security Testing, to ensure that the app doesn't crash if it's given a corrupted or malicious image file.
Option 4: Usability Testing, to see if the user finds it easy to select and edit images from their device's gallery.

Question Text: A tester uses a "Proxy Tool" (like Charles Proxy or Fiddler) to intercept and modify the app's network traffic. This is a common technique in:
Option 1: Security and API Testing, to check for vulnerabilities like "Man-in-the-Middle" attacks or poor data validation.
Option 2: Performance Testing, to see how the app behaves when the network traffic is delayed or throttled.
Option 3: Usability Testing, to observe how the app's UI changes when different data is received from the server.
Option 4: Regression Testing, to ensure that the app's network requests haven't changed between different versions.

Question Text: In "Unit Testing," what is "Code Coverage"?
Option 1: The percentage of the mobile app's features that are currently covered by at least one manual test case.
Option 2: A metric that measures how many lines or branches of the source code are executed by the automated unit tests.
Option 3: The total number of devices in the "Device Farm" that are currently being used for automated testing.
Option 4: The percentage of the app's UI elements that have been assigned a unique ID for automation purposes.

Question Text: You are testing a "Smart Home" app that controls lights via Bluetooth. You need to verify the connection range. This is:
Option 1: Hardware-Software Integration Testing, requiring physical movement to test signal strength and distance.
Option 2: Compatibility Testing, to see if the app works with different brands of Bluetooth-enabled light bulbs.
Option 3: Performance Testing, to see if there is any lag between clicking the button in the app and the light turning on.
Option 4: Security Testing, to ensure that unauthorized users cannot take control of the lights via Bluetooth.

Question Text: When writing a "Bug Report," why is it important to include "Steps to Reproduce"?
Option 1: To prove to the developer that the tester actually found a bug and didn't just make it up.
Option 2: To allow the developer to follow the exact same path to see the bug for themselves and then fix it.
Option 3: To fill up the bug report with more information so it looks more professional and detailed to management.
Option 4: To provide a "History" of the testing process so that other testers can see what has already been tried.

Question Text: You find that the app's "Sign Up" button is partially covered by the "System Navigation Bar" on phones with "Notches." This is a:
Option 1: UI/UX defect related to "Safe Area" insets, requiring the layout to adjust based on screen hardware.
Option 2: Functional defect, as the user might still be able to click the part of the button that is still visible.
Option 3: Compatibility defect, as the notch is only present on certain newer models of Android and iOS devices.
Option 4: Performance defect, as the app is taking too long to calculate the correct position of the button on the screen.

Question Text: What is "Data-Driven Testing" in mobile automation?
Option 1: A testing approach where the same test script is run multiple times using different sets of input data from a file.
Option 2: A testing approach where the QA team uses data from the app's database to create their manual test cases.
Option 3: A technique where the automation scripts are written in a way that they automatically generate their own test data.
Option 4: A process of collecting data about how users use the app and then using that data to improve the test plan.

Question Text: You are testing an app for a global audience. You need to ensure it uses the correct currency and date formats based on the device's locale. This is:
Option 1: Internationalization (i18n) and Localization (l10n) testing, focused on cultural and regional settings.
Option 2: Compatibility Testing, as different countries use different mobile carriers and network frequencies.
Option 3: Usability Testing, to see if users in different countries find the app's layout and design to be intuitive.
Option 4: Functional Testing, as the app must correctly convert and display the currency and date values.

Question Text: What is the main goal of "Smoke Testing" a new mobile build?
Option 1: To find as many bugs as possible in the new features that were added in the current development cycle.
Option 2: To quickly verify that the most critical functions of the app work and the build is stable enough for further testing.
Option 3: To perform a full regression of the entire application to ensure that no existing features have been broken.
Option 4: To check if the app's "Smoke" animations are working correctly and don't cause any performance issues.

Question Text: While testing a "Video Streaming" app, you notice the audio and video are out of sync after 10 minutes of playback. This is:
Option 1: A Performance/Synchronization issue, possibly related to buffer management or CPU throttling over time.
Option 2: A Functional issue, as the app is not correctly playing the video file as it was intended to be seen.
Option 3: A Compatibility issue, because the sync might be perfect on some devices but not on others with slower processors.
Option 4: A Usability issue, as the user will find it very annoying to watch a video where the audio and video are not synced.

Question Text: In "Mobile App Testing," what is a "Crash Log"?
Option 1: A document that lists all the features that have "crashed" or failed during the current testing cycle.
Option 2: A file generated by the OS when an app terminates unexpectedly, containing the stack trace and state at the time of failure.
Option 3: A list of all the times the testers' computers have crashed while they were trying to run the automated tests.
Option 4: A report that shows how many times the app has been downloaded and installed by users in the last month.

Question Text: You are testing an "Authentication" module. You need to verify that the "Session Token" is invalidated after the user logs out. This is:
Option 1: Security Testing, to prevent "Session Hijacking" where an attacker could use an old token to gain access.
Option 2: Functional Testing, to ensure the logout button works and takes the user back to the login screen.
Option 3: Performance Testing, to see how quickly the server can invalidate the token and update its database.
Option 4: Usability Testing, to see if the user finds it easy to log out of their account from the settings menu.

Question Text: What is "Alpha Testing"?
Option 1: Testing performed by the end-users in their own environment to find any final bugs before the official release.
Option 2: Testing performed by the internal development and QA teams in a controlled environment early in the lifecycle.
Option 3: A type of testing where only the "Alpha" or most important features of the application are being tested.
Option 4: The first time the automated tests are run on a new build of the application to check for major issues.

Question Text: You are testing a "Shopping" app. You need to ensure the "Cart" is saved even if the app is killed by the OS due to low memory. This is:
Option 1: Data Persistence testing, ensuring the app's state is saved to local storage or the cloud at regular intervals.
Option 2: Stress Testing, by manually killing the app many times to see if the cart data eventually gets corrupted.
Option 3: Load Testing, to see if the server can handle saving the cart data for thousands of users at the same time.

Question Text: What is "Idempotency Key" in API design?
Option 1: A unique identifier sent by the client to ensure that a request is processed only once by the server.
Option 2: A special password that the user must enter every time they want to delete a resource from the API.
Option 3: A cryptographic key used to encrypt the entire body of a JSON request for security purposes.
Option 4: A value that determines the order in which a client should call the different endpoints of an API.

Question Text: What is "Content Delivery Network" (CDN)?
Option 1: A group of developers who manually deliver physical hard drives to customers around the world.
Option 2: A geographically distributed group of servers which work together to provide fast delivery of Internet content.
Option 3: A specialized type of network cable that is used to connect servers inside a single data center.
Option 4: A television channel that broadcasts news about the latest updates in the world of microservices.

Question Text: What is "Resource Quota" in Kubernetes?
Option 1: The maximum number of hours a developer is allowed to spend working on Kubernetes each week.
Option 2: Constraints that limit aggregate resource consumption per namespace in a Kubernetes cluster.
Option 3: A rule that says every pod must use at least 10GB of RAM, even if it doesn't need it.
Option 4: The total number of servers that a company is allowed to buy from a cloud provider like AWS.

Question Text: What is "Ambient Mesh" in Istio?
Option 1: A new Istio data plane mode that does not require sidecars for every single application pod.
Option 2: A decorative pattern that is painted on the walls of the data center to make it look more modern.
Option 3: A type of network cable that changes color based on the amount of traffic flowing through it.
Option 4: A security feature that requires all developers to wear a special mesh vest while in the office.

Question Text: What is "Semantic Monitoring"?
Option 1: Monitoring a system by running a subset of the application's business logic against it to verify correctness.
Option 2: A process of checking the spelling and grammar of all the log messages generated by a service.
Option 3: A type of monitoring that only tracks the names of the services and ignores their performance metrics.
Option 4: A tool that automatically translates the monitoring dashboard into 50 different world languages.

Question Text: A startup needs to deploy a simple static landing page with global reach and low latency without managing any virtual servers or complex networking. Which approach is most efficient?
Option 1: Host the static files on a Cloud Storage bucket (like S3 or GCS) and distribute them via a Content Delivery Network (CDN).
Option 2: Provision a small Virtual Machine instance with an Nginx server to serve the static HTML, CSS, and JS files manually.
Option 3: Deploy a Kubernetes cluster to manage the containerized version of the static site to ensure high availability and scaling.
Option 4: Use a Backend-as-a-Service (BaaS) provider to build the landing page using a drag-and-drop interface with integrated logic.

Question Text: During a traffic surge, your web application's frontend is responsive, but users report that form submissions are failing or taking too long to process. What is the most likely bottleneck?
Option 1: The client-side JavaScript bundle is too large and is taking too long for the browser to parse and execute during the surge.
Option 2: The backend API or database is unable to handle the concurrent write requests, leading to timeouts or connection pool exhaustion.
Option 3: The User Interface (UI) lacks a loading spinner, causing users to click the submit button multiple times and flooding the network.
Option 4: The CSS media queries are not optimized for mobile devices, causing the layout to break and preventing successful form interactions.

Question Text: You are tasked with improving the security of a Cloud-Based Web App that currently stores user passwords in plain text within a relational database. What is the industry-standard fix?
Option 1: Encrypt the passwords using a symmetric encryption algorithm like AES-256 and store the key in a local environment file.
Option 2: Hash the passwords using a strong, salted, one-way cryptographic algorithm like Argon2 or bcrypt before storing them in the database.
Option 3: Implement a client-side JavaScript function to mask the password field so that it is not visible to anyone looking at the screen.
Option 4: Move the database to a private subnet in the cloud so that it is not accessible from the public internet, keeping the text plain.

Question Text: A developer is choosing between a Relational (SQL) and a Non-Relational (NoSQL) database for a project involving complex, deeply nested social media post data with varying structures. Which is better?
Option 1: SQL, because it enforces a strict schema that ensures data integrity and makes it easier to perform complex JOIN operations.
Option 2: NoSQL (Document Store), because its flexible schema allows for storing heterogeneous data structures without migrations.
Option 3: SQL, because it is inherently faster at horizontal scaling than NoSQL databases when dealing with high-velocity write operations.
Option 4: NoSQL (Key-Value), because it provides the strongest consistency models required for social media interactions and comments.

Question Text: When implementing an API for a mobile app, you need to ensure that the backend does not get overwhelmed by too many requests from a single malicious user. Which mechanism should you use?
Option 1: Implement Rate Limiting or Throttling at the API Gateway level to restrict the number of requests a user can make per minute.
Option 2: Increase the instance size of the backend server to ensure it has enough CPU and RAM to handle any amount of incoming traffic.
Option 3: Use a different URL for the mobile app API so that web users cannot find it and accidentally contribute to the traffic load.
Option 4: Rewrite the backend logic in a lower-level language like C++ to increase the raw processing speed of individual API requests.

Question Text: You are designing a system where users upload large video files that need to be transcoded into different formats. Which architecture is most "cloud-native" and scalable?
Option 1: Process the video on the main web server immediately after upload to ensure the user gets the result as fast as possible.
Option 2: Save the video to cloud storage, trigger an asynchronous Serverless function or background job via a Message Queue for processing.
Option 3: Block the user's browser session until the backend finishes the transcoding process to ensure the data is fully processed.
Option 4: Store the videos in the database as Binary Large Objects (BLOBs) and use a database trigger to initiate the transcoding.

Question Text: An application is experiencing "Slow Boot" times when scaling out new instances in a serverless environment (Cold Starts). How can a developer mitigate this for a Java-based API?
Option 1: Increase the memory allocation for the function, as cloud providers often allocate more CPU power proportionally with memory.
Option 2: Rewrite the entire application in a more complex language like Assembly to ensure the binary size is as small as possible.
Option 3: Disable all logging and monitoring within the function to reduce the amount of code that needs to be loaded during initialization.
Option 4: Hard-code all database credentials and API keys into the source code to avoid the overhead of fetching them from a secret manager.

Question Text: Your team is practicing DevOps and wants to ensure that every code change is automatically tested and deployed to a staging environment. What is this process called?
Option 1: Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment (CI/CD), which automates the build, test, and release phases of development.
Option 2: Manual Quality Assurance (QA), where a dedicated team of testers checks the code before it is manually moved to production.
Option 3: Waterfall Model, where each phase of the project is completed in a linear sequence before moving to the next deployment step.
Option 4: Hot-swapping, where developers directly edit the production code on the live server to fix bugs as they are reported by users.

Question Text: A web app needs to provide real-time updates for a stock market dashboard without the user refreshing the page. Which technology is most appropriate for bi-directional communication?
Option 1: WebSockets, which provide a persistent, full-duplex communication channel between the client's browser and the backend server.
Option 2: Long Polling, where the client repeatedly sends HTTP requests to the server to check for new data at short, fixed intervals.
Option 3: HTTP GET requests triggered by a setInterval timer in JavaScript to fetch the latest data from a RESTful API endpoint.
Option 4: Server-Side Rendering (SSR), where the entire page is re-generated on the server and sent to the client every time data changes.

Question Text: To optimize the performance of a global web application, you want to cache frequently accessed but rarely changed data close to the user. Where should this cache live?
Option 1: On an Edge Location or Content Delivery Network (CDN) to reduce the physical distance and network hops the data must travel.
Option 2: In the primary relational database's internal cache to ensure that the data is always consistent with the latest updates.
Option 3: On the user's local hard drive using the File System API to ensure that the application can work entirely offline if needed.
Option 4: In the server's RAM as a global variable, so that every request to that specific instance can access the data instantly.

Question Text: Your application experiences a massive read-heavy load during sales events, causing the primary relational database to slow down significantly. What is the most cost-effective architectural change?
Option 1: Implement Read Replicas of the database to offload query traffic from the primary instance while keeping the primary for write operations.
Option 2: Scale up the primary database instance to the largest available hardware tier to handle the combined read and write traffic on one node.
Option 3: Migrate the entire database to a NoSQL architecture overnight to take advantage of inherent horizontal scaling capabilities of document stores.
Option 4: Disable all foreign key constraints and indexing in the production database to reduce the overhead during high-traffic read periods.

Question Text: A developer needs to ensure that sensitive environment variables like API keys and database passwords are not exposed in the version control system (Git). What is the best practice?
Option 1: Use a dedicated Secret Management service (like AWS Secrets Manager or HashiCorp Vault) and inject variables at runtime during deployment.
Option 2: Commit a ".env" file to the public repository but use a very complex naming convention for the keys so that unauthorized users cannot guess them.
Option 3: Hard-code the secrets directly into the source code but use a private repository so that only authorized team members can see the credentials.
Option 4: Print the secrets to the console logs during the application startup so that developers can verify they are being loaded correctly in production.

Question Text: When designing a microservices architecture, how should services communicate to ensure that a failure in one service does not immediately crash the others (Cascading Failure)?
Option 1: Use an asynchronous Message Broker (like RabbitMQ or SNS/SQS) to decouple the services and allow for retries and eventual consistency.
Option 2: Use synchronous REST calls for every interaction to ensure that the data is always perfectly synchronized across all services at all times.
Option 3: Increase the timeout settings on all HTTP clients to 60 seconds so that services wait longer for a response before reporting an error.
Option 4: Deploy all microservices on a single massive virtual machine so they can share the same memory space and avoid network-related failures.

Question Text: You are using a Serverless function that needs to access a private database located inside a Virtual Private Cloud (VPC). What configuration is required?
Option 1: Configure the Serverless function to run within the same VPC and assign it to the appropriate private subnets and security groups.
Option 2: Open the database's security group to allow all incoming traffic from '0.0.0.0/0' so the serverless function can connect from any public IP.
Option 3: Move the database to a public subnet and give it a public IP address so that it can be reached via the open internet without a VPN.
Option 4: Tunnel the database connection through a third-party proxy service that does not require any VPC or networking configuration.

Question Text: An application requires a persistent storage solution for user profile pictures that are frequently accessed and must be served via the web. Which cloud service is most suitable?
Option 1: Object Storage (like Amazon S3 or Azure Blob Storage) because it is designed for unstructured data and provides high durability and scalability.
Option 2: A Relational Database (RDS) where the image data is converted to Base64 strings and stored in a 'TEXT' or 'BLOB' column in a table.
Option 3: The local ephemeral storage of the web server instance, which is fast and does not require any additional network calls for retrieval.
Option 4: A Distributed Cache like Redis, storing the raw binary data of every image in RAM to ensure the fastest possible page load times for users.

Question Text: To improve User Experience (UX), a developer wants to implement "Optimistic UI" updates for a social media "Like" button. What does this technique involve?
Option 1: Updating the UI locally to show the "Liked" state immediately before the backend server confirms that the API call was successful.
Option 2: Waiting for the backend to return a 200 OK response and then refreshing the entire page to show the updated like count to the user.
Option 3: Disabling the button after the first click to prevent the user from clicking it again until the server responds with a success message.
Option 4: Showing a full-screen loading overlay that prevents any other user interaction until the database write operation is fully completed.

Question Text: Your CI/CD pipeline fails during the 'Build' stage because of a dependency conflict. What is the most effective way to ensure consistent environments across Dev, Staging, and Production?
Option 1: Use Containerization (like Docker) to package the application and its dependencies into a single image that runs identically in any environment.
Option 2: Write a detailed 50-page manual for developers explaining exactly which versions of Node.js or Python they must install on their machines.
Option 3: Delete the 'node_modules' or 'venv' folder on the production server and let the server download the latest available packages during every boot.
Option 4: Use a shared remote desktop where all developers log in to the same machine to write and test their code in a single environment.

Question Text: A globally distributed application is experiencing high latency for users in Europe, while the backend is hosted in North America. What is the best solution?
Option 1: Deploy the application in multiple Cloud Regions and use a Latency-based Routing policy in the DNS settings to direct users to the nearest node.
Option 2: Upgrade the North American server to use a faster Fiber Optic connection to the internet to reduce the time it takes for packets to travel.
Option 3: Tell the European users to use a VPN that has a server located in North America to make their connection appear local to the application.
Option 4: Compress all the HTML and JavaScript files into a single ZIP folder that the user must download and extract before viewing the application.

Question Text: When performing a "Blue-Green" deployment, what is the primary benefit of this strategy regarding risk management and application downtime?
Option 1: It allows for near-zero downtime and instant rollback by switching traffic between two identical environments (one live, one new).
Option 2: It reduces the cost of cloud infrastructure by only running one environment at a time and deleting the old one before starting the new one.
Option 3: It automatically fixes bugs in the source code by comparing the 'Blue' version with the 'Green' version and selecting the best logic.
Option 4: It ensures that the database schema is automatically migrated and backward compatible without any intervention from the DBA team.

Question Text: A web application needs to implement OAuth 2.0 for "Login with Google" functionality. Which component is responsible for issuing the Access Token after the user approves?
Option 1: The Authorization Server (Google's Identity Provider), which verifies the user's credentials and the application's request for access.
Option 2: The Client-side Browser, which generates a secure token using a random number generator and sends it to the backend for storage.
Option 3: The Application's Backend Database, which creates a new row in the 'tokens' table and sends the ID back to the Google API for validation.
Option 4: The User's Internet Service Provider (ISP), which intercepts the login request and provides a secure handshake between the two parties.

Question Text: A developer is integrating a third-party payment gateway that uses webhooks to notify the app about successful transactions. How should the application securely verify these incoming requests?
Option 1: Check for a cryptographic signature in the request headers provided by the gateway and verify it using a shared secret key.
Option 2: Rely solely on the source IP address of the request to ensure it is coming from a known range of the payment provider's servers.
Option 3: Assume any request sent to the /webhook endpoint is valid as long as the payload contains a valid transaction ID from the database.
Option 4: Use a basic username and password in the URL query parameters of the webhook endpoint to authenticate the payment provider.

Question Text: When building a RESTful API, you realize that a GET request for a 'User' object returns 50 fields, but the mobile app only needs 3. What is the most standard way to solve this in REST?
Option 1: Implement field filtering using query parameters (e.g., ?fields=name,email) to allow the client to request only the specific data it needs.
Option 2: Create 50 different API endpoints, one for each specific field of the User object, so the client can call only the ones they need.
Option 3: Ignore the extra data as modern mobile networks are fast enough to handle large JSON payloads without impacting the user experience.
Option 4: Compress the entire JSON response using GZIP at the server level so that even with 50 fields, the payload size is significantly smaller.

Question Text: Your application is susceptible to Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) attacks. Which of the following is the most effective mitigation for a web app using cookie-based sessions?
Option 1: Implement Anti-CSRF tokens that are unique per session and must be sent by the client in a custom header for all state-changing requests.
Option 2: Encrypt the entire body of every HTTP request so that an attacker cannot see what data is being sent to the server from the browser.
Option 3: Use a very short session timeout of 5 minutes so that an attacker has a limited window of time to perform a CSRF attack on the user.
Option 4: Shift from using Cookies to using LocalStorage for session storage, as browsers automatically prevent all scripts from reading LocalStorage data.

Question Text: A team needs to build a search feature that allows users to query millions of products with complex filters and full-text search capabilities. Which database technology is most appropriate?
Option 1: A Search Engine like Elasticsearch or Solr, which uses inverted indexing to provide high-performance full-text search and complex filtering.
Option 2: A standard Relational Database (like PostgreSQL) using the LIKE operator with wildcard characters for every search query performed by the user.
Option 3: A Key-Value store like Redis, storing every possible search combination as a unique key with the results as the corresponding value.
Option 4: A flat CSV file stored in a cloud bucket that the application downloads and parses in memory every time a user performs a search.

Question Text: In a serverless environment, you have a function that frequently times out because it waits for a long-running external API. What is the best architectural refactor to handle this?
Option 1: Use a "Task Queue" or "Job Pattern" where the function triggers the task and the user is notified later via a WebSocket or Polling.
Option 2: Increase the timeout setting of the serverless function to its maximum limit (e.g., 15 minutes) to ensure it always finishes the task.
Option 3: Run the long-running task in a loop within the frontend browser using JavaScript until the external API finally returns a successful result.
Option 4: Provision a high-CPU virtual machine instance to run the task, as the extra processing power will make the external API respond faster.

Question Text: To prevent Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attacks in a React or Vue.js application, what is the most important practice when rendering user-generated content?
Option 1: Ensure that all user input is properly sanitized or escaped, and avoid using functions like dangerouslySetInnerHTML without extreme caution.
Option 2: Install a firewall on the user's computer to block any malicious scripts from being downloaded from the internet into the browser.
Option 3: Use only GET requests for all application features so that no data is ever sent to the server that could contain a malicious script.
Option 4: Encode the entire frontend source code into a binary format so that an attacker cannot read the logic and find potential XSS vulnerabilities.

Question Text: You are designing a system that must be "Highly Available" across different geographical locations even if an entire cloud region goes offline. What is the best strategy?
Option 1: Implement a Multi-Region architecture with a Global Load Balancer that can automatically failover traffic to a healthy secondary region.
Option 2: Store all data on a single high-performance physical server in a high-security data center and use a very fast backup generator for power.
Option 3: Set up a "Multi-Cloud" strategy where the frontend is on AWS and the backend is on Azure, assuming both clouds won't fail at the exact same time.
Option 4: Buy more domain names and point them to different IP addresses so that users can manually try a different URL if the main one is down.

Question Text: When using JWT (JSON Web Tokens) for authentication, where is the most secure place to store the token on the client side to prevent XSS-based theft?
Option 1: In an HttpOnly and Secure Cookie, which prevents client-side JavaScript from accessing the token and ensures it is only sent over HTTPS.
Option 2: In the browser's localStorage, because it is easy to access via JavaScript and persists even after the user closes the browser window.
Option 3: As a global variable in the JavaScript code so that it is cleared from memory as soon as the user refreshes the page or navigates away.
Option 4: In the URL as a query parameter for every request, so the backend can easily extract it without needing to parse any complex headers.

Question Text: A developer wants to implement a "Dark Mode" feature that persists even after the user logs out and logs in from a different device. Where should the state be stored?
Option 1: In the backend database as a user preference setting, which is fetched upon login and applied to the frontend theme configuration.
Option 2: In the browser's sessionStorage, because it is fast to access and automatically clears when the user closes the browser tab or window.
Option 3: In a local JSON file on the user's desktop, which the web application prompts the user to upload every time they visit the site.
Option 4: In the application's CSS file using a media query that detects the time of day and automatically switches the theme to dark at night.

Question Text: Your API is being abused by bots that are scraping data at an unsustainable rate. You want to block them without affecting real users. What is the most effective tool?
Option 1: A Web Application Firewall (WAF) with bot-protection rules that can identify and block traffic based on behavioral patterns and signatures.
Option 2: A JavaScript "alert" box that asks the user if they are a bot, and only allows them to proceed if they click the "No" button in the popup.
Option 3: Changing the API endpoint names every hour so that the bots cannot find the data, and updating the frontend code to match the new names.
Option 4: Reducing the server's bandwidth to 1Mbps so that the bots take much longer to download the data, effectively slowing down their scraping rate.

Question Text: When migrating a monolithic application to microservices, you find that data is now scattered across multiple databases. How do you handle a "Join" across services?
Option 1: Implement an API Gateway or a specialized service that aggregates data from multiple microservices and returns a single unified response.
Option 2: Direct the frontend to make 10 separate API calls to 10 different services and then perform the complex data joining logic in the user's browser.
Option 3: Give every microservice direct read-access to every other microservice's private database to allow for standard SQL JOIN queries.
Option 4: Merge all the microservice databases back into one single large database to simplify the query logic while keeping the code separate.

Question Text: A startup wants to use "Infrastructure as Code" (IaC) to manage their cloud resources. What is the primary advantage of this approach over manual configuration?
Option 1: It allows for version-controlled, repeatable, and automated deployment of infrastructure, reducing the risk of human error and configuration drift.
Option 2: It makes the cloud resources run 50% faster because the code is compiled into machine language before being sent to the cloud provider.
Option 3: It eliminates the need for any security settings, as the code itself is inherently secure and cannot be hacked once it is deployed.
Option 4: It allows developers to use their favorite programming language to write the frontend of the application while the backend is generated.

Question Text: You are using an Object Storage service (like S3) and want to give a user temporary permission to upload a file directly without making your bucket public. How?
Option 1: Generate a "Pre-signed URL" that grants limited-time write access to a specific object path without requiring the user to have cloud credentials.
Option 2: Temporarily change the bucket policy to 'Public Read/Write' and then change it back to 'Private' once the user confirms they have finished.
Option 3: Ask the user to send their file to you via email, and then manually upload it to the cloud bucket using your administrator credentials.
Option 4: Give the user your root cloud account's username and password so they can log in to the console and upload the file to the bucket.

Question Text: A web app needs to perform a heavy calculation that takes 30 seconds. To keep the UI responsive, where should this logic ideally reside?
Option 1: In a background worker or a serverless function, with the frontend using a loading state or a progress bar to inform the user.
Option 2: In the main thread of the browser using a while(true) loop until the calculation is complete to ensure the user stays on the page.
Option 3: Inside a CSS animation keyframe, because modern browsers use the GPU to render animations, making the calculation much faster.
Option 4: In a synchronous SQL stored procedure that blocks the database connection until the calculation is finished and the result is returned.

Question Text: What is the purpose of a "Health Check" endpoint (e.g., /health) in a cloud-based web application managed by a Load Balancer?
Option 1: To allow the Load Balancer to verify if the instance is functioning correctly and automatically remove it from the rotation if it fails.
Option 2: To provide a dashboard for the users to see how much CPU and RAM the application is currently using on the server in real-time.
Option 3: To allow the developers to remotely restart the server by sending a specific 'POST' request to that endpoint whenever a bug is found.
Option 4: To act as a honeypot for hackers so that they waste their time attacking a fake endpoint while the real application stays secure.

Question Text: Your team is using a "Canary Deployment" strategy. How does this differ from a standard "Rolling Update" deployment?
Option 1: A Canary deployment sends a small percentage of traffic to the new version first to test stability before rolling it out to everyone.
Option 2: A Canary deployment involves taking the entire site offline for 2 hours to perform a deep-clean of the database before the new version starts.
Option 3: A Canary deployment uses a different programming language for the new version to see if it performs better than the old version's language.
Option 4: A Canary deployment is only used for experimental features that are intended to be deleted after 24 hours regardless of their performance.

Question Text: Why is it considered a security risk to return detailed stack traces in an API's error response (500 Internal Server Error) in a production environment?
Option 1: It can leak sensitive information about the application's internal structure, library versions, and database schema to potential attackers.
Option 2: It takes up too much network bandwidth, causing the user's data plan to be exhausted quickly by large error messages from the server.
Option 3: Stack traces are written in a specific font that is not supported by all browsers, causing the UI to crash when the error is displayed.
Option 4: It makes the API documentation look messy because the error responses don't match the expected JSON schema defined in the Swagger file.

Question Text: A web app uses a "Micro-frontend" architecture. What is the primary goal of this specific architectural pattern for a large development team?
Option 1: To allow different teams to work on, deploy, and scale different parts of the user interface independently using different technologies.
Option 2: To reduce the total number of lines of CSS code in the application by sharing a single massive stylesheet across all the different teams.
Option 3: To ensure that the entire application is rendered on a single HTML canvas element to provide a smoother gaming-like user experience.
Option 4: To force all developers to use the same version of the same framework to ensure that the code is completely uniform across the company.

Question Text: When integrating with a GraphQL API, what is the primary purpose of using "Fragments" in your client-side queries?
Option 1: To define reusable sets of fields that can be shared across multiple queries, making the code cleaner and easier to maintain.
Option 2: To split a large query into smaller pieces that are sent over different network connections to improve the speed of the data transfer.
Option 3: To encrypt specific parts of the query so that the GraphQL server cannot see the sensitive fields being requested by the user.
Option 4: To tell the GraphQL server to ignore certain fields if the database is currently under a high load and cannot fulfill the full request.

Question Text: You are troubleshooting a "Memory Leak" in a Node.js backend. Which tool or technique would be most effective in identifying the cause?
Option 1: Taking a Heap Snapshot and comparing it over time to see which objects are growing in memory and not being garbage collected.
Option 2: Increasing the physical RAM of the server every time it crashes until the application eventually has enough memory to never crash again.
Option 3: Adding console.log statements after every line of code to see exactly which line is taking the longest to execute during the leak.
Option 4: Rewriting the entire backend in a language that does not have a garbage collector, like C, so that memory management is manual.

Question Text: You are designing a data archival system for a healthcare provider where records must be kept for 7 years but are almost never accessed. Which storage class is most cost-effective?
Option 1: Archive/Glacier storage, which offers the lowest storage cost but has a longer retrieval time (minutes to hours).
Option 2: Standard Object Storage, which provides instant access to all files but has a higher monthly cost per gigabyte of data.
Option 3: High-performance Block Storage attached to a persistent virtual machine that remains running to serve requests.
Option 4: In-memory caching using Redis to ensure that even 7-year-old records can be retrieved by doctors in under 10 milliseconds.

Question Text: A serverless function is failing because it exceeds its memory limit while processing a 2GB CSV file. What is the most memory-efficient way to handle this?
Option 1: Stream the file from cloud storage and process it line-by-line or in small chunks instead of loading the entire file into the function's RAM.
Option 2: Increase the function's memory limit to the maximum possible setting (e.g., 10GB) so the entire file can be stored in an array for processing.
Option 3: Split the CSV file into 2,000 separate files of 1MB each and trigger 2,000 separate serverless functions to process them simultaneously.
Option 4: Convert the CSV file into a high-resolution image format and use an OCR library to read the data, as image processing uses less memory.

Question Text: Your NoSQL database is experiencing "Hot Partition" issues where a single shard is overloaded because all users from one city have the same partition key. How do you fix this?
Option 1: Redesign the partition key to include a more granular attribute, like a unique User ID or a combination of City and Timestamp.
Option 2: Delete the existing database and move the data back to a single-node SQL database that does not use sharding or partitioning.
Option 3: Ask the users in that specific city to stop using the application during peak hours to reduce the load on that specific database shard.
Option 4: Increase the global write throughput of the entire database cluster until the single overloaded shard can handle the concentrated traffic.

Question Text: A developer wants to ensure that files uploaded to a public S3 bucket cannot be accidentally deleted by anyone, including the account owner. Which feature should they enable?
Option 1: Object Lock in "Compliance Mode," which prevents version deletion for a fixed duration and cannot be bypassed by any user.
Option 2: Bucket Versioning, which keeps a history of all changes but allows the account administrator to delete the entire bucket at any time.
Option 3: Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) Delete, which requires a physical token to be present whenever a user tries to delete a specific file version.
Option 4: Server-side Encryption (SSE-KMS), which makes the files unreadable to unauthorized users but does not actually prevent them from being deleted.

Question Text: You are using a serverless "Function-as-a-Service" (FaaS) model. What happens to the local file system (/tmp) once the function execution is complete and the container is destroyed?
Option 1: The local file system is ephemeral and all data is lost; persistent data must be written to an external database or cloud storage.
Option 2: The cloud provider automatically saves the /tmp folder to a hidden backup bucket and restores it the next time the function is called.
Option 3: The data remains in the physical server's RAM and can be accessed by other users' functions, which is why it is a major security risk.
Option 4: The local file system is automatically synchronized with the developer's local machine via the cloud provider's command-line interface.

Question Text: When implementing a "CQRS" (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) pattern, why are the read and write models often stored in different databases?
Option 1: To allow the read database to be optimized for complex queries (e.g., NoSQL) while the write database remains optimized for transactions (e.g., SQL).
Option 2: To ensure that if the write database crashes, the read database can automatically take over the write operations without any data loss.
Option 3: To comply with international privacy laws that require user 'names' (reads) to be stored in a different country than user 'passwords' (writes).
Option 4: Because modern cloud providers charge less for two small databases than they do for one large database with the same total storage capacity.

Question Text: An e-commerce app uses a serverless function to send order confirmation emails. During a "Flash Sale," the function fails due to API rate limits from the email provider. Fix it?
Option 1: Introduce a Message Queue (like SQS) between the order function and the email function to buffer requests and process them at a controlled rate.
Option 2: Wrap the email sending code in a try-catch block and use a while(true) loop to keep retrying the API call until it eventually succeeds.
Option 3: Increase the number of concurrent serverless functions so that more functions are trying to send emails at the same time during the sale.
Option 4: Switch the email provider to a local SMTP server running on a small Raspberry Pi in the office to avoid external API rate limits entirely.

Question Text: Your application needs to store "Event Sourcing" data. What is the defining characteristic of an Event Store compared to a traditional state-based database?
Option 1: It stores a sequence of immutable state-changing events instead of just the current "snapshot" or final state of an object.
Option 2: It automatically deletes data after 24 hours to ensure that the database remains small and fast for the latest incoming web requests.
Option 3: It only allows 'Update' and 'Delete' operations and strictly forbids 'Insert' operations to maintain the integrity of the existing data.
Option 4: It is a special type of RAM-only database that does not persist data to disk, making it 100 times faster than a standard SQL database.

Question Text: In a serverless architecture, "Function Chaining" (calling one function from another directly) is often discouraged for long workflows. What is the preferred alternative?
Option 1: Use a Workflow Orchestrator (like AWS Step Functions or Azure Logic Apps) to manage state, retries, and parallel execution between functions.
Option 2: Consolidate all the logic from the different functions into one giant "Mega-Function" that runs for 30 minutes to ensure everything finishes.
Option 3: Use a global variable in a shared database that each function updates to signal the next function in the chain to start its execution.
Option 4: Hard-code the IP address of the next function's container into the previous function to ensure the fastest possible network handoff.

Question Text: A database "Read Replica" is falling behind the "Primary" instance (high Replica Lag) during heavy write traffic. How does this affect the application's users?
Option 1: Users might see stale data (e.g., an old balance) if their request is routed to the replica immediately after they performed a write operation.
Option 2: Users will be unable to log in because the replica lag will cause the authentication tokens to become invalid across the entire system.
Option 3: The application will automatically crash with a "500 Internal Server Error" because the primary database will stop accepting new writes.
Option 4: The primary database will slow down its own write speed to match the slow replica, ensuring that the data is always perfectly in sync.

Question Text: You are building a globally distributed NoSQL database. According to the CAP Theorem, if you prioritize "Availability" and "Partition Tolerance," what must you sacrifice?
Option 1: Consistency; some nodes may return slightly older data during a network partition until the system eventually synchronizes.
Option 2: Performance; the system will become extremely slow because every write must be confirmed by every node on the planet before finishing.
Option 3: Security; the database will disable all password checks during a network partition to ensure that users can still access their data.
Option 4: Storage; the database will delete half of its records to save space and ensure that the remaining data can be replicated faster.

Question Text: A serverless function needs to maintain a "warm" connection to a relational database to avoid the overhead of creating a new connection on every request. How?
Option 1: Initialize the database connection object outside the main function handler so that it is reused across multiple "warm" invocations.
Option 2: Use a setInterval timer inside the function code to ping the database every 1 second, even when the function is not being actively called.
Option 3: Disable the cloud provider's "auto-scaling" feature so that only one single instance of the function ever runs at any given time.
Option 4: Write the database password in a text file on the function's local disk so that the connection can be established without a network handshake.

Question Text: Your web app allows users to search for documents. You want to implement "Autocomplete" that is extremely fast (<20ms). Where should the index for autocomplete live?
Option 1: In a Distributed In-Memory Cache like Redis using Sorted Sets or a specialized search service with edge caching enabled.
Option 2: In a standard relational database table using a SELECT * FROM docs WHERE title LIKE '%search%' query on every single keystroke.
Option 3: In a hidden HTML <div> on the frontend that contains the names of every single document in the system, loaded when the user logs in.
Option 4: On a physical DVD that is mailed to the user when they sign up, which the web application reads using a browser-based driver.

Question Text: When scaling a relational database "Vertically," what is the primary limitation you will eventually encounter compared to "Horizontal" scaling?
Option 1: You will eventually hit a physical hardware ceiling (maximum CPU/RAM) and the cost per unit of performance increases exponentially.
Option 2: Vertical scaling requires you to change your entire SQL schema to a NoSQL format, which is a very time-consuming and risky process.
Option 3: Cloud providers do not allow vertical scaling for relational databases; they only allow you to add more replicas (horizontal scaling).
Option 4: Vertical scaling makes the database 100% consistent, which the CAP theorem says is impossible for any modern web application to handle.

Question Text: You are using "Database Sharding" to scale. What is the biggest challenge when you need to perform a query that requires data from two different shards?
Option 1: Cross-shard joins are complex and slow; you usually have to perform multiple queries and merge the data at the application layer.
Option 2: Sharding a database makes it impossible to use primary keys, so you have to identify every row using a randomly generated string.
Option 3: Once a database is sharded, you can no longer use the SQL language and must switch to a custom proprietary query language.
