Option 3: A church that has been in existence for at least one thousand years without changing.
Option 4: A religion that worships giant statues of ancient gods and goddesses.

Question Text: In "Historical Sociology," what is "The Longue Durée"?
Option 1: A French term for a very long bread that was eaten by peasants during the revolution.
Option 2: A perspective that focuses on slow-changing, long-term social structures and trends.
Option 3: The study of how people's lives were shorter in the past than they are today.
Option 4: A method of dating historical artifacts by looking at how long they have been buried.

Question Text: A "Medical Anthropologist" studies "The Social Life of Medicines." What does this mean?
Option 1: How medicines are manufactured in a factory and then shipped to different stores.
Option 2: How the meaning and value of a drug change as it moves through different social contexts.
Option 3: The way different chemicals in a pill interact with each other inside the human body.
Option 4: The study of why some people prefer to take pills while others prefer liquid medicine.

Question Text: In "Sociology of Education," what is "Social Reproduction"?
Option 1: The biological process of having children and raising them to be healthy adults.
Option 2: The way schools help to perpetuate existing social and economic inequalities.
Option 3: The requirement that all students must take a class on how to interact with others.
Option 4: The process of teachers being replaced by new teachers as they reach retirement age.

Question Text: A "Cultural Anthropologist" studies "Reciprocity." What is "Negative Reciprocity"?
Option 1: An exchange where one party tries to get something for as little as possible (like theft).
Option 2: An exchange where people give gifts to each other but neither person is happy about it.
Option 3: A system where people refuse to trade with each other because they are enemies.
Option 4: The process of returning a gift to the person who gave it to you because you don't like it.

Question Text: In "Demography," what is "The Replacement Level Fertility"?
Option 1: The number of children a couple must have to replace themselves in the population.
Option 2: The process of replacing older workers with younger workers as they retire.
Option 3: The rate at which new houses are built to replace older houses that have been torn down.
Option 4: The number of people who move into a country to replace those who have moved out.

Question Text: An "Economic Sociologist" studies "Commodification." What is happening here?
Option 1: Things that were not previously sold (like human organs or water) are given a price.
Option 2: The process of making a product look more attractive so that more people will buy it.
Option 3: The study of how different commodities are transported across the ocean in ships.
Option 4: The legal requirement that all products must have a label showing their ingredients.

Question Text: In "Social Theory," what is "Symbolic Interactionism"?
Option 1: The study of how big social structures like the government affect the lives of individuals.
Option 2: A micro-level theory that focuses on how people create meaning through daily interactions.
Option 3: The belief that symbols like flags are more important than the people they represent.
Option 4: The study of how different symbols are used in advertising to trick people into buying things.

Question Text: A "Visual Anthropologist" uses "Indigenous Media." What is the goal of this?
Option 1: To show indigenous people how to use modern technology to watch Hollywood movies.
Option 2: To give indigenous groups the tools to represent their own culture and perspectives.
Option 3: To study how indigenous people are portrayed in mainstream news and television.
Option 4: To sell indigenous art and music to a global audience for the highest possible price.

Question Text: In "Criminology," what is "White-Collar Crime"?
Option 1: Crimes committed by people of high social status in the course of their occupation.
Option 2: Crimes that involve stealing white clothing or other luxury items from a store.
Option 3: Crimes that are committed in the winter when there is a lot of white snow on the ground.
Option 4: The study of how people who work in offices are more likely to be victims of crime.

Question Text: A "Physical Anthropologist" looks at "Clines." What are they measuring?
Option 1: The different types of tools that were used by early humans in different parts of the world.
Option 2: The gradual change in a biological trait (like skin color) across a geographic area.
Option 3: The speed at which a person can climb a mountain at different stages of their life.
Option 4: The number of different languages that are spoken in a single geographic region.

Question Text: In "Urban Sociology," what is "Suburbanization"?
Option 1: The process of turning a large city into a series of smaller, independent villages.
Option 2: The movement of people from the central city to the surrounding residential areas.
Option 3: The study of how people live in underground houses to save space in a crowded city.
Option 4: The trend of building more parks and gardens in the middle of a very busy city.

Question Text: A "Medical Sociologist" studies "The Health Belief Model." What does this model predict?
Option 1: Which people are most likely to become doctors based on their family background.
Option 2: Whether a person will take action to prevent or treat a disease based on their perceptions.
Option 3: The total number of people who will get sick during a specific time of the year.
Option 4: The amount of money a government should spend on building new hospitals and clinics.

Question Text: In "Sociology of Family," what is "Kinship"?
Option 1: The legal documents that prove a person is related to someone else in their family.
Option 2: A social network of people who are related by blood, marriage, or adoption.
Option 3: The feeling of being "kin" or close friends with someone who is not a relative.
Option 4: The study of how different animals take care of their young in the wild.

Question Text: A "Linguistic Anthropologist" studies "Language Revitalization." What is the objective?
Option 1: To teach everyone in the world to speak a single, universal language like Esperanto.
Option 2: To prevent a language from dying out by teaching it to new generations of speakers.
Option 3: To find the original language that was spoken by the very first human beings.
Option 4: To translate all the famous books of the world into as many languages as possible.

Question Text: In "Political Sociology," what is "Social Movement Theory" concerned with?
Option 1: The way people move from one social class to another during their lifetime.
Option 2: Why and how groups of people organize to bring about or resist social change.
Option 3: The study of how different types of exercise can improve the health of a society.
Option 4: The way the government moves people from one part of the country to another.

Question Text: In a clinical intake session, a client describes persistent feelings of worthlessness and a loss of interest in activities for three weeks. Which immediate action aligns with the standard biopsychosocial assessment protocol?
Option 1: Administer a standardized depression inventory to quantify symptom severity.
Option 2: Immediately prescribe a low-dose SSRI to manage the symptoms.
Option 3: Advise the client to take a vacation to reduce environmental stress.
Option 4: Refer the client to a neurologist for an MRI to check for structural brain changes.

Question Text: An Industrial-Organizational psychologist is hired to reduce high turnover in a tech firm. Which research-backed intervention would most likely address intrinsic motivation?
Option 1: Implementing a "Top Performer" monetary bonus system based on monthly sales.
Option 2: Redesigning roles to increase employee autonomy and task significance.
Option 3: Increasing the frequency of mandatory team-building retreats on weekends.
Option 4: Installing high-end coffee machines and gaming zones in the common areas.

Question Text: During a Social Psychology study on conformity, a participant notices others giving the wrong answer. According to Asch’s findings, what factor would most significantly decrease the likelihood of the participant conforming?
Option 1: Increasing the group size from three members to seven members.
Option 2: Having one other person in the group provide the correct answer.
Option 3: Making the task more difficult and the stimulus more ambiguous.
Option 4: Ensuring all group members are of a higher perceived social status.

Question Text: A developmental psychologist is observing a 4-year-old child who believes that because they can see a toy, everyone else in the room can see it too, regardless of their position. This demonstrates which Piagetian concept?
Option 1: The lack of object permanence regarding hidden physical items.
Option 2: The concept of conservation of volume and mass in liquids.
Option 3: Egocentrism, characteristic of the preoperational stage of development.
Option 4: Concrete operational logic applied to spatial reasoning tasks.

Question Text: A Cognitive Psychologist is designing a user interface for a safety-critical monitoring system. To minimize "attentional blink" and ensure signals are not missed, the designer should:
Option 1: Ensure critical signals are spaced at least 500 milliseconds apart.
Option 2: Place all important icons in the peripheral vision area of the screen.
Option 3: Use only one color for all alerts to avoid distracting the operator.
Option 4: Increase the speed of rapid serial visual presentation of the data.

Question Text: In a Forensic Psychology context, a psychologist is asked to assess a defendant's competency to stand trial. What is the primary focus of this specific evaluation?
Option 1: Determining if the defendant suffered from a mental defect at the time of the crime.
Option 2: Evaluating the defendant's current ability to understand the legal proceedings.
Option 3: Predicting the likelihood of the defendant committing future violent acts.
Option 4: Deciding the appropriate rehabilitative sentence for the convicted individual.

Question Text: A Health Psychologist is working with a patient who has a chronic heart condition but refuses to quit smoking. Using the Transtheoretical Model, if the patient says "I know it's bad, but I'm not ready to think about quitting," they are in which stage?
Option 1: The Action stage, where they are actively trying to reduce cigarette count.
Option 2: The Precontemplation stage, where there is no intention to take action.
Option 3: The Maintenance stage, where they have already quit but feel a relapse.
Option 4: The Preparation stage, where they are looking for resources to quit.

Question Text: A Biopsychologist is studying the effects of chronic stress on the brain. Which structural change is most commonly observed in the hippocampus following prolonged exposure to high cortisol levels?
Option 1: An increase in the density of dendritic spines in the prefrontal cortex.
Option 2: Significant atrophy and reduction in volume of hippocampal neurons.
Option 3: The rapid growth of the amygdala leading to better emotional regulation.
Option 4: Improved myelination of the axons connecting the two hemispheres.

Question Text: In Sports Psychology, an athlete experiences "choking" during high-stakes competitions. A psychologist suggests "quiet eye" training. What is the primary mechanism of this intervention?
Option 1: Teaching the athlete to close their eyes and visualize success before a play.
Option 2: Extending the final ocular fixation on a target to improve motor control.
Option 3: Encouraging the athlete to ignore the crowd by focusing on a distant point.
Option 4: Using auditory cues to distract the athlete from internal physiological stress.

Question Text: A Neuropsychologist is evaluating a patient who can speak fluently but the sentences make no sense and they cannot understand spoken language. Damage is likely in:
Option 1: Broca’s area, located in the posterior portion of the frontal lobe.
Option 2: Wernicke’s area, located in the superior temporal gyrus of the left hemisphere.
Option 3: The basal ganglia, responsible for the coordination of motor speech.
Option 4: The primary visual cortex, responsible for interpreting non-verbal cues.

Question Text: An Educational Psychologist wants to apply "scaffolding" in a classroom setting. Which action by the teacher best exemplifies this Lev Vygotsky-inspired technique?
Option 1: Giving students a final exam without any prior practice or hints.
Option 2: Providing temporary support that is gradually removed as the student gains mastery.
Option 3: Grouping students by their IQ scores to ensure uniform learning speeds.
Option 4: Using a strict reward-and-punishment system to manage classroom behavior.

Question Text: A Counseling Psychologist is working with a couple. The therapist focuses on identifying and changing the "demand-withdraw" pattern in their communication. This approach is most likely:
Option 1: Based on psychoanalytic theories focusing on childhood trauma.
Option 2: A behavioral intervention aimed at reinforcing positive speech patterns.
Option 3: A systems-based approach focusing on the dynamics of the interaction.
Option 4: A biological approach looking for hormonal imbalances in the partners.

Question Text: In Personality Psychology, a researcher uses the "Big Five" model. A candidate scores very high on "Conscientiousness." What workplace behavior is this score most likely to predict?
Option 1: The tendency to be outgoing and seek social stimulation during breaks.
Option 2: The likelihood of being organized, dependable, and disciplined in tasks.
Option 3: The ability to remain calm and resilient under high-pressure situations.
Option 4: The inclination to be creative and open to unconventional ideas.

Question Text: An Evolutionary Psychologist is explaining why humans have a universal preference for sweet and fatty foods. What is the most likely adaptive explanation provided?
Option 1: Humans evolved to prefer these foods because they were scarce and energy-dense.
Option 2: Sweet foods were historically used as a primary currency in ancient trade.
Option 3: Fatty foods were preferred because they prevented the development of allergies.
Option 4: These preferences are purely cultural and have no biological or evolutionary basis.

Question Text: In Community Psychology, a practitioner wants to implement "primary prevention." Which of the following programs would be the best example of this approach?
Option 1: Providing intensive therapy for individuals already diagnosed with PTSD.
Option 2: Opening a crisis center for victims of domestic violence to seek immediate aid.
Option 3: Implementing a city-wide nutrition and exercise program in all public schools.
Option 4: Running a rehabilitation clinic for long-term drug users to prevent relapse.

Question Text: A Positive Psychologist is designing an intervention to increase "flow" in the workplace. According to Csikszentmihalyi, what is a necessary condition for achieving a flow state?
Option 1: The task must be extremely easy so the worker never feels any stress.
Option 2: There must be a balance between the challenge of the task and the person's skills.
Option 3: The worker must be constantly interrupted by feedback from their supervisor.
Option 4: The task must be performed in a high-traffic, loud environment to boost arousal.

Question Text: A Quantitative Psychologist is checking the "Internal Consistency" of a new 50-item personality scale. Which statistical measure is most appropriate for this specific purpose?
Option 1: Pearson’s r correlation between the scale and an external criterion.
Option 2: Cronbach’s Alpha, to see how well the items on the test correlate with each other.
Option 3: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) to compare the means of different groups.
Option 4: The Chi-square test to determine the goodness of fit for categorical data.

Question Text: In Environmental Psychology, a researcher finds that "crowding" in an office leads to decreased performance. What is the psychological distinction between "density" and "crowding"?
Option 1: Density is the physical number of people; crowding is the subjective feeling of too little space.
Option 2: Crowding is the physical measure of square footage; density is the social impact.
Option 3: There is no distinction; both terms refer to the number of people per unit area.
Option 4: Density refers to the noise level, while crowding refers to the lack of privacy.

Question Text: A Comparative Psychologist is studying "Theory of Mind" in non-human primates. Which experimental setup would best test if a chimpanzee understands another's perspective?
Option 1: Seeing if the chimpanzee can use a stick to reach a piece of fruit.
Option 2: Checking if the chimpanzee hides food from a competitor who cannot see the hiding spot.
Option 3: Measuring the chimpanzee's reaction to their own reflection in a mirror.
Option 4: Training the chimpanzee to use sign language to request different types of food.

Question Text: A Behavioral Psychologist is using "Systematic Desensitization" to treat a phobia. What is the underlying principle that makes this counter-conditioning technique effective?
Option 1: Flooding the patient with the feared stimulus until they are too exhausted to react.
Option 2: Associating a deep relaxation response with a gradually increasing hierarchy of fears.
Option 3: Providing a monetary reward every time the patient looks at the feared object.
Option 4: Explaining the irrationality of the fear until the patient cognitively accepts it.

Question Text: In Abnormal Psychology, a clinician is distinguishing between Bipolar I and Bipolar II. What is the definitive clinical difference regarding the "manic" phase?
Option 1: Bipolar I requires a full manic episode; Bipolar II involves only hypomania.
Option 2: Bipolar II requires a full manic episode; Bipolar I involves only hypomania.
Option 3: Bipolar I is defined by rapid cycling, while Bipolar II is defined by seasonal onset.
Option 4: Bipolar II involves hallucinations, while Bipolar I is strictly mood-based.

Question Text: A Forensic Psychologist is analyzing a "false confession." Which interrogation technique is most likely to lead an innocent person to internalize a crime they did not commit?
Option 1: Presenting the suspect with false evidence or "failed" polygraph results.
Option 2: Allowing the suspect to have a lawyer present during all questioning phases.
Option 3: Using a "good cop" who offers the suspect a glass of water and a break.
Option 4: Recording the entire interview to ensure all legal procedures are followed.

Question Text: An Environmental Psychologist suggests "Biophilic Design" for a hospital. Which feature is a hallmark of this approach to improve patient recovery rates?
Option 1: Using sterile, white walls and bright fluorescent lighting to ensure cleanliness.
Option 2: Integrating natural elements like plants, water, and natural light into the ward.
Option 3: Reducing the number of windows to prevent outside noise from disturbing patients.
Option 4: Utilizing high-tech, metallic finishes on all furniture to appear modern.

Question Text: In Psychometrics, a "Speed Test" differs from a "Power Test" primarily because in a Speed Test:
Option 1: The items are so difficult that no one is expected to get them all right.
Option 2: The items are relatively easy but the time limit is strictly enforced.
Option 3: The test measures physical reaction time rather than cognitive ability.
Option 4: The scoring is based on the quality of the essay rather than multiple choice.

Question Text: A Neuropsychologist observes a patient with "Anosognosia" following a right-hemisphere stroke. This condition is characterized by the patient's:
Option 1: Total loss of ability to recognize familiar faces (prosopagnosia).
Option 2: Inability to speak fluently despite understanding what is being said.
Option 3: Denying the existence of their physical disability or paralysis.
Option 4: Intense fear of leaving their home or entering open public spaces.

Question Text: A Cognitive Psychologist is investigating "Change Blindness." In a real-world application, which scenario most dangerously exemplifies this phenomenon?
Option 1: A driver failing to notice a pedestrian entering a crosswalk while they are focused on a changing traffic light.
Option 2: A student failing to remember the specific color of a textbook they used for an entire semester.
Option 3: An office worker not noticing that a coworker has changed their hairstyle or glasses over the weekend.
Option 4: A person forgetting where they parked their car in a large, multi-level shopping mall garage.

Question Text: In Counseling Psychology, a therapist uses "Reflective Listening." If a client says, "I feel like I'm drowning in work," which response best demonstrates this skill?
Option 1: "You should probably talk to your boss about reducing your current project load."
Option 2: "It sounds like you are feeling completely overwhelmed by your professional responsibilities."
Option 3: "I felt the same way last year when I was completing my doctoral dissertation."
Option 4: "Why do you think you feel that way? Is it because you are procrastinating too much?"

Question Text: An Industrial-Organizational Psychologist is implementing "360-degree feedback." What is the primary advantage of this method over traditional supervisor-only appraisals?
Option 1: It significantly reduces the time required for HR to process annual performance reviews.
Option 2: It provides a comprehensive view of performance from peers, subordinates, and supervisors.
Option 3: It guarantees that every employee will receive a promotion or salary increase within a year.
Option 4: It allows the supervisor to avoid having difficult conversations with their direct reports.

Question Text: In Behavioral Psychology, a clinician uses "Response Cost" to manage a child's disruptive behavior. Which of the following is an example of this technique?
Option 1: Giving the child a sticker every time they sit quietly for more than ten minutes.
Option 2: Removing a previously earned token or privilege following a specific undesirable behavior.
Option 3: Ignoring the child completely until they stop screaming and start playing with toys.
Option 4: Assigning an extra chore to the child immediately after they break a household rule.

Question Text: A Social Psychologist is studying "Social Loafing" in virtual teams. To mitigate this effect, the team leader should ensure that:
Option 1: All team members are given the exact same generic tasks to complete simultaneously.
Option 2: Individual contributions are identifiable and evaluated by the rest of the group.
Option 3: The team size is increased to at least twenty people to share the workload.
Option 4: No deadlines are set, allowing team members to work at their own natural pace.

Question Text: In Clinical Psychology, a patient presents with "Glove Anesthesia" (loss of sensation only in the hand). Why does this suggest a Conversion Disorder?
Option 1: It corresponds exactly to the physical distribution of the ulnar and radial nerves.
Option 2: It is anatomically impossible based on the actual pathway of nerves in the arm.
Option 3: It is a common side effect of long-term use of anti-anxiety medications like benzodiazepines.
Option 4: It indicates a severe bacterial infection that has specifically targeted the skin of the hand.

Question Text: A Developmental Psychologist is applying the "Strange Situation" procedure. A child who ignores their mother upon her return is classified as having:
Option 1: Secure attachment, indicating a healthy and trusting relationship with the caregiver.
Option 2: Anxious-avoidant attachment, often seen when caregivers are consistently unresponsive.
Option 3: Anxious-ambivalent attachment, typically resulting from inconsistent caregiving styles.
Option 4: Disorganized attachment, which is frequently associated with childhood trauma or abuse.

Question Text: In Educational Psychology, a teacher uses "Differentiated Instruction." This means the teacher is primarily focused on:
Option 1: Delivering the exact same lecture to all students regardless of their prior knowledge.
Option 2: Tailoring the content, process, and products of learning to meet diverse student needs.
Option 3: Using only one specific type of intelligence, such as logical-mathematical, for all tasks.
Option 4: Ensuring that every student is graded on a strict curve to maintain high standards.

Question Text: A Forensic Psychologist is asked to use the "PCL-R" (Psychopathy Checklist-Revised). What is a core trait measured by Factor 1 (Interpersonal/Affective)?
Option 1: A long history of juvenile delinquency and frequent violations of conditional release.
Option 2: A lack of remorse or guilt and a callous disregard for the feelings of others.
Option 3: A tendency to experience frequent and intense bouts of clinical depression and anxiety.
Option 4: The consistent ability to maintain long-term, stable, and healthy romantic relationships.

Question Text: In Health Psychology, the "Stress-Buffering Hypothesis" suggests that social support is most beneficial to an individual's health when:
Option 1: The individual is experiencing very low levels of daily stress and high levels of life satisfaction.
Option 2: The individual is facing high levels of stress, acting as a protective resource against illness.
Option 3: The individual lives in a rural area with limited access to modern medical facilities.
Option 4: The individual has a genetic predisposition to chronic inflammatory diseases like arthritis.

Question Text: A Sports Psychologist works with a golfer on "External Focus of Attention." Which instruction aligns best with this evidence-based strategy?
Option 1: "Focus specifically on the movement of your wrists during the middle of the swing."
Option 2: "Focus on the trajectory of the ball and the target spot on the green ahead of you."
Option 3: "Think about the tension in your shoulder muscles as you prepare to strike the ball."
Option 4: "Try to remember the mechanics of the perfect swing you read about in the manual."

Question Text: In Positive Psychology, the concept of "Post-Traumatic Growth" (PTG) suggests that individuals may experience:
Option 1: A total return to their exact personality state prior to the traumatic event occurring.
Option 2: Positive psychological changes as a result of struggling with highly challenging life crises.
Option 3: An inevitable decline into chronic mental illness following any major stressful experience.
Option 4: The ability to completely erase the memory of the trauma through sheer willpower.

Question Text: A Neuropsychologist is testing a patient’s "Executive Functions." Which task is most appropriate for assessing the ability to inhibit a dominant response?
Option 1: The Stroop Task, where the patient names the ink color of words that spell different colors.
Option 2: A simple reaction time test where the patient presses a button whenever a light flashes.
Option 3: A vocabulary test asking the patient to define increasingly complex and rare words.
Option 4: A digit span task requiring the patient to repeat a sequence of numbers in order.

Question Text: In Quantitative Psychology, a researcher uses "Factor Analysis." The primary goal of this statistical technique is to:
Option 1: Determine if the mean scores of three different groups are significantly different from each other.
Option 2: Reduce a large number of observed variables into a smaller number of underlying constructs.
Option 3: Predict the exact value of a dependent variable based on a single independent variable.
Option 4: Calculate the probability that a specific event will occur within a given timeframe.

Question Text: An Evolutionary Psychologist discusses "Kin Selection." This theory explains why humans are more likely to:
Option 1: Compete aggressively with their own siblings for limited resources like food or money.
Option 2: Perform altruistic acts for close relatives, thereby increasing their shared genetic success.
Option 3: Adopt children from different cultural backgrounds to increase genetic diversity in the group.
Option 4: Avoid all social interactions with family members to prevent the spread of diseases.

Question Text: In Biopsychology, "Long-Term Potentiation" (LTP) is considered the cellular basis for learning. It involves:
Option 1: The weakening of synaptic connections between two neurons that are rarely used.
Option 2: A long-lasting increase in synaptic strength following high-frequency stimulation.
Option 3: The physical death of neurons that contain incorrect or outdated information.
Option 4: The growth of new brain regions in response to learning a new physical skill.

Question Text: A Community Psychologist is using "Photovoice" in a project. What is the primary purpose of this participatory action research method?
Option 1: To take professional portraits of community leaders for a local government website.
Option 2: To empower marginalized groups to document their reality and advocate for social change.
Option 3: To use high-speed photography to study the movement patterns of people in public parks.
Option 4: To sell artistic photographs to raise funds for building a new community community center.

Question Text: In Comparative Psychology, researchers study "Delayed Gratification" in crows. If a crow chooses a better future reward over an immediate smaller one, it shows:
Option 1: Instinctive behavior that has no relationship to cognitive planning or self-control.
Option 2: Complex cognitive abilities similar to those seen in "The Marshmallow Test" with humans.
Option 3: A lack of hunger, meaning the crow is not motivated by the food stimulus provided.
Option 4: That the crow has been accidentally trained by a human to perform this specific trick.

Question Text: A Forensic Psychologist evaluates "Malingering." In this context, malingering refers to:
Option 1: The genuine experience of physical symptoms that have no clear medical cause.
Option 2: The intentional production of false or exaggerated physical or psychological symptoms.
Option 3: A rare neurological condition where the patient loses the ability to feel physical pain.
Option 4: The tendency for witnesses to unintentionally change their story over a period of time.

Question Text: In Human Factors (Cognitive Psychology), "Mental Workload" is often measured using the NASA-TLX. This scale assesses:
Option 1: The physical weight of the equipment an operator must carry during a typical shift.
Option 2: Subjective ratings of task demands, effort, performance, and frustration levels.
Option 3: The exact number of neurons firing in the prefrontal cortex during a specific task.
Option 4: The amount of electrical energy consumed by a computer system during high usage.

Question Text: An Industrial-Organizational Psychologist applies "Equity Theory" to workplace morale. An employee is likely to feel "under-rewarded" if:
Option 1: They perceive their ratio of inputs to outcomes is lower than that of a comparison peer.
Option 2: They receive a large bonus but feel that they did not work hard enough to earn it.
Option 3: Their manager gives them more autonomy and responsibility than they previously had.
Option 4: They are paid exactly the same as everyone else in the company regardless of seniority.

Question Text: In Clinical Psychology, the "Dodo Bird Verdict" refers to the controversial claim that:
Option 1: All psychotropic medications are equally effective regardless of the specific diagnosis.
Option 2: All established psychotherapies are roughly equal in their effectiveness for patients.
Option 3: Children are easier to treat than adults because their brains are more neuroplastic.
Option 4: Most mental health disorders will resolve themselves over time without any intervention.

Question Text: A Health Psychologist is helping a patient manage chronic pain using "Gate Control Theory." The goal is to:
Option 1: Completely sever the nerves responsible for transmitting pain signals to the brain.
Option 2: Use non-painful input (like massage) to "close the gate" to painful signals in the spinal cord.
Option 3: Convince the patient that the pain is purely psychological and does not actually exist.
Option 4: Increase the patient's dosage of opioid medications until all pain sensation is gone.

Question Text: In Personality Psychology, a "Projective Test" like the Rorschach Inkblot Test is based on the assumption that:
Option 1: People will reveal their unconscious motives and conflicts when interpreting ambiguous stimuli.
Option 2: Standardized multiple-choice questions are the only way to accurately measure personality.
Option 3: Brain structure is the sole determinant of how a person behaves in social situations.
Option 4: A person's signature and handwriting style can predict their future career success.

Question Text: A Neuropsychologist is assessing "Prosopagnosia." This condition specifically involves the inability to:
Option 1: Recognize familiar faces, even though basic vision and intellectual function are intact.
Option 2: Understand the meaning of written words despite being able to read them aloud.
Option 3: Coordinate fine motor movements required for tasks like buttoning a shirt or writing.
Option 4: Regulate emotional responses, leading to frequent and sudden outbursts of anger.

Question Text: In Social Psychology, "Groupthink" is most likely to occur when a group:
Option 1: Is highly diverse and encourages dissenting opinions from all of its members.
Option 2: Is highly cohesive and under significant pressure to reach a unanimous decision.
Option 3: Has no clear leader and allows members to work independently on separate tasks.
Option 4: Is composed of individuals who have never met each other before the meeting.

Question Text: A Developmental Psychologist discusses "Object Permanence." At what age does a child typically understand that an object exists even when it is out of sight?
Option 1: During the first month of life, as an innate reflex present from birth.
Option 2: By approximately 8 to 12 months of age, during the sensorimotor stage.
Option 3: Not until the child reaches the formal operational stage at age 12 or later.
Option 4: Only after the child has started attending primary school and learned to read.

Question Text: In Educational Psychology, "Intrinsic Motivation" is best fostered when a student:
Option 1: Is promised a monetary reward for every "A" grade they receive on a report card.
Option 2: Engages in a task because they find it inherently interesting and personally rewarding.
Option 3: Is threatened with detention if they do not complete their homework on time.
Option 4: Is constantly compared to the top-performing students in their classroom.

Question Text: A Biopsychologist explains the "All-or-None Law" of neural firing. This principle states that:
Option 1: A neuron will fire at varying intensities depending on the strength of the stimulus.
Option 2: A neuron either fires completely or does not fire at all, with no in-between state.
Option 3: All neurons in a specific brain region must fire at the exact same time for a thought to occur.
Option 4: A neuron can only fire once every twenty-four hours to prevent over-exhaustion.

Question Text: In Community Psychology, "Empowerment" is defined as a process where people:
Option 1: Rely entirely on outside experts to solve all of the problems in their neighborhood.
Option 2: Gain mastery over their lives and participate in decisions that affect their community.
Option 3: Are given free resources without having to participate in any planning or work.
Option 4: Move to a different city to avoid dealing with local social and economic issues.

Question Text: A Counseling Psychologist uses "Unconditional Positive Regard." According to Carl Rogers, this involves:
Option 1: Agreeing with every single action or decision the client makes, even if it is harmful.
Option 2: Accepting and valuing the client as they are, without judgment or evaluation.
Option 3: Providing the client with constant praise and compliments to boost their self-esteem.
Option 4: Keeping a professional distance so the therapist's own emotions are never involved.

Question Text: In Forensic Psychology, a "Threat Assessment" differs from a "Risk Assessment" because it:
Option 1: Focuses on the likelihood of a specific person carrying out a targeted act of violence.
Option 2: Only looks at the personality traits of the individual rather than their recent behaviors.
Option 3: Is used exclusively for individuals who have already been convicted of a violent crime.
Option 4: Does not require any clinical interview or review of the individual's past records.

Question Text: An Environmental Psychologist studies "Wayfinding" in complex buildings like airports. A key design feature to improve wayfinding is:
Option 1: Using a symmetrical layout where every hallway looks identical to the others.
Option 2: Providing clear "landmarks" and consistent signage at all major decision points.
Option 3: Removing all windows to prevent travelers from being distracted by the outside.
Option 4: Changing the color of the walls every day to keep the environment interesting.

Question Text: In Sports Psychology, "Self-Efficacy" refers to an athlete's:
Option 1: Objective level of physical fitness as measured by a standardized treadmill test.
Option 2: Belief in their own capability to execute the actions required for a specific performance.
Option 3: Total number of medals and trophies they have won during their professional career.
Option 4: Genetic predisposition toward having high levels of fast-twitch muscle fibers.

Question Text: A Positive Psychologist recommends "Gratitude Journaling." Research suggests this practice primarily increases:
Option 1: A person's ability to remember negative events with much greater clarity and detail.
Option 2: Subjective well-being and life satisfaction while reducing symptoms of depression.
Option 3: The speed at which a person can complete complex mathematical and logic puzzles.
Option 4: The physical strength of the immune system against viral infections like the flu.

Question Text: In Behavioral Psychology, "Shaping" is a process used to:
Option 1: Punish a subject every time they move away from the desired final behavior.
Option 2: Reinforce successive approximations of a target behavior until the behavior is achieved.
Option 3: Ensure that a behavior is learned instantly without the need for multiple trials.
Option 4: Mold a person's physical appearance through exercise and strict dietary changes.

Question Text: A Cognitive Psychologist explains the "Availability Heuristic." This mental shortcut leads people to:
Option 1: Estimate the frequency of an event based on how easily examples come to mind.
Option 2: Carefully weigh every possible outcome before making a logical financial decision.
Option 3: Ignore all new information that contradicts their previously held personal beliefs.
Option 4: Assume that because something is natural, it must be healthier or better for them.

Question Text: In Industrial-Organizational Psychology, "Job Enrichment" involves:
Option 1: Adding more tasks of the same difficulty level to an employee's daily routine.
Option 2: Increasing the depth of a job by giving employees more control and responsibility.
Option 3: Offering a higher salary for a job that is considered boring or highly repetitive.
Option 4: Providing free snacks and gym memberships to all employees in the organization.

Question Text: A Developmental Psychologist identifies a "Critical Period." This is a specific timeframe during which:
Option 1: An individual is most likely to experience a mid-life crisis and change careers.
Option 2: Certain experiences must occur for a particular developmental milestone to be reached.
Option 3: A person is completely immune to the effects of environmental stress or trauma.
Option 4: The brain stops growing and begins to lose neurons at a very rapid pace.

Question Text: In Clinical Psychology, "Cognitive Restructuring" is a core technique in CBT used to:
Option 1: Identify and challenge irrational or maladaptive thoughts to change emotional states.
Option 2: Hypnotize the patient so they can remember repressed memories from their infancy.
Option 3: Use electrical stimulation to change the physical structure of the frontal lobes.
Option 4: Teach the patient how to suppress all of their emotions through deep meditation.

Question Text: A Health Psychologist studies "Burnout" in medical professionals. Which of the following is one of the three core dimensions of burnout?
Option 1: High levels of physical energy and enthusiasm for work tasks.
Option 2: Depersonalization, often manifesting as a cynical attitude toward patients.
Option 3: An increase in personal accomplishment and professional self-esteem.
Option 4: The ability to maintain a perfect work-life balance without any effort.

Question Text: In Social Psychology, "Cognitive Dissonance" is the discomfort felt when:
Option 1: Two people in a relationship have a minor disagreement about a trivial topic.
Option 2: A person holds two conflicting beliefs or acts in a way that contradicts their beliefs.
Option 3: An individual is unable to solve a difficult puzzle after multiple attempts.
Option 4: A person forgets an important piece of information right when they need it.

Question Text: A Forensic Psychologist conducts an "Autopsy of a Crime." In criminal profiling, this refers to:
Option 1: A literal medical examination of a deceased victim to determine the cause of death.
Option 2: A detailed analysis of the crime scene to infer the personality traits of the offender.
Option 3: A psychological evaluation of a witness to see if they are telling the truth.
Option 4: The process of interviewing a suspect's family members to find a motive for the crime.

Question Text: In Neuropsychology, "Hemi-spatial Neglect" usually results from damage to the:
Option 1: Left frontal lobe, causing the patient to ignore the right side of their body.
Option 2: Right parietal lobe, causing the patient to ignore the left side of their space.
Option 3: Occipital lobe, leading to total blindness in both the left and right eyes.
Option 4: Cerebellum, resulting in a total loss of balance and physical coordination.

Question Text: An Educational Psychologist applies "Metacognition" in the classroom. This involves:
Option 1: Thinking about one's own thinking processes and monitoring one's understanding.
Option 2: Memorizing as many facts as possible without understanding the concepts behind them.
Option 3: Following a teacher's instructions perfectly without ever asking any questions.
Option 4: Using a calculator to solve basic arithmetic problems instead of doing them mentally.

Question Text: In Comparative Psychology, "Social Learning" in animals is often tested using:
Option 1: A mirror, to see if the animal can recognize itself as a distinct individual.
Option 2: An observer animal watching a demonstrator solve a puzzle to get a reward.
Option 3: A maze, to see how long it takes for a single animal to find the exit alone.
Option 4: A loud noise, to measure the startle response of different species of birds.

Question Text: A Counseling Psychologist identifies "Transference" in a therapy session. This occurs when:
Option 1: The therapist shares their own personal problems with the client to build rapport.
Option 2: The client projects feelings about a significant person in their life onto the therapist.
Option 3: The therapist refers the client to a different specialist for medical treatment.
Option 4: The client stops coming to therapy because they feel they have been cured.

Question Text: In Personality Psychology, "Locus of Control" refers to whether a person believes:
Option 1: They are the most important person in their social circle or organization.
Option 2: Success is determined by their own efforts or by external forces like luck.
Option 3: They have the physical strength to complete a difficult marathon or race.
Option 4: They can accurately predict the personality of a stranger just by looking at them.

Question Text: In Biopsychology, the "Amygdala" is most closely associated with the processing of:
Option 1: Complex mathematical equations and logical reasoning tasks.
Option 2: Emotions, particularly fear and the detection of potential threats.
Option 3: The regulation of body temperature and the sensation of hunger.
Option 4: The fine motor control needed to play a musical instrument like the piano.

Question Text: A Quantitative Psychologist explains "Effect Size." This statistical concept tells us:
Option 1: If a result is statistically significant at the p < .05 level or not.
Option 2: The practical magnitude or strength of the relationship between variables.
Option 3: The exact number of participants who dropped out of a longitudinal study.
Option 4: The total cost of conducting a large-scale research project in the field.

Question Text: In Community Psychology, "Social Capital" refers to the:
Option 1: Total amount of money a community has in its local bank and government fund.
Option 2: Networks, norms, and trust that enable participants to act together effectively.
Option 3: Physical buildings and infrastructure, such as roads and bridges, in a city.
Option 4: Number of individuals in a neighborhood who have a university degree.

Question Text: An Environmental Psychologist researches "Personal Space." This "bubble" around a person:
Option 1: Is a fixed distance that never changes regardless of the culture or situation.
Option 2: Expands or contracts based on cultural norms and the nature of the relationship.
Option 3: Is only present in humans and has never been observed in any other animal species.
Option 4: Disappears completely when a person is in a very dark or quiet environment.

Question Text: In Sports Psychology, "Imagery" is most effective for athletes when it:
Option 1: Involves only the visual sense and ignores all other physical sensations.
Option 2: Includes multiple senses and mimics the actual timing of the performance.
Option 3: Is done only once a year right before the most important competition.
Option 4: Focuses exclusively on the athlete failing so they know what to avoid.

Question Text: In Forensic Psychology, "Jury Nullification" occurs when a jury:
Option 1: Is unable to reach a verdict and the judge declares a mistrial in the case.
Option 2: Returns a "not guilty" verdict despite believing the defendant broke the law.
Option 3: Is dismissed by the judge because they were caught talking to the media.
Option 4: Decides the sentence for a defendant instead of leaving it to the judge.

Question Text: A Positive Psychologist defines "Resilience" as the ability to:
Option 1: Never experience any negative emotions, even during a major tragedy or loss.
Option 2: Bounce back from adversity and maintain functioning despite significant stress.
Option 3: Forget about a traumatic event as soon as it has finished occurring.
Option 4: Convince others that one's life is perfect even when it is actually falling apart.

Question Text: In Abnormal Psychology, "Negative Symptoms" of Schizophrenia include:
Option 1: Hallucinations, such as hearing voices that are not actually present.
Option 2: Avolition, which is a significant lack of motivation or ability to initiate tasks.
Option 3: Delusions of grandeur, where the person believes they have special powers.
Option 4: Disorganized speech, where the person jumps rapidly from one topic to another.

Question Text: A Cognitive Psychologist discusses "Working Memory." According to Baddeley’s model, the "Central Executive":
Option 1: Stores visual images for long periods of time in the permanent memory bank.
Option 2: Coordinates and regulates the flow of information between sub-systems.
Option 3: Is responsible only for processing sounds and spoken language patterns.
Option 4: Is a physical part of the brain located in the primary motor cortex.

Question Text: In Industrial-Organizational Psychology, "Work-Family Enrichment" occurs when:
Option 1: An employee is so stressed at work that they cannot interact with their family.
Option 2: Experiences in one role improve the quality of life in the other role.
Option 3: A company requires employees to bring their children to the office every day.
Option 4: An employee quits their job to spend all of their time with their family.

Question Text: A Developmental Psychologist observes a "Fine Motor Skill." Which action is an example?
Option 1: A toddler learning how to run across a grassy field without falling down.
Option 2: A child using their thumb and forefinger to pick up a small piece of cereal.
Option 3: An adolescent playing a game of soccer and kicking the ball into the net.
Option 4: An adult lifting a heavy box and carrying it up a flight of stairs.

Question Text: In Clinical Psychology, "Exposure and Response Prevention" (ERP) is the gold standard for:
Option 1: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder, by preventing the ritual after the trigger.
Option 2: Major Depressive Disorder, by forcing the patient to attend social events.
Option 3: Anorexia Nervosa, by making the patient watch others eat a large meal.
Option 4: Antisocial Personality Disorder, by placing the patient in a group therapy setting.

Question Text: In Health Psychology, "Self-Monitoring" in weight management involves:
Option 1: Having a doctor weigh the patient once every six months at a clinic.
Option 2: The patient keeping a detailed daily log of their food intake and exercise.
Option 3: Watching television shows about healthy cooking and fitness routines.
Option 4: Ignoring one's weight and focusing only on how one feels emotionally.

Question Text: In Social Psychology, the "Fundamental Attribution Error" is the tendency to:
Option 1: Overestimate situational factors when explaining the behavior of other people.
Option 2: Underestimate situational factors and overestimate traits when explaining others.
Option 3: Blame oneself for every negative event that happens in one's personal life.
Option 4: Assume that everyone else shares the same opinions and beliefs that we do.

Question Text: In Forensic Psychology, a "Lethality Assessment" for domestic violence checks:
Option 1: If the victim is likely to leave the relationship within the next week.
Option 2: The presence of high-risk factors that predict a fatal outcome in the future.
Option 3: The total amount of money the couple has in their joint savings account.
Option 4: How many times the police have been called to the house in the past year.

Question Text: In Neuropsychology, "Executive Dysfunction" is most commonly caused by damage to the:
Option 1: Occipital lobes, which are responsible for the processing of visual data.
Option 2: Prefrontal cortex, which handles planning, decision-making, and control.
Option 3: Temporal lobes, which are primarily involved in hearing and memory.
Option 4: Brainstem, which regulates basic life functions like breathing and heart rate.

Question Text: In Educational Psychology, "Self-Regulated Learning" means the student:
Option 1: Only learns when a teacher is present and providing direct instructions.
Option 2: Sets goals, monitors their progress, and adjusts their study strategies.
Option 3: Attends a school where there are no grades or formal assessments of any kind.
Option 4: Memorizes the textbook word-for-word to ensure they get a perfect score.

Question Text: In Comparative Psychology, "Aping" or true imitation in primates is different from "Emulation" because:
Option 1: In imitation, the animal copies the exact motor actions used by the demonstrator.
Option 2: In emulation, the animal ignores the demonstrator and solves the task by luck.
Option 3: Imitation is only found in humans, while all other animals use emulation.
Option 4: Emulation involves copying the exact sounds made by the demonstrator animal.

Question Text: In Counseling Psychology, "Termination" is the phase of therapy where:
Option 1: The therapist decides to stop working with the client because they are too difficult.
Option 2: The client and therapist work together to end the relationship as goals are met.
Option 3: The client's insurance company refuses to pay for any more therapy sessions.
Option 4: The therapist moves to a different city and cannot see the client anymore.

Question Text: In Personality Psychology, "Self-Actualization" in Maslow's hierarchy is:
Option 1: The most basic need for food and water that must be met before anything else.
Option 2: The fulfillment of one's unique potential after all other needs are met.
Option 3: The desire to be famous and recognized by everyone in one's local community.
Option 4: The need to feel safe and secure in one's physical environment at all times.

Question Text: In Biopsychology, "Neuroplasticity" refers to the brain's ability to:
Option 1: Remain exactly the same from the moment of birth until the end of life.
Option 2: Change its structure and function in response to experience or injury.
Option 3: Function perfectly even after all of the neurons have been surgically removed.
Option 4: Predict the future behavior of an individual based on their genetic code.

Question Text: In Quantitative Psychology, "Validity" in testing refers to:
Option 1: Whether the test produces consistent results every time it is administered.
Option 2: Whether the test actually measures what it is intended to measure.
Option 3: How many people can finish the test within the allotted time limit.
Option 4: The physical appearance of the test and the quality of the paper used.

Question Text: In Community Psychology, "Prevention" is prioritized over "Treatment" because it:
Option 1: Is much more expensive and requires more highly trained medical staff.
Option 2: Addresses the root causes of problems before they develop into crises.
Option 3: Is only effective for physical health issues and not for mental health issues.
Option 4: Requires the community to stop using all forms of modern technology.

Question Text: In Environmental Psychology, "Defensible Space" theory suggests that:
Option 1: Crime is higher in areas where people have no sense of ownership or control.
Option 2: All public parks should be turned into private gardens to prevent loitering.
Option 3: People should carry weapons at all times to defend themselves from attackers.
Option 4: High-rise buildings are the safest place for families with young children to live.

Question Text: In Sports Psychology, "Team Cohesion" is composed of two main types:
Option 1: Social cohesion (liking each other) and Task cohesion (working toward a goal).
Option 2: Physical cohesion (being the same height) and Financial cohesion (same pay).
Option 3: Genetic cohesion (being related) and Academic cohesion (same degree).
Option 4: Temporal cohesion (working same hours) and Spatial cohesion (living together).

Question Text: In Forensic Psychology, "Victim Impact Statements" are used during:
Option 1: The initial police investigation to find the person who committed the crime.
Option 2: The sentencing phase, to allow the victim to describe the harm they suffered.
Option 3: The jury selection process, to see if the jurors are biased against the victim.
Option 4: The trial itself, to prove that the defendant is guilty of the crime beyond doubt.

Question Text: In Positive Psychology, "PERMA" is an acronym for the five elements of well-being. What does the "R" stand for?
Option 1: Resilience, the ability to bounce back from a difficult or traumatic life event.
Option 2: Relationships, the presence of supportive and positive social connections.
Option 3: Rationality, the ability to make logical decisions without being influenced by emotion.
Option 4: Relaxation, the amount of time a person spends sleeping or resting each day.

Question Text: A local government official is faced with a budget deficit and must choose between cutting public library hours or reducing park maintenance. Which principle of Public Administration is most relevant here?
Option 1: Prioritizing utilitarian outcomes by maintaining the service with the highest documented foot traffic.
Option 2: Eliminating both services equally to ensure that no specific demographic feels unfairly targeted by cuts.
Option 3: Increasing local property taxes immediately without a public hearing to cover the total deficit.
Option 4: Outsourcing all library management to a private firm regardless of the existing labor contracts.

Question Text: In a Comparative Politics study, you observe two countries with high ethnic diversity; one is stable while the other is in conflict. What institutional feature should you analyze first?
Option 1: The specific type of electoral system, such as Proportional Representation versus Majoritarian "First-Past-The-Post."
Option 2: The total number of years since the country gained independence from its former colonial power.
Option 3: The average annual rainfall and its impact on the agricultural output of the minority ethnic regions.
Option 4: The color of the national flag and its symbolic representation of the various ethnic groups involved.

Question Text: You are a junior diplomat tasked with analyzing a border dispute using the Realist paradigm of International Relations. What is your primary focus for the report?
Option 1: The expansion of international trade agreements and cultural exchange programs between the two nations.
Option 2: The shift in the balance of military power and the strategic security dilemma created by troop movements.
Option 3: The role of non-governmental organizations in mediating a peaceful resolution through soft power.
Option 4: The personal psychological profile and childhood upbringing of the current heads of state in both countries.

Question Text: During a Public Policy evaluation, a "Stakeholder Analysis" reveals that a proposed dam will displace indigenous tribes but provide electricity to millions. How should a policy analyst proceed?
Option 1: Ignore the indigenous tribes as they represent a small percentage of the total voting population.
Option 2: Facilitate a deliberative process to find compensatory mechanisms or alternative energy sites.
Option 3: Proceed with the dam immediately to maximize the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth of the nation.
Option 4: Cancel the project entirely without looking for alternatives to avoid any form of social confrontation.

Question Text: A researcher uses a "Randomized Control Trial" (RCT) in Political Methodology to test if cash transfers increase voter turnout. What is the main advantage of this method?
Option 1: It allows the researcher to establish a causal relationship by isolating the effect of the cash transfer.
Option 2: It is the least expensive method and requires very little data collection compared to qualitative interviews.
Option 3: It guarantees that every single person in the country will eventually receive the cash transfer.
Option 4: It eliminates the need for any theoretical framework because the data speaks entirely for itself.

Question Text: In the context of Political Economy, a country is experiencing "Stagflation." What unique challenge does this present to the central bank and policy makers?
Option 1: Prices are falling too rapidly while employment is at an all-time high, causing a surplus of cash.
Option 2: Simultaneous high inflation and stagnant economic growth, making traditional interest rate tools risky.
Option 3: The government has too much revenue and does not know how to spend it on infrastructure.
Option 4: International trade is so balanced that there is no need for any domestic economic intervention.

Question Text: A campaign manager is studying Psephology to understand "voter volatility." Which scenario best describes this specific phenomenon?
Option 1: A large group of voters consistently voting for the same party for over forty years without fail.
Option 2: Voters who frequently switch their party preference between different election cycles based on issues.
Option 3: The process of redrawing district boundaries to favor one specific political party over another.
Option 4: The legal requirement for all citizens to show a specific form of identification before casting a ballot.

Question Text: You are analyzing a "Security Dilemma" in Global Politics. Why might an increase in Country A’s defensive capabilities lead to an arms race?
Option 1: Because Country B perceives the defensive build-up as a potential threat to its own security interests.
Option 2: Because Country A has explicitly stated it intends to invade Country B within the next three months.
Option 3: Because international law requires all countries to have exactly the same number of tanks and aircraft.
Option 4: Because the United Nations provides subsidies to any country that increases its military spending.

Question Text: In a Legislative Studies internship, you are asked to track "Logrolling" in a new infrastructure bill. What are you looking for?
Option 1: The process where two or more legislators agree to vote for each other's bills to ensure mutual passage.
Option 2: The physical act of carrying a large scroll of paper to the floor of the house for a final vote.
Option 3: A situation where the President uses a pocket veto to kill a bill after the session has ended.
Option 4: The use of a filibuster to prevent a vote from ever taking place on the legislative floor.

Question Text: Applying Political Psychology, how might "Confirmation Bias" affect a citizen's consumption of political news during an election?
Option 1: They will actively seek out diverse viewpoints to ensure they have a balanced understanding of the issues.
Option 2: They will favor information that aligns with their existing beliefs and ignore contradictory evidence.
Option 3: They will stop watching news altogether to avoid being influenced by any form of political messaging.
Option 4: They will only believe news that is published in physical newspapers rather than on digital platforms.

Question Text: A city planner in Urban Politics is dealing with "Gentrification." What is the primary social justice concern regarding this process?
Option 1: The increase in property values that might displace long-term, low-income residents from their homes.
Option 2: The fact that more trees are being planted, which might attract unwanted birds to the city center.
Option 3: The installation of high-speed internet which makes the neighborhood too modern for older residents.
Option 4: The decrease in traffic congestion which makes it too easy for people to drive through the area.

Question Text: In Public Law, the principle of "Stare Decisis" is fundamental. If a judge follows this principle, how will they decide a new case?
Option 1: By creating a completely new law based on their personal moral feelings about the current situation.
Option 2: By looking at previous judicial decisions (precedents) in similar cases to guide their current ruling.
Option 3: By asking the legislative branch to tell them exactly how to rule before the trial begins.
Option 4: By flipping a coin to ensure that the judicial process remains entirely unbiased and random.

Question Text: A Human Rights advocate is citing "Non-Refoulement." In which scenario would this international legal principle be most applicable?
Option 1: When a state is considering deporting a refugee to a country where they face a high risk of persecution.
Option 2: When a government is deciding whether to increase the minimum wage for all its domestic workers.
Option 3: When a corporation is looking to move its headquarters to a country with lower environmental standards.
Option 4: When a city council is debating whether to build a new prison in a residential neighborhood.

Question Text: In Environmental Politics, the "Tragedy of the Commons" explains why shared resources are often overexploited. What is a common policy solution?
Option 1: Allowing every individual to use as much of the resource as they want without any oversight.
Option 2: Implementing regulations, such as quotas or private property rights, to manage resource use.
Option 3: Closing the resource entirely and never allowing anyone to use it for any purpose again.
Option 4: Encouraging everyone to use the resource faster before someone else gets the chance to use it.

Question Text: A researcher in Political Sociology is studying "Social Capital." How would high social capital most likely impact a local community?
Option 1: It would lead to higher levels of trust and cooperation among citizens, facilitating collective action.
Option 2: It would cause people to become more isolated as they focus entirely on their own financial wealth.
Option 3: It would result in a total breakdown of the local government as citizens stop following any rules.
Option 4: It would require the government to spend more money on policing because people do not trust each other.

Question Text: You are evaluating a "Federal" vs "Unitary" system in State & Local Government. Which feature is unique to a Federal system?
Option 1: The central government has all the power and can abolish local governments at its own whim.
Option 2: Power is constitutionally divided between a central government and regional or state governments.
Option 3: There is no executive branch, and all decisions are made by a large committee of citizens.
Option 4: The country is ruled by a single monarch who inherits the position from their parents.

Question Text: In Gender & Politics, the concept of the "Glass Ceiling" is often discussed. What does this term specifically refer to?
Option 1: The actual physical glass roofs found in many modern government buildings and parliaments.
Option 2: The invisible barriers that prevent women from rising to the highest levels of political leadership.
Option 3: A policy that requires all political debates to be held in transparent rooms for public viewing.
Option 4: The high cost of heating large government offices that have too many windows and glass doors.

Question Text: A student of Peace & Conflict Studies is analyzing "Positive Peace." How does this differ from "Negative Peace"?
Option 1: Negative peace is the absence of war, while positive peace involves the presence of social justice.
Option 2: Positive peace is when a country wins a war, while negative peace is when a country loses a war.
Option 3: Negative peace is a situation where everyone is angry, while positive peace is where everyone is happy.
Option 4: There is no difference; both terms refer exactly to the same state of a lack of physical violence.

Question Text: In American Politics, what is the primary function of the "Electoral College" in the process of electing a President?
Option 1: To provide a direct popular vote where the person with the most individual votes always wins.
Option 2: To serve as a body of electors who formally cast votes for the President based on state results.
Option 3: To act as a school where new Presidents go to learn about the Constitution after being elected.
Option 4: To count the number of colleges and universities in each state to determine federal funding levels.

Question Text: An analyst in Political Geography is looking at "Gerrymandering." What is the main goal of this practice in a democracy?
Option 1: To ensure that all districts are perfectly square in shape to make them easier to map.
Option 2: To manipulate the boundaries of an electoral district to favor one party or class over another.
Option 3: To increase the number of voters who are able to reach their polling place within ten minutes.
Option 4: To make sure that every district has exactly the same number of parks and public schools.

Question Text: In Executive Politics, what does the "Unitary Executive Theory" suggest about the power of the President?
Option 1: The President should have near-total control over the executive branch without legislative interference.
Option 2: The President must share all executive powers with a committee of twelve elected governors.
Option 3: The President has no power over the military and must ask Congress for permission to move troops.
Option 4: The President is only a figurehead and all actual decisions are made by the Chief of Staff.

Question Text: A researcher in Judicial Process is studying "Judicial Activism." Which of the following best describes this approach?
Option 1: Judges who strictly follow the literal text of the Constitution and avoid making new policies.
Option 2: Judges who are willing to overturn laws and create new policies to protect individual rights.
Option 3: Judges who refuse to hear any cases that involve political parties or election disputes.
Option 4: Judges who are elected by the public every two years to ensure they remain popular.

Question Text: In Global Politics, what is a "Failed State"?
Option 1: A state that has lost its monopoly on the legitimate use of force and cannot provide basic services.
Option 2: A state that has failed to win a gold medal in the most recent Olympic Games.
Option 3: A state that has decided to change its name and its national anthem at the same time.
Option 4: A state that has more than three different political parties running in a local election.

Question Text: In Public Policy, what is the "Agenda Setting" stage of the policy cycle?
Option 1: The final stage where the policy is evaluated to see if it actually worked as intended.
Option 2: The stage where certain issues are identified as requiring government attention and action.
Option 3: The stage where the government writes the checks to pay for the new policy programs.
Option 4: The stage where the Supreme Court decides if the new policy is constitutional or not.

Question Text: A Political Theory student is reading Hobbes' "Leviathan." What is the primary reason Hobbes argues for a strong sovereign?
Option 1: To ensure that everyone has an equal amount of wealth and property throughout their lives.
Option 2: To avoid the "state of nature," which he describes as a war of every man against every man.
Option 3: To promote the development of the arts and sciences through heavy government subsidies.
Option 4: To ensure that the church has more power than the government in all daily affairs.

Question Text: In Comparative Politics, what is "Consociationalism"?
Option 1: A power-sharing arrangement in deeply divided societies to ensure stability and democracy.
Option 2: A system where only one political party is allowed to exist to prevent any form of social conflict.
Option 3: A method of voting where people use colored stones instead of paper ballots to choose leaders.
Option 4: A type of government where the military makes all decisions regarding the national economy.

Question Text: In International Relations, what does "Soft Power" refer to, as coined by Joseph Nye?
Option 1: The ability to get what you want through attraction and persuasion rather than coercion or payment.
Option 2: The use of lightweight military equipment that is easy to transport across international borders.
Option 3: The economic power a country has when it produces a lot of software and digital technology.
Option 4: The power a country has when it has a very small population and a very large land area.

Question Text: In Public Administration, what is "New Public Management" (NPM)?
Option 1: An approach that applies private sector management techniques to the public sector for efficiency.
Option 2: A rule that says only people under the age of thirty can hold high-level management positions.
Option 3: A system where all government decisions are made by a computer algorithm to avoid human bias.
Option 4: A movement to return to traditional 19th-century methods of government record-keeping.

Question Text: In Political Methodology, what is a "Type I Error"?
Option 1: Failing to reject a null hypothesis that is actually false (a false negative).
Option 2: Rejecting a null hypothesis that is actually true (a false positive).
Option 3: Forgetting to write down the names of the participants in a political survey.
Option 4: Using a pen instead of a pencil to fill out a data collection form in the field.

Question Text: In Political Economy, what is the "Dependency Theory"?
Option 1: The idea that poor countries are poor because they are not working hard enough to succeed.
Option 2: The idea that resources flow from poor "periphery" states to wealthy "core" states, enriching the latter.
Option 3: The idea that all countries will eventually become equally wealthy if they just use the same currency.
Option 4: The idea that governments should depend entirely on international aid to fund their schools.

Question Text: In Political Psychology, what is "Groupthink"?
Option 1: A situation where a group makes better decisions because they have so many different opinions.
Option 2: A psychological phenomenon where the desire for harmony in a group results in irrational decision-making.
Option 3: A new type of social media platform designed for political activists to share their ideas.
Option 4: The process of teaching students how to think critically about political advertisements.

Question Text: In Political Sociology, what is "Elite Theory"?
Option 1: The belief that a small minority, consisting of members of the economic elite, holds the most power.
Option 2: The belief that every single person in a democracy has exactly the same amount of political power.
Option 3: The theory that only people with university degrees should be allowed to vote in elections.
Option 4: The idea that the most talented athletes should be the ones who run the government.

Question Text: In Public Law, what is "Administrative Law"?
Option 1: The body of law that governs the activities of administrative agencies of government.
Option 2: The set of rules that tells government employees what time they must arrive at their desks.
Option 3: The law that requires all government buildings to have a front desk for visitors.
Option 4: The rules used by private companies to manage their human resources departments.

Question Text: In American Politics, what is "Federalism"?
Option 1: A system where the national government has all the power and states have none.
Option 2: The division of power between the national government and the state governments.
Option 3: A type of government where only the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) can make laws.
Option 4: The process of combining all the states into one single mega-state with no borders.

Question Text: In Global Politics, what is "Interdependence"?
Option 1: A situation where countries are mutually reliant on each other for security and prosperity.
Option 2: A situation where one country refuses to talk to any other country in the world.
Option 3: The process of a country becoming completely self-sufficient in all its food and energy needs.
Option 4: A war between two countries that have absolutely no trade or diplomatic links.

Question Text: In Human Rights & Justice, what is "Restorative Justice"?
Option 1: A system of justice that focuses on the rehabilitation of offenders through reconciliation with victims.
Option 2: A system where the offender is punished as harshly as possible to set an example for others.
Option 3: A law that says all old government buildings must be restored to their original appearance.
Option 4: The process of returning stolen property to its original owner without any court involvement.

Question Text: In Security Studies, what is "Human Security"?
Option 1: An approach that prioritizes the security of individuals and communities rather than just the state.
Option 2: The process of making sure that all humans have a secure password for their email accounts.
Option 3: A military strategy that involves using human shields to protect important government buildings.
Option 4: The study of how to make sure that robots do not take over the jobs of human security guards.

Question Text: In Environmental Politics, what is "Sustainable Development"?
Option 1: Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations.
Option 2: Building as many factories as possible as quickly as possible to increase the current GDP.
Option 3: A policy of never building anything new and living only in existing structures.
Option 4: The process of moving all human populations to the moon to protect the Earth's environment.

Question Text: In Gender & Politics, what is "Intersectionality"?
Option 1: The study of how different social identities, such as race and gender, overlap and create unique experiences.
Option 2: The process of building new roads that cross each other in the center of a large city.
Option 3: A political strategy where two different parties agree to merge into one single party.
Option 4: The study of how many men and women are standing at a street intersection at any given time.

Question Text: In Urban Politics, what is "Zoning"?
Option 1: The practice of dividing land in a municipality into zones in which certain land uses are permitted.
Option 2: The process of creating different time zones within a single city to manage traffic flow.
Option 3: A type of exercise that city employees are required to do every morning before work.
Option 4: The act of painting different parts of a city in different colors to make them look nice.

Question Text: In Political Geography, what is a "Buffer State"?
Option 1: A small neutral country situated between two larger hostile countries to prevent conflict.
Option 2: A state that has a lot of extra money saved up in case of a natural disaster or emergency.
Option 3: A country that produces a lot of floor buffers and cleaning equipment for export.
Option 4: A state where the internet speed is very slow and videos are always buffering.

Question Text: In Electoral Studies, what is "Duverger's Law"?
Option 1: The principle that plurality-rule elections structured within single-member districts tend to favor a two-party system.
Option 2: The law that says every citizen must vote in every election or they will be fined.
Option 3: The idea that the person who spends the most money on advertising always wins the election.
Option 4: The rule that says political candidates must be at least forty years old to run for office.

Question Text: In Peace & Conflict Studies, what is "Mediation"?
Option 1: A process where a neutral third party helps conflicting parties reach a voluntary agreement.
Option 2: A process where a third party joins the war on the side of the country that is losing.
Option 3: A type of deep breathing exercise that soldiers do to stay calm during a battle.
Option 4: The act of writing a long letter to a world leader to tell them why they are wrong.

Question Text: In State & Local Government, what is "Home Rule"?
Option 1: The power of a local city or county to set up its own system of self-government within state limits.
Option 2: A rule that says all government employees must work from their own homes.
Option 3: The law that says the governor of a state must live in the capital city at all times.
Option 4: A policy where the government provides a free house to every person who is elected to office.

Question Text: In Legislative Studies, what is a "Select Committee"?
