Option 2: Providing a balanced view of the student's strengths, areas for improvement, and social growth.
Option 3: Comparing the student's marks with the marks of the "Topper" of the class to create competition.
Option 4: Giving only a "Satisfactory" or "Unsatisfactory" rating without providing any specific details or examples.

Question Text: How can a teacher ensure "Safety and Well-being" during an outdoor school excursion?
Option 1: Let the students run around freely as it is their "play time" and the teacher's "break time."
Option 2: Conduct a risk assessment, establish clear rules, and maintain a constant headcount of students.
Option 3: Only take the students who have the highest grades to minimize the risk of any behavioral issues.
Option 4: Tell the students that if they get lost, it is their own responsibility to find their way back home.

Question Text: What is "Differentiated Assessment"?
Option 1: Giving the students who are "struggling" much easier questions so that they can also get 100% marks.
Option 2: Allowing students to demonstrate their understanding through various formats like posters, speeches, or tests.
Option 3: Assessing only the students who participate in class and ignoring those who are quiet or shy.
Option 4: Creating a different exam for every single student in the class based on their favorite hobbies.

Question Text: A teacher wants to improve "Parental Engagement." Which of the following is a proactive strategy?
Option 1: Only calling parents when their child has done something wrong or has failed an important test.
Option 2: Sending a weekly newsletter or digital update about what the students are learning in class.
Option 3: Inviting parents to come to the school and clean the classrooms every Saturday morning.
Option 4: Asking parents to write the students' homework for them to ensure it is always neat and correct.

Question Text: In the context of "Professional Ethics," what should a teacher do if they witness a colleague being physically aggressive with a student?
Option 1: Mind their own business as every teacher has their own "unique" way of managing a classroom.
Option 2: Report the incident immediately to the school authorities according to the child protection policy.
Option 3: Wait until the end of the year and then mention it anonymously in a teacher's suggestion box.
Option 4: Tell the student's parents about it in secret and ask them not to mention the teacher's name.

Question Text: Which of the following is a characteristic of "Effective Lesson Design"?
Option 1: Including a clear learning objective, varied activities, and a method for checking understanding.
Option 2: Making sure the lesson takes exactly 40 minutes and that every student copies five pages of notes.
Option 3: Using only the textbook and ensuring that no outside information or resources are introduced.
Option 4: Planning a lesson that is so difficult that only the top 5% of the students can understand it.

Question Text: How does "Collaborative Learning" benefit primary students?
Option 1: It allows the lazy students to get good grades by riding on the efforts of the hardworking students.
Option 2: It develops social skills, empathy, and the ability to view problems from different perspectives.
Option 3: It makes the teacher's job easier because they don't have to teach while the students are talking.
Option 4: It creates a loud and chaotic environment where no actual learning or academic work can take place.

Question Text: What is the role of "Play" in the primary curriculum according to modern pedagogical standards?
Option 1: Play is a waste of time and should be replaced with extra hours of Math and Science coaching.
Option 2: Play is a fundamental way through which young children explore, learn, and develop social skills.
Option 3: Play should only be allowed as a reward for students who finish their written work very quickly.
Option 4: Play is only for the "Pre-Primary" section and should be completely stopped once a child enters Grade 1.

Question Text: A teacher wants to use "Inquiry-Based Learning" for a topic on "Plants." What should they do?
Option 1: Give students a diagram of a plant and ask them to label the parts (root, stem, leaf) from memory.
Option 2: Ask students to observe different plants in the garden and come up with their own questions about them.
Option 3: Read a chapter on plants from the textbook and then give a 20-minute lecture on photosynthesis.
Option 4: Tell students to memorize the Latin names of 50 different plants found in the local geographical area.

Question Text: How should a teacher handle "Multi-level" learning in a single classroom?
Option 1: Teach to the "middle" of the class and hope that the top students don't get bored and the bottom don't get lost.
Option 2: Use flexible grouping and tiered assignments to meet the different learning needs of all students.
Option 3: Spend all the time with the slowest learners and let the rest of the class do whatever they want.
Option 4: Focus only on the gifted students as they are the ones who will bring "glory" to the school's reputation.

Question Text: What is the importance of "Environmental Studies" (EVS) in the primary years in India?
Option 1: To make students memorize the names of all the National Parks and Wildlife Sanctuaries in India.
Option 2: To develop an awareness and appreciation of the natural and social environment and the need for its protection.
Option 3: To prepare students for careers in civil engineering and urban development from a very young age.
Option 4: To teach students how to draw perfect maps of the world without using any reference or tracing paper.

Question Text: When using "Positive Reinforcement," which of the following is most effective?
Option 1: Giving a chocolate to every student who stays quiet for more than five minutes during the lesson.
Option 2: Providing specific praise like "I like how you used different colors to show the data in your chart."
Option 3: Telling the whole class that "You are all very good children" every morning during the assembly.
Option 4: Promising the students that there will be no homework for a month if they all pass the unit test.

Question Text: A student is very shy and never speaks in class. How can the teacher support their "Communication Skills"?
Option 1: Force the student to stand on the desk and give a 10-minute speech to "break" their shyness.
Option 2: Provide opportunities for the student to share in small groups or through written/visual means first.
Option 3: Ignore the student completely and only focus on the students who are loud and participate often.
Option 4: Tell the parents that the student is "socially awkward" and needs to be sent to a special school.

Question Text: Which of the following is a "Reflective Question" a teacher might ask themselves after a lesson?
Option 1: "Did I manage to finish the entire chapter and all the back-exercises within the 40-minute period?"
Option 2: "Which part of the lesson did the students find most engaging, and how can I tell they understood?"
Option 3: "How many students were talking while I was writing on the board, and who should I punish tomorrow?"
Option 4: "Will the Principal be happy with the amount of written work I have assigned to the students today?"

Question Text: In "Student Support," what is the role of the teacher regarding a child's "Emotional Intelligence"?
Option 1: To tell the students to keep their emotions at home and only focus on "logic" while they are at school.
Option 2: To help students identify, understand, and manage their own emotions and empathize with others.
Option 3: To grade students on a scale of 1 to 10 based on how "happy" they appear to be during the lunch break.
Option 4: To ensure that no student ever feels "sad" or "angry" by giving them whatever they want at all times.

Question Text: How can a teacher best use "Peer Feedback" in a Grade 5 writing assignment?
Option 1: Ask students to give their partners a grade from 1 to 10 based on how much they like their handwriting.
Option 2: Provide a simple checklist for students to use when looking at a peer's work to provide constructive comments.
Option 3: Tell the students to find and circle every single mistake in their partner's work using a bright red pen.
Option 4: Use peer feedback as a way to rank the students from "Best Writer" to "Worst Writer" in the classroom.

Question Text: What is the purpose of a "Lesson Plan" in primary education?
Option 1: To provide a rigid script that the teacher must follow exactly, even if the students are confused.
Option 2: To serve as a roadmap that ensures learning objectives are met while allowing for some flexibility.
Option 3: To show the school administration that the teacher is busy and has done some "paperwork" for the day.
Option 4: To give to the students so they can teach themselves while the teacher handles other responsibilities.

Question Text: A teacher wants to teach "Financial Literacy" to Grade 4 students. Which activity is best?
Option 1: Asking students to memorize the names of the Governors of the Reserve Bank of India since 1947.
Option 2: Setting up a "Classroom Store" where students use "play money" to buy and sell small items.
Option 3: Showing a 2-hour documentary on the history of the global stock market and its recent fluctuations.
Option 4: Giving a lecture on the complex mathematical formulas used to calculate compound interest rates.

Question Text: How should a teacher handle a "Conflict" between two students in the playground?
Option 1: Take both students to the Principal's office and demand that they both be suspended for three days.
Option 2: Listen to both sides, help them understand each other's feelings, and guide them toward a resolution.
Option 3: Tell the students that "fighting is natural" and let them figure it out on their own without any help.
Option 4: Pick the student you like more and tell the other student to apologize immediately or face a penalty.

Question Text: Which ICT application is best for "Collaborative Storytelling" in a primary classroom?
Option 1: A shared digital document where students take turns adding sentences or paragraphs to a story.
Option 2: A simple word processor where one student types while the others sit and watch in silence.
Option 3: A printer that the teacher uses to print out stories they have written for the students to read.
Option 4: A calculator that students use to count the number of words they have written in their notebooks.

Question Text: What is the significance of "Gender Sensitivity" in a primary school classroom?
Option 1: Ensuring that boys and girls sit in separate rows and never interact during any classroom activities.
Option 2: Challenging stereotypes and ensuring equal opportunities and respect for all students regardless of gender.
Option 3: Telling the girls that they are better at "Arts" and the boys that they are naturally better at "Math."
Option 4: Making sure all the classroom decorations are pink for girls and blue for the boys to feel "at home."

Question Text: How can a teacher promote "Active Listening" among students?
Option 1: By shouting "Listen to me!" every time the teacher wants to say something important to the class.
Option 2: By modeling active listening themselves when students speak and using engaging, varied teaching methods.
Option 3: By giving a 5-mark "Listening Test" every day where students have to repeat the teacher's exact words.
Option 4: By punishing any student who looks away from the teacher's face for more than ten seconds at a time.

Question Text: In "Professional Knowledge," what is "Pedagogical Content Knowledge" (PCK)?
Option 1: Knowing the subject matter so well that you don't need to know anything about how children learn.
Option 2: Knowing how to represent and formulate the subject in a way that makes it understandable to others.
Option 3: Memorizing the entire textbook of the subject you are teaching so you never have to look at it in class.
Option 4: The ability to write very difficult exam papers that ensure at least 50% of the students fail the test.

Question Text: A teacher wants to introduce "Coding" to Grade 3 students. What is the most appropriate starting point?
Option 1: Writing complex lines of Java or Python code on the chalkboard for students to copy into their books.
Option 2: Using "Unplugged" activities or block-based visual programming tools like Scratch Jr or similar.
Option 3: Giving a 10-page reading assignment on the history of computer science and the first microprocessors.
Option 4: Asking students to build a fully functional website for the school using HTML and CSS in one week.

Question Text: What is "Scaffolding" in the context of a "Zone of Proximal Development" (ZPD)?
Option 1: Tasks that are so easy that the student can do them without any help or even thinking about them.
Option 2: Support given to a student to perform a task they cannot yet do alone but can do with guidance.
Option 3: A task that is so difficult that even with the teacher's help, the student will never be able to finish it.
Option 4: A physical barrier placed between students to ensure they do not copy from each other during an exam.

Question Text: How should a teacher handle a "Highly Gifted" student who finishes all tasks ahead of others?
Option 1: Give them more of the same easy work to keep them "busy" and prevent them from talking to others.
Option 2: Provide enrichment activities that challenge their thinking and allow them to dive deeper into the topic.
Option 3: Tell the student to sit quietly and wait for the rest of the class, even if it takes another 30 minutes.
Option 4: Ask the student to go to the next grade's classroom and sit there for the remainder of the period.

Question Text: Which of the following is an example of "Community Engagement"?
Option 1: Inviting a local potter to the school to demonstrate their craft during a lesson on "Work We Do."
Option 2: Asking students to bring 50 rupees each to pay for the teacher's birthday celebration at a restaurant.
Option 3: Telling students to stay inside the school gates at all times and never interact with anyone from "outside."
Option 4: Sending a letter to the parents asking them to buy more expensive textbooks for the next academic year.

Question Text: In "Classroom Instruction," what is "Checks for Understanding" (CFUs)?
Option 1: A final exam at the end of the year that covers everything the students have learned in the last 10 months.
Option 2: Techniques used during a lesson to see if students are following along, like "Thumbs Up/Down."
Option 3: Asking the smartest student in the class if they understood and assuming everyone else did too.
Option 4: Looking at the students' faces to see if they look "happy" or "confused" and then moving on quickly.

Question Text: What is the ethical responsibility of a teacher regarding "Student Privacy" on social media?
Option 1: Posting photos of students' "funny mistakes" on their personal Instagram to get likes from their friends.
Option 2: Never posting images or personal information of students without explicit permission from school and parents.
Option 3: Tagging the students' parents in every single post about what is happening in the classroom daily.
Option 4: Creating a public Facebook group for the class where anyone can see the students' grades and names.

Question Text: How can "Teamwork" among teachers improve the "School Culture"?
Option 1: By sharing a common vision, supporting each other, and creating a positive, collaborative environment.
Option 2: By forming small "groups" or "cliques" that compete against each other for the Principal's favor.
Option 3: By ensuring that no teacher ever helps another teacher, so that everyone's "individual" work is clear.
Option 4: By complaining about the students together in the staff room to release the stress of teaching daily.

Question Text: A teacher is teaching "Directions" to Grade 3. Which activity is most effective?
Option 1: Making students memorize the definitions of "North, South, East, and West" from a dictionary.
Option 2: Using a compass or the position of the sun in the morning to find directions in the school playground.
Option 3: Giving students a map of the world and asking them to find the "North Pole" and "South Pole" on it.
Option 4: Writing the names of the four directions on the board and asking students to copy them ten times.

Question Text: What is "Differentiated Instruction" NOT?
Option 1: Tailoring the teaching to meet the individual needs, interests, and abilities of every single student.
Option 2: Providing three different levels of a worksheet so that every student can work at their own level.
Option 3: Giving the "slower" students much more work to do so that they can "catch up" with the "faster" ones.
Option 4: Changing the way a concept is taught based on whether a student is a visual, auditory, or kinesthetic learner.

Question Text: How should a teacher use "Assessment Data"?
Option 1: To rank students from 1 to 40 and post the list on the school notice board for everyone to see.
Option 2: To identify learning gaps and adjust their teaching strategies to better meet the students' needs.
Option 3: To decide which students should be allowed to go on the school trip and which ones should stay home.
Option 4: To prove to the parents that their child is "not smart enough" for the current grade they are in.

Question Text: Which of the following is a "Professionalism" trait?
Option 1: Arriving at school 15 minutes late every day because the teacher's "personal work" is more important.
Option 2: Being well-prepared, punctual, respectful to colleagues, and committed to student learning.
Option 3: Only teaching the students whose parents have given the teacher "extra gifts" during the festivals.
Option 4: Using the school's internet and printer for personal work during the time they are supposed to be teaching.

Question Text: A student is being raised by a single parent. How should the teacher handle "Family-themed" lessons?
Option 1: Only talk about "Traditional Families" (Mother, Father, Child) and ignore any other family structures.
Option 2: Use inclusive language that acknowledges that families can look different (grandparents, single parents).
Option 3: Ask the student to leave the room whenever "Mothers" or "Fathers" are being discussed in the class.
Option 4: Tell the student that their family is "not complete" and they should try to find another parent soon.

Question Text: What is "Metacognition" in a primary classroom?
Option 1: Thinking about one's own thinking and learning processes (e.g., "How did I solve this problem?").
Option 2: Memorizing a list of 500 scientific terms without knowing what any of those terms actually mean.
Option 3: Being able to recite a 10-page poem perfectly without making a single mistake or even stopping for breath.
Option 4: The ability to write with both the left and the right hand at the exact same speed and level of neatness.

Question Text: In "Curriculum Adaptation," what is "Universal Design for Learning" (UDL) primarily about?
Option 1: Ensuring that every student in the country is using the exact same textbook and taking the same exam.
Option 2: Providing multiple means of engagement, representation, and expression to reach all types of learners.
Option 3: Designing a classroom that has no walls or furniture so that students can move around freely all day.
Option 4: Only teaching the "core" subjects like Math and Science and skipping "Arts" and "Physical Education."

Question Text: How can a teacher foster a "Growth Mindset" in their students?
Option 1: By telling students that they are "born smart" and don't need to work hard to get good grades in school.
Option 2: By praising effort, persistence, and the process of learning rather than just the final correct answer.
Option 3: By comparing students to their peers who are doing better to make them feel "ashamed" of their effort.
Option 4: By giving students only the tasks that they can already do perfectly to avoid any "failure" or mistakes.

Question Text: A teacher is planning a lesson on "Healthy Food." Which approach is most "Inclusive"?
Option 1: Telling students that only expensive, "organic" food is healthy and anything else is "bad" for them.
Option 2: Discussing a variety of locally available, affordable, and nutritious foods from different cultures.
Option 3: Showing pictures of "international" foods that most students have never seen or heard of in their lives.
Option 4: Making a list of "Forbidden Foods" and telling students they will be punished if they ever eat them.

Question Text: What is the value of "Storytelling" in a primary classroom?
Option 1: It is a way to pass the time when the teacher hasn't prepared a lesson or is feeling a bit tired.
Option 2: It develops imagination, language skills, and helps children make sense of the world around them.
Option 3: It should only be used as a reward for the students who have finished all their "real" academic work.
Option 4: It is a "pre-primary" activity and has no place in a "serious" Grade 4 or Grade 5 classroom environment.

Question Text: How should a teacher handle "Digital Citizenship" for Grade 5 students?
Option 1: Telling students that the internet is a "dangerous place" and they should never, ever use a computer.
Option 2: Teaching students about online safety, respect, and how to identify credible sources of information.
Option 3: Giving students their own social media accounts and encouraging them to post their daily school life.
Option 4: Ignoring the topic because students are "too young" to understand anything about the digital world.

Question Text: What is "Collaborative Teaching"?
Option 1: Two teachers working together to plan, teach, and assess the same group of students effectively.
Option 2: One teacher teaching the class while the other teacher sits at the back and grades the notebooks.
Option 3: Two teachers competing to see whose class can get the highest average mark in the final examination.
Option 4: A teacher asking a student to teach the rest of the class while they take a 30-minute coffee break.

Question Text: A teacher wants to use "Role Play" to teach "Social Skills." Which scenario is most effective?
Option 1: Asking students to act out a scene where they have to resolve a disagreement about a shared toy.
Option 2: Having students memorize a 20-page script about the history of the Indian Parliament's formation.
Option 3: Telling students to stand in the front of the class and pretend to be a tree for ten minutes in silence.
Option 4: Asking students to mimic the teacher's behavior when they are angry with the class for being too loud.

Question Text: What is "Holistic Assessment"?
Option 1: Assessing only the academic marks of a student and ignoring their social, emotional, and physical growth.
Option 2: Evaluating a student's development across various domains, including academics, arts, and behavior.
Option 3: Giving a single "percentage" score at the end of the year that defines the student's entire personality.
Option 4: Asking the parents to write a "report card" for the teacher based on how much they like the teacher.

Question Text: How can a teacher ensure "Equity" in a classroom with students from different socio-economic backgrounds?
Option 1: By expecting every student to bring their own expensive tablet and high-speed internet connection.
Option 2: By providing equal access to resources and support tailored to each student's specific circumstances.
Option 3: By only focusing on the students from wealthy families as they are more likely to succeed in life.
Option 4: By treating every student exactly the same, even if some of them need extra help or more resources.

Question Text: Which of the following is a "Reflective Practice" tool?
Option 1: A teaching journal where the teacher writes down what went well and what could be improved in a lesson.
Option 2: A wooden stick that the teacher uses to point at things on the chalkboard during a science lesson.
Option 3: A loud whistle that the teacher uses to get the students' attention during the physical education class.
Option 4: A large red pen that the teacher uses to cross out every single mistake in the students' notebooks.

Question Text: What is the primary goal of "Classroom Management"?
Option 1: To ensure that students are so afraid of the teacher that they never dare to speak or even move.
Option 2: To create a structured environment where students can focus on learning and feel safe and respected.
Option 3: To make sure the teacher has to do as little "actual work" as possible during the 6-hour school day.
Option 4: To organize the students in a way that makes the classroom look "perfect" for the Principal's visit.

Question Text: A teacher is teaching "Environment" and wants to reduce waste. What is the most practical action?
Option 1: Telling students that they should never use any paper and should do all their work in their heads.
Option 2: Setting up a classroom "Recycling Corner" and encouraging students to use both sides of their paper.
Option 3: Asking students to bring 100 empty plastic bottles from home to build a large "plastic wall" in the class.
Option 4: Giving a 1-hour lecture on the "Chemistry of Plastic" and why it takes 500 years to decompose.

Question Text: How should a teacher handle "Student Feedback" about their own teaching?
Option 1: Punish any student who suggests that the teacher's lesson was "boring" or "too difficult to follow."
Option 2: Listen to the feedback, thank the students, and consider how to make the lessons more engaging.
Option 3: Ignore the feedback entirely because "students don't know anything about how to teach a class."
Option 4: Tell the students that if they don't like the teaching, they should go to a different school instead.

Question Text: What is "Inclusive Education"?
Option 1: A system where students with disabilities are taught in a separate building far away from others.
Option 2: An approach where all students, regardless of their challenges, learn together in the same classroom.
Option 3: A school where only the "smartest" and "richest" students are allowed to enroll and study together.
Option 4: A policy that says every student must wear the exact same uniform and have the exact same haircut.

Question Text: In the context of "Professional Ethics," what is "Confidentiality"?
Option 1: Keeping a student's personal and academic information private and only sharing it with relevant people.
Option 2: Telling the other teachers in the staff room all the "juicy secrets" about a student's family life.
Option 3: Writing a public blog post about a student's behavioral issues and naming the student and the school.
Option 4: Giving the class's contact list to a private coaching center in exchange for a "referral fee."

Question Text: How can a teacher use "Gamification" in a primary classroom?
Option 1: Making students play video games for five hours a day instead of learning Math, Science, or English.
Option 2: Using game-like elements like points, badges, or challenges to motivate and engage students in learning.
Option 3: Turning every single lesson into a "fight" where the winner gets a prize and the loser gets a penalty.
Option 4: Telling the students that their entire life is a "game" and only those who get 100% marks can "win."

Question Text: What is the "Spiral Curriculum"?
Option 1: A curriculum where students learn a topic once and then never see it or hear about it ever again.
Option 2: An approach where students revisit topics over time, with each visit increasing in depth and complexity.
Option 3: A curriculum designed in the shape of a spiral that students have to trace with their fingers daily.
Option 4: A system where students move from one classroom to another in a "spiral" pattern every 30 minutes.

Question Text: How should a teacher handle a student who is "Gifted" in Art but "Struggling" in Mathematics?
Option 1: Tell the student to stop doing Art until they can get at least 90% in every single Mathematics test.
Option 2: Recognize the student's talent in Art while providing extra, tailored support for their Math learning.
Option 3: Assume the student is "just an artist" and stop trying to teach them any Mathematics at all.
Option 4: Make the student stay back after school and do Math problems while the others are in the Art room.

Question Text: What is the importance of "Active Learning"?
Option 1: It is a way to make sure students are physically "active" (running, jumping) during every single lesson.
Option 2: It involves students in the learning process through activities, discussions, and hands-on experiences.
Option 3: It is a method where the teacher talks for 40 minutes and the students "actively" copy every word.
Option 4: It means that students are "active" on social media and posting about what they are learning in class.

Question Text: A teacher wants to teach "Empathy." Which activity is most suitable for Grade 4?
Option 1: Asking students to read a story and then discuss how the different characters might be feeling.
Option 2: Making students memorize the dictionary definition of the word "Empathy" and its synonyms.
Option 3: Telling students to "be nice to everyone" and then punishing anyone who is seen "not being nice."
Option 4: Showing a movie about a person who is very mean and then asking students to count their mistakes.

Question Text: What is the role of "Scaffolded Writing" for Grade 2 students?
Option 1: Providing a blank piece of paper and telling them to write a 10-page story about their last summer holiday.
Option 2: Providing sentence starters or a "word bank" to help students structure their own original sentences.
Option 3: Writing a story on the board and asking the students to copy it exactly as it is without any changes.
Option 4: Telling the students to "just write whatever comes to your mind" and not worrying about any grammar.

Question Text: How can a teacher use "Formative Assessment" to improve "Reading Skills"?
Option 1: By giving a single "Reading Exam" at the end of the year and failing any student who can't read fast.
Option 2: By listening to students read individually and providing immediate, constructive feedback on their errors.
Option 3: By asking students to read a book at home and then having their parents sign a "Reading Log" daily.
Option 4: By making the students who can't read well stand in the front of the class and read a difficult text.

Question Text: What is "Continuous and Comprehensive Evaluation" (CCE)?
Option 1: A system of assessment that covers all aspects of a student's development on a continuous basis.
Option 2: A test that happens every single day of the year and takes at least three hours to complete daily.
Option 3: A way to ensure that students are "continuously" under pressure to perform better than their peers.
Option 4: An evaluation that only looks at a student's "comprehensive" knowledge of the History of India.

Question Text: How should a teacher handle "Cyberbullying" if they become aware of it among their students?
Option 1: Ignore it because it is happening "outside of school hours" and "on the students' own time."
Option 2: Address the situation immediately, support the victim, and educate the class on digital respect.
Option 3: Tell the victim to "just delete their account" and then everything will go back to being "normal."
Option 4: Join in the "fun" so that the students feel like the teacher is "cool" and "understands them."

Question Text: Which of the following is a "Differentiated Instruction" strategy for a visual learner?
Option 1: Providing a long audio recording of a lecture for the student to listen to several times at home.
Option 2: Using diagrams, charts, and videos to explain a concept rather than just using spoken words.
Option 3: Asking the student to stand up and act out the concept in front of the whole class for ten minutes.
Option 4: Telling the student to close their eyes and "visualize" the concept while the teacher is talking.

Question Text: What is the benefit of "Reflective Journaling" for a primary school student?
Option 1: It helps them develop their handwriting and ensures they can write at least 500 words per day.
Option 2: It allows them to reflect on their learning, their feelings, and their own personal growth over time.
Option 3: It provides the teacher with "evidence" that can be used to punish the student for their thoughts.
Option 4: It is a way for students to practice their spelling of "difficult" and "academic" vocabulary words.

Question Text: As an "Industry Ready" primary teacher, what is your ultimate goal for your students?
Option 1: To ensure that 100% of the students get an "A" grade in every single subject in the final exam.
Option 2: To foster a love for learning, develop essential life skills, and prepare them for future challenges.
Option 3: To make sure the students can recite the entire textbook from memory without making any mistakes.
Option 4: To ensure that the students are so well-disciplined that they never ask any questions in the class.

Question Text: While planning a lesson on the Indian Freedom Struggle for Grade 8, you notice the textbook is very text-heavy. What is the most effective way to prepare for diverse learners?
Option 1: Stick strictly to the textbook to ensure all curriculum points are covered for the final board examinations.
Option 2: Create a multimedia presentation with maps, archival footage, and a timeline to supplement the text.
Option 3: Ask the students to read the chapter at home and come prepared to answer the back-of-chapter questions.
Option 4: Skip the complex parts of the chapter to ensure the syllabus is completed within the allotted time frame.

Question Text: A teacher is designing a curriculum for a new interdisciplinary unit on 'Sustainability'. Which approach best ensures students understand the real-world impact?
Option 1: Assigning a 20-page research paper where students list definitions of environmental terms from the dictionary.
Option 2: Conducting a lecture-only series where the teacher explains the theoretical concepts of global warming.
Option 3: Integrating a project where students audit the school’s waste management and propose actionable improvements.
Option 4: Organizing a one-time drawing competition where students paint trees without discussing the science behind it.

Question Text: During a classroom instruction session on 'Democracy', students start arguing about a recent local election. How should the teacher handle this?
Option 1: Immediately stop the discussion and punish the students for being disruptive and straying from the lesson.
Option 2: Facilitate a structured debate focusing on democratic principles like free speech and the electoral process.
Option 3: Take a side in the argument to show the students which political party provides the best governance.
Option 4: Ignore the argument and continue reading the textbook aloud until the class period ends.

Question Text: In a Grade 6 class, you have three students with dyslexia. How do you implement differentiated instruction during a literature assessment?
Option 1: Provide them with the same written test as everyone else but give them five extra minutes to finish.
Option 2: Excuse them from the assessment entirely so they do not feel pressured or stressed by the grades.
Option 3: Offer an alternative assessment format, such as an oral presentation or a visual story-map of the plot.
Option 4: Ask them to sit at the back of the class and copy the answers from a high-performing peer’s sheet.

Question Text: A student consistently disrupts the class by making jokes while you are explaining a complex mathematical theorem. What is the best classroom management strategy?
Option 1: Send the student to the principal's office immediately every time they speak without permission.
Option 2: Shout at the student in front of the whole class to assert your authority and stop the disruption.
Option 3: Have a private conversation to understand the behavior and set clear, consistent expectations for participation.
Option 4: Ignore the student completely and hope that the lack of attention will make them stop the behavior.

Question Text: You are evaluating a student's project on 'Ancient Civilizations'. What is the most constructive way to provide feedback for improvement?
Option 1: Write "Good job" at the top of the paper without any specific comments on the content or structure.
Option 2: Cross out the errors with a red pen and give a low grade without explaining what was wrong.
Option 3: Provide a rubric-based feedback sheet highlighting strengths and specific areas for further research.
Option 4: Compare their work to the best student in the class and tell them they need to be more like that peer.

Question Text: You notice a student who was previously high-performing has become withdrawn and is suddenly failing tests. What is your first step in student support?
Option 1: Inform the student that their grades are slipping and they will be detained if they don't improve.
Option 2: Reach out to the student privately to offer support and check if there are personal or health issues.
Option 3: Assume the student is being lazy and tell the parents that the student is not paying attention in class.
Option 4: Ignore the change in behavior as long as the student is not being disruptive during the lecture.

Question Text: A parent asks you to give their child extra marks in the internal assessment in exchange for a gift. What is the correct professional and ethical response?
Option 1: Accept the gift but do not change the marks, as this ensures the student is still graded fairly.
Option 2: Politely decline the gift and explain the school’s strict policy on grading integrity and ethics.
Option 3: Accept the gift and increase the marks slightly, as it helps build a good relationship with the parent.
Option 4: Report the parent to the police immediately without attempting to explain the professional boundary.

Question Text: During a parent-teacher meeting (PTM), a parent is angry about their child's low grades in Social Studies. How should you communicate?
Option 1: Argue back and tell the parent that their child is not studying enough at home and it's their fault.
Option 2: Listen empathetically to the parent’s concerns and share data-driven evidence and a plan for improvement.
Option 3: Tell the parent that you are too busy to talk and that they should schedule an appointment next month.
Option 4: Blame the school administration for the difficult curriculum and agree that the grading is unfair.

Question Text: You want to use ICT to teach 'Geography' to 9th graders. Which of the following is the most effective use of technology?
Option 1: Showing a 45-minute long movie every day so that you don't have to prepare for the lecture.
Option 2: Using Google Earth to virtually explore landforms and climates while students record their observations.
Option 3: Asking students to type out the definitions from the textbook into a Word document and printing them.
Option 4: Playing a loud pop song during the class to keep the students awake while they read the textbook.

Question Text: Reflective practice is essential for a teacher's growth. After a lesson goes poorly, what should a professional teacher do?
Option 1: Blame the students for being unintelligent and decide to teach the same way the next day.
Option 2: Write a reflection note analyzing what didn't work and how to modify the approach for the next class.
Option 3: Decide that the subject is too difficult for the students and skip the remaining part of the syllabus.
Option 4: Ask the department head to change the class section because these students are too difficult to handle.

Question Text: You are assigned to co-teach a History unit with a colleague who has a very different teaching style. What is the best way to collaborate?
Option 1: Insist that your style is superior and demand that the colleague follows your lesson plan exactly.
Option 2: Divide the class into two groups and teach them separately in different rooms to avoid conflict.
Option 3: Meet regularly to align objectives, share resources, and use each other's strengths to benefit the students.
Option 4: Complain to the Principal about the colleague's methods instead of speaking to them directly.

Question Text: How can a teacher effectively integrate extracurricular activities into a Civics lesson on 'Community Service'?
Option 1: Assign a chapter to read about NGOs and take a written test on the names of famous social workers.
Option 2: Organize a local community clean-up drive and have students write a reflection on their experience.
Option 3: Tell students to join a club after school and not mention community service during the regular class.
Option 4: Show a picture of a park and ask students to color it during the class time instead of studying.

Question Text: When adapting the curriculum for a student with a hearing impairment, which modification is most appropriate for a Humanities class?
Option 1: Speaking louder and slower while facing the blackboard so the student can hear the vibrations.
Option 2: Providing written transcripts of lectures and using visual aids like subtitles for any video content used.
Option 3: Excusing the student from all discussions and asking them to only read the textbook in the library.
Option 4: Moving the student to the very back of the classroom so they aren't distracted by the teacher's voice.

Question Text: You discover that a group of students is bullying a peer on a WhatsApp group. What is your responsibility as an educator?
Option 1: Ignore it because it is happening outside of school hours and on a private social media platform.
Option 2: Address the issue through a workshop on digital citizenship and follow the school’s anti-bullying policy.
Option 3: Delete the WhatsApp group yourself by taking the students' phones without informing the parents.
Option 4: Tell the victim to "toughen up" and learn how to handle social situations better on their own.

Question Text: You are planning a lesson on "Physical Features of India." How do you ensure the lesson is culturally responsive for students from different states?
Option 1: Use only the examples provided in the national NCERT textbook to maintain uniformity across the country.
Option 2: Incorporate local geographical landmarks and stories from the various regions represented by your students.
Option 3: Focus exclusively on the geography of the state where the school is located to make it relevant.
Option 4: Ask students from other states to explain their geography because you haven't prepared that section.

Question Text: While designing a 10th-grade curriculum for "Social Justice," you find the content might be sensitive for some families. How do you proceed?
Option 1: Remove the sensitive topics entirely to avoid any potential conflict with parents or the school board.
Option 2: Send an introductory note to parents explaining the learning objectives and the balanced approach you will take.
Option 3: Teach the content in a biased manner that supports only the most popular opinion in the local community.
Option 4: Tell the students to skip the chapter and read it on their own if they are interested in the topic.

Question Text: A student uses an AI tool to write an entire essay on "The Impact of the Industrial Revolution." How should you handle this?
Option 1: Give the student a zero and report them for permanent expulsion without explaining the reason why.
Option 2: Use it as a teaching moment to discuss academic integrity and the proper way to use AI as a research aid.
Option 3: Accept the essay as it is, as long as it looks professional and covers all the required historical points.
Option 4: Tell the whole class that AI is evil and ban all electronic devices from the school premises immediately.

Question Text: You notice that female students are rarely participating in your 9th-grade Political Science debates. What is the best instructional fix?
Option 1: Force every female student to speak for five minutes by calling their names in alphabetical order.
Option 2: Implement small-group discussions first to build confidence before moving to a whole-class debate format.
Option 3: Assume that the female students are naturally shy and let the male students dominate the conversation.
Option 4: Tell the male students to stop talking entirely so the female students are forced to fill the silence.

Question Text: In an inclusive classroom, a student with ADHD finds it difficult to sit through a 40-minute lecture. What is a proactive strategy?
Option 1: Make the student stand in the corner of the room so they don't distract others while they move around.
Option 2: Incorporate short "brain breaks" and kinesthetic activities that allow all students to move and refocus.
Option 3: Assign a staff member to sit next to the student and hold them down during the lecture period.
Option 4: Tell the parents that the student cannot attend regular classes until they are "calm enough" to sit still.

Question Text: A parent complains that you are "wasting time" with group activities and should focus on "rote learning" for the board exams.
Option 1: Agree with the parent and switch back to traditional lecturing to ensure everyone is satisfied.
Option 2: Explain the pedagogical benefits of active learning in developing critical thinking and long-term retention.
Option 3: Ignore the parent's email and continue with your plans without offering any explanation or context.
Option 4: Complain to the student about their parent’s attitude during the next classroom session.

Question Text: You find a colleague is leaking question paper details to their private tuition students. What is your ethical obligation?
Option 1: Ignore the situation because it is not your business and you want to maintain a good relationship with your peer.
Option 2: Report the matter to the school authorities or the ethics committee as it compromises academic integrity.
Option 3: Ask the colleague to share the leaked questions with your students as well to be fair to everyone.
Option 4: Hint to your students that they should join that colleague's private tuitions to get better marks.

Question Text: During a "Mock Parliament" session, a student makes a derogatory remark about a specific community. How do you react?
Option 1: Laugh it off as a joke and tell the class that "politics is a dirty game" to keep the mood light.
Option 2: Pause the session to address why the remark is harmful and reinforce the importance of respectful discourse.
Option 3: Immediately expel the student from the class and refuse to let them participate in any future activities.
Option 4: Ignore the remark and continue the session as if nothing happened to avoid making the student feel bad.

Question Text: You want to assess students' understanding of "The Mughal Empire" beyond a written test. Which assessment is most valid?
Option 1: A multiple-choice quiz that asks for the exact dates of every single minor battle fought in the era.
Option 2: A role-play activity where students simulate a court session and debate administrative policies of the time.
Option 3: Asking students to draw a map of the empire and color it without labeling any of the major cities.
Option 4: Having students copy the entire summary of the chapter from the back of the book five times.

Question Text: A student is being raised by a single parent and is often late because they have to help with a younger sibling.
Option 1: Punish the student with extra homework every time they are late to teach them the value of punctuality.
Option 2: Meet with the student and parent to find a flexible solution that supports the student’s education and home reality.
Option 3: Inform the student that their personal problems are not an excuse for missing the first ten minutes of class.
Option 4: Tell the student to drop out of school and join an open school system if they cannot be on time.

Question Text: Which of the following is an example of "Assessment AS Learning" in a Humanities classroom?
Option 1: The teacher giving a surprise test at the end of the week to see who was paying attention in class.
Option 2: Students using a checklist to self-evaluate their own essays before submitting the final draft to the teacher.
Option 3: The final term-end examination that determines whether a student is promoted to the next grade.
Option 4: A parent checking the student's homework and correcting all the mistakes before the student goes to school.

Question Text: You are using a digital simulation to teach "Urban Planning." Some students have no internet at home. How do you ensure equity?
Option 1: Only assign the simulation as homework for the rich students and give the others a textbook reading.
Option 2: Provide dedicated time in the school’s computer lab for all students to complete the simulation activity.
Option 3: Cancel the activity for everyone so that the students without internet do not feel left out or inferior.
Option 4: Tell the students without internet that it is their responsibility to find a cyber cafe to do their work.

Question Text: How does a "Reflective Journal" help a teacher who is struggling with classroom discipline in a Grade 9 class?
Option 1: It allows the teacher to vent their frustrations and write down the names of the students they dislike most.
Option 2: It helps the teacher track patterns in student behavior and analyze which of their own triggers or actions affect the class.
Option 3: It serves as a legal document that can be used to prove to the principal that the students are "unteachable."
Option 4: It is a waste of time that takes away from the time the teacher could spend grading papers or planning.

Question Text: You are asked to lead a "Value Education" workshop for the whole school. What is the most effective way to engage 10th graders?
Option 1: Reading out a list of 50 rules that the students must follow if they want to be considered "good citizens."
Option 2: Using real-life case studies and dilemmas that allow students to debate and arrive at ethical conclusions.
Option 3: Showing a two-hour long documentary without any discussion or follow-up activity afterward.
Option 4: Bringing in a guest speaker who shouts at the students about the importance of discipline and tradition.

Question Text: Collaborative teaching involves two teachers in the same room. What is a common pitfall to avoid?
Option 1: One teacher acting as the "lead" while the other is treated like an "assistant" who only handles behavior.
Option 2: Both teachers planning together and taking turns to lead different sections of the same lesson.
Option 3: Using a "station teaching" model where students rotate between the two teachers for different tasks.
Option 4: Communicating openly about student progress and sharing the grading workload equally between both.

Question Text: How should a teacher integrate "Art-Integrated Learning" (AIL) into a History lesson on the "Bhakti Movement"?
Option 1: Asking students to memorize the birth dates of all the saints and poets mentioned in the chapter.
Option 2: Having students compose a poem or create a painting that reflects the philosophy of a specific Bhakti saint.
Option 3: Telling students to look at the pictures in the book for five minutes while the teacher checks their attendance.
Option 4: Asking the Art teacher to teach the History lesson instead so the History teacher can take a break.

Question Text: A student with a physical disability cannot participate in the "Field Trip" to a mountain fort. What should you do?
Option 1: Leave the student at school with a librarian and tell them it's "too dangerous" for them to come along.
Option 2: Select an alternative site that is accessible or ensure the logistics are in place to include the student fully.
Option 3: Cancel the trip for the entire class so that you don't have to deal with the logistical difficulty of one student.
Option 4: Tell the parents that they must accompany the student and carry them up the mountain themselves.

Question Text: What is the best way to handle "Curriculum Overload" when you are running behind the school’s academic calendar?
Option 1: Speed-read through the remaining chapters and tell the students to mark the important lines for the exam.
Option 2: Identify "Power Standards" or core concepts that are essential and focus on teaching those deeply.
Option 3: Skip the last three chapters entirely and tell the students they are "not important" for the final boards.
Option 4: Ask the students to come to school on Sundays for four hours to finish the syllabus in a hurry.

Question Text: In the context of "Continuous Professional Development" (CPD), which activity is most beneficial for a 21st-century teacher?
Option 1: Attending a one-day lecture where they sit and listen to an expert talk about old teaching methods.
Option 2: Participating in a Professional Learning Community (PLC) where they peer-observe and share modern strategies.
Option 3: Buying a book on "How to be a Great Teacher" and keeping it on their shelf without ever reading it.
Option 4: Doing the same thing every year for twenty years and assuming that "experience" is the only thing that matters.

Question Text: You find that your "Standardized Test" results show that 70% of the class failed a specific section on "Economics."
Option 1: Blame the students for not studying that section and move on to the next topic to stay on schedule.
Option 2: Re-teach the concept using a different instructional strategy and then provide a re-assessment.
Option 3: Assume the test was too hard and just add 10 "grace marks" to everyone’s score to fix the average.
Option 4: Tell the students that they are clearly not suited for the Humanities stream and should switch to Arts.

Question Text: A student expresses a radical political view during a class on "Nationalism" that makes other students feel unsafe. How do you intervene?
Option 1: Shaming the student publicly to ensure they never express such an opinion in your classroom again.
Option 2: Reminding the class of the ground rules for respectful dialogue and asking the student to provide evidence-based arguments.
Option 3: Reporting the student to the local police immediately as a threat to national security and safety.
Option 4: Ignoring the comment entirely and quickly changing the subject to something less controversial like the weather.

Question Text: You are using "Flipped Classroom" for a lesson on "The Constitution of India." What should the students do before coming to class?
Option 1: Watch a pre-recorded lecture or read the primary text of the Preamble to gain foundational knowledge.
Option 2: Sit in the classroom and wait for the teacher to arrive and explain everything from the very beginning.
Option 3: Take a high-stakes final examination to prove they already know everything about the Indian Constitution.
Option 4: Do nothing at all, as the "Flipped" model means the teacher does all the work while students relax at home.

Question Text: You notice a "clique" in your 8th-grade class is systematically excluding a student from a marginalized background during group projects.
Option 1: Tell the excluded student to "make more effort" to be likable so that the other students will include them.
Option 2: Explicitly design heterogeneous groups and use cooperative learning roles to ensure every student is valued.
Option 3: Let the students choose their own groups every time, as forcing them to work together creates unnecessary friction.
Option 4: Move the excluded student to a different section of the school so they don't have to deal with the clique anymore.

Question Text: When designing a rubric for an "Oral History" project, which criterion is most important for a Humanities student?
Option 1: The quality of the expensive recording equipment the student used to interview their grandparents.
Option 2: The student’s ability to analyze the interview data and connect it to broader historical themes and contexts.
Option 3: The physical appearance and dressing style of the student during the final presentation of the project.
Option 4: Whether the student managed to interview a famous person or just a regular member of their own family.

Question Text: A student tells you in confidence that they are feeling extreme pressure from their parents to score 95% in the 10th-grade boards.
Option 1: Agree with the parents and tell the student that anything less than 95% is a failure in the current job market.
Option 2: Listen to the student, offer stress-management tips, and suggest a joint meeting with the counselor and parents.
Option 3: Tell the student to ignore their parents and stop studying entirely to prove a point about mental health.
Option 4: Inform the whole class about the student's personal conversation to show why "over-studying" is a bad idea.

Question Text: In a "History of Art" lesson, you want to use the "VTS" (Visual Thinking Strategies) method. What is the first question you should ask?
Option 1: "Who is the artist who painted this and in what year was it painted according to the textbook?"
Option 2: "What is going on in this picture?" followed by "What do you see that makes you say that?"
Option 3: "How much do you think this painting would sell for in a modern auction house in London?"
Option 4: "Which of you can draw better than this artist, and why do you think your style is more modern?"

Question Text: You are a middle school teacher. You realize that the textbook's version of a historical event is biased. What is the most "industry-ready" action?
Option 1: Teach the textbook version only, because that is what will be asked in the board examinations.
Option 2: Present multiple perspectives on the event and encourage students to analyze the sources and biases involved.
Option 3: Tell the students to tear the page out of the book and write their own version based on Wikipedia.
Option 4: Complain to the Education Minister on social media instead of addressing the bias within the classroom.

Question Text: During a "Peer Feedback" session, a student is being overly harsh and insulting to their classmate's essay on "Climate Change."
Option 1: Cancel all future peer feedback sessions because students are clearly not mature enough for this task.
Option 2: Model how to give "Constructive Feedback" using the "Warm and Cool" feedback method (Praise and Suggestions).
Option 3: Tell the student who was insulted to hit back with a similar insult to even the playing field.
Option 4: Give the harsh student a "10/10" for honesty and tell the other student to stop being so sensitive about their work.

Question Text: You are integrating "Game-Based Learning" (GBL) in Geography. What is the main goal of using a game like "Civilization" or "SimCity"?
Option 1: To keep the students entertained so the teacher can finish their administrative paperwork in peace.
Option 2: To allow students to experience complex systems, resource management, and the consequences of geographical decisions.
Option 3: To see which student is the fastest at clicking buttons and has the best gaming reflexes in the class.
Option 4: To replace the teacher entirely with a computer program so the school can save money on salaries.

Question Text: A student with a visual impairment joins your 7th-grade Social Science class. How do you adapt your "Map Work" lesson?
Option 1: Exempt the student from the lesson and ask them to sit quietly while others work on their maps.
Option 2: Use tactile maps with raised lines and textures so the student can "feel" the boundaries and features.
Option 3: Describe the map out loud for 40 minutes without giving the student any physical materials to interact with.
Option 4: Ask the student's neighbor to draw the map for them and give both students the same grade.

Question Text: What is the hallmark of a "Learner-Centered" classroom management style in a secondary school?
Option 1: The teacher sits on a high chair and uses a microphone to ensure their voice is the only one heard.
Option 2: The teacher and students collaboratively develop a "Classroom Constitution" with shared rights and responsibilities.
Option 3: The teacher uses a system of "Negative Reinforcement" where the slowest student is punished every day.
Option 4: The teacher allows students to do whatever they want, including leaving the room without permission at any time.

Question Text: You are planning a "Field Visit" to a local museum. What is the most important "Pre-Visit" activity?
Option 1: Collecting the money for the bus and making sure every student has a matching uniform for the trip.
Option 2: Setting clear learning objectives and providing a "Scavenger Hunt" or inquiry sheet to guide their observation.
Option 3: Telling the students that the trip is a holiday and they don't need to bring any notebooks or pens.
Option 4: Ensuring the museum has a high-quality cafeteria so the students can eat a large lunch during the visit.

Question Text: A student is caught "Cyberbullying" a teacher on a public forum. As a member of the "Discipline Committee," what is your stance?
Option 1: Demand the student be banned from using the internet for life and be removed from the school immediately.
Option 2: Follow a "Restorative Justice" approach that focuses on understanding the harm, apology, and behavioral change.
Option 3: Ignore the post and hope that if no one talks about it, the post will eventually be deleted by the platform.
Option 4: Create a fake account to bully the student back so they understand how it feels to be targeted online.

Question Text: When evaluating "Professionalism," how should a teacher handle a mistake they made during a lecture on "Economic Policies"?
Option 1: Never admit the mistake, as it will make the students lose respect for the teacher’s authority and knowledge.
Option 2: Acknowledge the error in the next class, provide the correct information, and thank the student who spotted it.
Option 3: Blame the textbook or the internet for providing wrong information and refuse to take any personal responsibility.
Option 4: Punish the student who pointed out the mistake for being "disrespectful" and "interrupting the flow" of the lesson.

Question Text: Which of the following best describes "Differentiated Assessment" in a 9th-grade English Literature class?
Option 1: Giving the same essay prompt to every student but grading the struggling students more leniently.
Option 2: Offering a choice between writing an essay, creating a comic strip, or performing a monologue of a scene.
Option 3: Making the boys write about war and the girls write about romance to suit their "natural interests."
Option 4: Only assessing the top 10% of the class and giving the rest a "pass" grade to save time on marking.

Question Text: A student consistently misses school on Fridays for religious reasons. How do you ensure they don't fall behind in "Social Studies"?
Option 1: Tell the student that school is more important than religion and they must attend or they will fail the year.
Option 2: Upload lesson notes and assignments to the school's LMS so the student can access them asynchronously.
Option 3: Ask the other students to stop talking to the student so they realize that missing school has social costs.
Option 4: Ignore the student’s absence and refuse to provide any extra help, as it was their choice to stay at home.

Question Text: In "Collaborative Teaching," what is "Parallel Teaching"?
Option 1: One teacher teaches the lesson while the other teacher stands at the back and checks their email.
Option 2: The class is split into two groups, and each teacher teaches the same content to one group simultaneously.
Option 3: One teacher teaches History in Room 1, while the other teacher teaches Geography in Room 2 at different times.
Option 4: Both teachers speak at the exact same time to the whole class to see who the students listen to more.

Question Text: You want to teach "Media Literacy." What is the most effective classroom activity for 10th graders?
Option 1: Having students memorize the names of the top five news anchors in India and their respective channels.
Option 2: Analyzing two different news reports on the same event to identify bias, loaded language, and omitted facts.
Option 3: Watching a movie and writing a summary of the plot without discussing the director's intent or techniques.
Option 4: Banning all newspapers and news apps from the classroom to protect students from "fake news."

Question Text: What is the primary purpose of a "Teacher Portfolio" in the context of "Professional Development"?
Option 1: To keep a collection of all the "Thank You" cards and gifts received from students over the years.
Option 2: To document evidence of teaching practice, student growth, and reflections for career advancement and growth.
Option 3: To show other teachers that you are better than them by highlighting only your most expensive certificates.
Option 4: To have a place to store all the administrative forms and leave applications required by the school office.

Question Text: A "Inclusive Teaching" strategy for a student with "Social Anxiety" during a presentation might be:
Option 1: Forcing them to stand on the stage in front of 500 people to "cure" their fear of public speaking through shock.
Option 2: Allowing them to record their presentation at home or present it to a small group of trusted peers instead.
Option 3: Telling the student that they will receive a zero if they do not speak loudly and clearly in front of the class.
Option 4: Asking the class to laugh whenever the student stutters to encourage them to practice more at home.

Question Text: You are designing a lesson on "Gender Roles" for 8th graders. How do you ensure the curriculum doesn't reinforce stereotypes?
Option 1: Use examples where only men are shown as breadwinners and women as homemakers to reflect traditional society.
Option 2: Use diverse case studies showing individuals in non-traditional roles and discuss the evolution of gender equity.
Option 3: Avoid the topic entirely because it might be uncomfortable for students who come from conservative backgrounds.
Option 4: Show a Bollywood movie where gender roles are highly stereotyped and tell students to emulate the characters.

Question Text: A teacher wants to use "Inquiry-Based Learning" for a unit on 'Local Government'. What is the most appropriate starting point?
Option 1: Handing out a list of 50 facts about the Municipal Corporation for students to memorize for a surprise test.
Option 2: Posing a real-world problem, such as "Why is there a water shortage in our colony?" and having students investigate.
Option 3: Reading the chapter on 'Panchayati Raj' aloud and asking students to underline every difficult word they find.
Option 4: Telling students to stay at home and watch the news until they understand how the local government functions.

Question Text: You observe that a few students are "Gifted Learners" who finish their Humanities assignments much faster than others.
Option 1: Give them extra sets of repetitive worksheets to keep them busy while the rest of the class finishes the main task.
Option 2: Provide "Extension Activities" that require higher-order thinking, such as analyzing the long-term impact of a policy.
Option 3: Tell them to sit quietly and do nothing so they do not disturb the students who are still struggling with the work.
Option 4: Ask them to go to the next classroom and help the teacher there with administrative tasks like filing papers.

Question Text: During a classroom discussion on "Religious Diversity," a student makes a comment that is factually incorrect about a faith.
Option 1: Shout at the student for being ignorant and demand that they leave the room immediately for their insensitivity.
Option 2: Calmly provide corrected information using objective sources and explain the importance of factual accuracy in dialogue.
Option 3: Ignore the incorrect statement because correcting it might hurt the student's feelings or damage their self-esteem.
Option 4: Ask the other students to vote on whether they think the statement was true or false to decide the correct answer.

Question Text: What is the most effective way to use "Formative Assessment" data during a unit on "Indian Geography"?
Option 1: Using the quiz results to rank students from 'Best' to 'Worst' and posting the list on the school notice board.
Option 2: Adjusting the next day's lesson plan to re-teach the specific concepts that the majority of the class found difficult.
Option 3: Filing the results away in a folder and never looking at them again until the final report cards are being prepared.
Option 4: Giving a lecture to the parents about why their children are failing to understand basic geographical coordinates.

Question Text: A student who is a "Kinesthetic Learner" struggles with long lectures on "Ancient History." How can you adapt?
Option 1: Force the student to sit in the front row and keep their hands on the desk at all times during the 40-minute talk.
Option 2: Incorporate a "History Walk" or a role-play activity where students physically act out the daily life of a civilization.
Option 3: Tell the student that History is a "reading subject" and if they can't sit still, they should choose physical education.
Option 4: Assign the student the task of cleaning the blackboard every 5 minutes to keep them moving during your lecture.

Question Text: In a "Community Engagement" project, students are asked to interview local artisans. What is the primary ethical concern?
Option 1: Making sure the students get the highest quality photographs for their social media accounts and school website.
Option 2: Ensuring students treat the artisans with respect, obtain informed consent, and represent their stories accurately.
Option 3: Making sure the artisans give free samples of their work to the students as a reward for being interviewed.
Option 4: Ensuring the students finish the interview as quickly as possible so they don't miss their next math coaching class.

Question Text: You are a new teacher and find the "Staff Room" culture is highly cynical and resistant to new ICT tools.
Option 1: Join in the cynicism so that you can fit in with your colleagues and avoid being treated like an outsider.
Option 2: Continue using the tools effectively in your class and share the positive student outcomes during staff meetings.
Option 3: Report every single cynical colleague to the Principal daily until they are all fired for having a bad attitude.
Option 4: Stop using ICT tools altogether and go back to traditional methods to maintain peace in the staff room.

Question Text: When teaching "Civics," how do you explain the concept of "Equity" vs. "Equality" effectively to 7th graders?
Option 1: Tell them both words mean exactly the same thing and they can use them interchangeably in their exam papers.
Option 2: Use an illustration showing people of different heights trying to see over a fence with different levels of support.
Option 3: Give a complex 2-hour lecture using only legal jargon from the Supreme Court archives without any visual aids.
Option 4: Ask students to look up both words in a dictionary and write the definitions ten times in their notebooks.

Question Text: A student's parent is a high-ranking official who demands that you change their child's seating to the front row.
Option 1: Immediately move the student to the front row to avoid any professional trouble or conflict with the official.
Option 2: Explain the classroom's logical seating arrangement policy and how it supports all students' learning needs.
Option 3: Move the student to the very back of the room to prove that you are not intimidated by the parent's high status.
Option 4: Ask the parent for a bribe in exchange for moving the student to the most "premium" seat in the classroom.

Question Text: Which of the following is an example of "Interdisciplinary Teaching" involving the Humanities department?
Option 1: The History teacher and Math teacher both giving the same amount of homework on the same Tuesday evening.
Option 2: The English and History teachers collaborating on a unit about "Partition Literature" and its historical context.
Option 3: The Geography teacher taking a sick leave and the Physics teacher sitting in the class to maintain silence.
Option 4: The school organizing a sports day where students run races but do not discuss any academic subjects at all.

Question Text: You are using a "Scaffolding" technique to help students write a thesis statement. What does this look like?
Option 1: Writing the thesis statement for the student and telling them to copy it exactly into their final essay.
Option 2: Providing a "Sentence Starter" or a template that guides the student through the logical structure of the claim.
Option 3: Giving the student a blank piece of paper and telling them to "be creative" without providing any prior instructions.
Option 4: Telling the student to go to the library and not come back until they have written a perfect opening paragraph.

Question Text: A student consistently uses "Slang" and informal language in formal History essays. How do you provide feedback?
Option 1: Red-mark every informal word and give the student a failing grade for being "unprofessional" and "lazy."
Option 2: Explain the difference between "Formal" and "Informal" registers and provide examples of academic vocabulary.
Option 3: Start using slang yourself in your lectures to make the student feel more comfortable and "seen" in class.
Option 4: Ignore the language as long as the historical facts are correct, as language doesn't matter in a Humanities paper.

Question Text: What is the benefit of "Peer Observation" as part of a teacher’s "Continuous Professional Development"?
Option 1: It allows teachers to spy on each other and report minor mistakes to the management to get higher raises.
Option 2: It provides an opportunity to see different teaching styles and receive constructive, non-evaluative feedback.
Option 3: It is a way for the senior teachers to assert their dominance over the junior teachers in the department.
Option 4: It is a waste of time that should be spent on correcting notebooks and preparing for the next day's lesson.

Question Text: You want to foster "Metacognition" in your 10th-grade students after a unit on "The World Wars."
Option 1: Ask them to memorize the names of 20 different generals and the dates they were appointed to their positions.
Option 2: Ask them to write a "Reflection Note" on which study strategies helped them understand the complex causes of the war.
Option 3: Give them a long list of multiple-choice questions that only require them to recall basic facts from the book.
Option 4: Tell them that they should not think too much and just focus on what is written in the textbook for the exam.

Question Text: A student is being raised in a multilingual household. How can you use this as an asset in a "Language & Culture" lesson?
Option 1: Tell the student to forget their mother tongue and only speak English so they can "improve" their social status.
Option 2: Invite the student to share how certain concepts or idioms are expressed in their home language vs. English.
Option 3: Ignore the student's background and treat them exactly like a monolingual student to ensure "fairness."
Option 4: Ask the student to translate the entire textbook into their mother tongue as a special homework assignment.

Question Text: How should a teacher handle "Controversial Issues" (e.g., Caste, Religion) in an Indian Humanities classroom?
Option 1: Avoid them entirely to prevent any possible communal tension or complaints from the school management.
Option 2: Create a safe space for evidence-based discussion, emphasizing constitutional values and multiple perspectives.
Option 3: Use the opportunity to preach your own personal political and religious beliefs to the "impressionable" students.
Option 4: Let the students shout at each other until the loudest one wins, as that reflects "real-world" politics.

Question Text: Which of the following is a key feature of "Inclusive Education" for a student with "Low Vision"?
Option 1: Making the student sit in a dark corner of the room so the glare from the window doesn't bother their eyes.
Option 2: Providing "Large Print" materials, high-contrast visuals, and allowing the use of a magnifying device in class.
Option 3: Excusing the student from all reading tasks and asking them to just listen to the audiobooks during the class.
Option 4: Telling the other students to read the textbook aloud to the student with low vision during their lunch break.

Question Text: You are a "Class Teacher." You notice a student's lunch box is often empty and they look malnourished.
Option 1: Publicly ask the student why they are not bringing food so that other students might offer to share theirs.
Option 2: Discreetly inform the school counselor or principal to provide support through the school’s welfare program.
Option 3: Tell the student that they cannot focus on their studies if they don't eat and they should "be more responsible."
Option 4: Ignore the situation because as a Humanities teacher, your only job is to teach the curriculum, not look at lunch.

Question Text: In "Lesson Planning," what is the purpose of an "Anticipatory Set" (Hook)?
Option 1: To take attendance and make sure every student is wearing their tie and belt correctly before the lesson starts.
Option 2: To grab the students' attention and activate their prior knowledge at the very beginning of the class session.
Option 3: To give the students a long list of vocabulary words they need to copy into their notebooks before you speak.
Option 4: To punish the students who were late to the class by making them stand up for the first five minutes.

Question Text: You are planning a "Co-curricular" integration for a History unit on 'The Silk Route'. Which activity best reinforces the curriculum?
Option 1: Asking students to run 100 meters in the playground to show how long the traders had to travel on foot.
Option 2: Organizing a "Trade Fair" where students exchange goods, currencies, and ideas representing different regions.
Option 3: Having students sit in silence for the whole period to imagine how lonely the ancient traders must have felt.
Option 4: Telling the students to draw a silk worm in their biology notebooks and labeling its body parts in detail.

Question Text: A student with a "Specific Learning Disability" (SLD) struggles with handwriting but is very expressive orally.
Option 1: Force the student to write every assignment by hand to ensure they practice and eventually "overcome" the disability.
Option 2: Allow the use of "Speech-to-Text" software or a scribe for high-stakes assessments to reflect their true knowledge.
Option 3: Reduce the student's marks for "poor presentation" to motivate them to work harder on their penmanship.
Option 4: Tell the student that they should not have chosen Humanities if they cannot write long, handwritten essays.

Question Text: What is the most professional way to handle a disagreement with a senior colleague regarding a teaching methodology?
Option 1: Complain about the senior colleague to the students during class to gain their sympathy and support.
Option 2: Schedule a private meeting to discuss your perspectives respectfully, citing evidence-based pedagogical reasons.
